title: MotifJS Documentation
text: MotifJS is a UI framework for JavaScript and TypeScript, built for modern web applications, that brings speed, reactivity and a clear architecture together under one roof. Views are written in JSX, and the compiler turns them into component calls at build time. The same calls can also be written directly, without JSX, in TypeScript or JavaScript. Every tag in JSX becomes a component object that carries its own DOM element, and these objects live in the controls tree. A value bound to a getter updates only that property of the element it is bound to; the component is not rebuilt.

title: MotifJS Documentation
heading: What does MotifJS do differently?
text: In MotifJS the interface is a tree of component objects that live for as long as the application stays open. The view is built once, and from then on these objects carry it: bindings update values, the tree changes by hand or through bindings, and lifetimes are managed explicitly. Every tag is a component object. A <div> , a <button> , even a piece of plain text turns into a motifComponent call in the compiler. The resulting object has its own element , a controls collection that holds its children, and the bindings , class and attr members, plus motif , which handles events and visibility. The built element is not thrown away as a copy; it stays in hand for the life of the application, and you can find and change it in the tree through parent , siblings and $() . view() runs once. It is called while the component is being built, and bindings carry every change after that. On a component that is already built, controls.add(<div/>) builds the child right away and puts its element in place; on a component that is not built yet, the child is built together with its owner. The tree is edited at run time. controls.add , insert , move , moveToIndex and remove change the component tree directly. A component passed to another component's controls.add leaves its old place and moves to the new one, taking its state, bindings and events with it. remove disposes the component. detach , on the other hand, plays the leave transition if there is one and only takes the component out of the tree and the DOM; a detached component can be added again later. Access to the real element. Every component's element is created in the constructor, so you can reach it before the component is built and before it is added to the page. In a component without an element of its own (a fragment), element is a comment node. Fine-grained reactivity. When a state field changes, only the DOM node or attribute bound to that field is updated, not the whole component. Waiting and hidden components keep their place. x-wait does not build the component at all until its condition holds. x-display is the reverse of the same waiting: if it starts out false the component is not built, and if it turns false after the component is built, the component is hidden. In both cases the component leaves a comment marker in the DOM unless hideStrategy: "detach" is given, and it comes back to the same spot when shown. Lifetimes are managed explicitly. A disposed component shuts down its children, bindings and events, and resources tied to it with motif.register or motif.setDisposable are closed along with it. An application subscription opened through the component's context.on is removed on its own when the component is disposed. Service lifetimes follow route changes. When the router is in use, every route change opens its own service scope, and the components built during that change are tied to it. A service registered as scoped is created once per scope. When the new change completes, the previous change's scope closes together with its services, unless a kept page is still holding it. A page is not rebuilt every time you return to it. The component of a route given keepAlive: true is kept after its first build, and the same instance is shown when you come back. With stack navigation turned on ( app.useRouter({ …, stack: true }) ), pages left behind are kept for up to five steps by default; going back brings the same instances with their scroll positions. A slide transition ( animation: "slide" ) and swiping back from the edge ( swipeBack ) are options. Built-in infrastructure. Routing, dependency injection, lifecycle, animation and memory management come with the core. Frame , Lazy , Transport / TransportTo , ContentBody / ContentBlock , Virtualization , Resilience , Query and the List , Dictionary and LinkedList collections are part of the core as well. JavaScript or TypeScript, with or without JSX. Components are classes, functions or Options API objects, and the view is built with JSX or with the hand-written (imperative) form of the same calls. All three styles produce the same kind of component, and they sit side by side in the same tree. MotifJS is designed for long-lived, state-heavy interfaces. No planning has been done yet for server-side rendering (SSR); it may be considered in the future.

title: MotifJS Documentation
heading: Quick look
text: A notes list: NotesService keeps the notes in one place, and NotesPane shows the search box, the rows and an editor for the selected note. SettingsService holds the theme and density settings and is created when the application starts. The same component is written in six forms: class, function and Options API, each with JSX and without it. A few things worth noticing in the example: Each note is a single reactive object. When the title changes in the editor, the text in the row updates, and when pinning changes, so does the icon in the row; the list is not rebuilt. NotesService.create adds to the front of the list, and the rows follow that on their own. Bindings are fine-grained. x-model / bindings.model is a two-way binding, {() => …} / bindings.text is live text, x-display / bindings.display is visibility, and .map + key / bindings.list + indexkey is a list of rows. Rows are matched to the item object itself; key does not change that matching, and if the same key is used twice, development mode prints an MJX202 warning. In JSX, the compiler turns a field read such as {note.title} into a binding by itself; when writing without JSX, a value that has to stay live is passed as a getter, while setText("…") and plain values are written once. Services are registered while the application is being built. builder.services.addSingleton(NotesService, { useClass: NotesService }) registers the service before build() . A singleton given startup: true is created at the start of app.run() , before the root component is built, without waiting for a component to ask for it; on a service that is not a singleton this option is ignored and an MJX415 warning is printed. The other way to register is to mark the class with @Injectable({ lifetime: "singleton" }) . That mark enters the registry when the class's module is loaded: build() registers only the marked classes loaded up to that point, so a service whose module has not been loaded yet is not in the registry until the module loads and it is asked for the first time, and it is not created at startup even with startup: true . On a class that was registered in the builder, the mark is ignored. In the example the class component gets the service with this.getService , and the function and Options components with FromService ; the Options component can use this.getService too. The imperative form is the same core calls written by hand. motifComponent(tag, setup) creates a component, and the setup function runs once as initializeComponent . For an element that starts out hidden, the display binding is set up in preconfig so the element is not built until it becomes visible. Plain text is a "text" component: motifComponent("text", (node) => node.setText("…")) . The compiler produces whichever binding it picks for each expression ( bindings.method for live text, bindings.ternary for a ternary); when writing by hand, bindings.text is enough for live text. npx motif-explain file.tsx prints which call a JSX expression comes down to.

title: MotifJS Documentation
heading: Next step
text: To begin, go on to Getting Started .

title: Getting Started
text: This section covers setting up the MotifJS build chain, writing the first component and getting the application on screen. The examples come in two forms: with JSX ( .tsx ) and without JSX, using component calls directly ( .ts ).

title: Getting Started
heading: Requirements
text: Vite (the recommended bundler) or Rollup TypeScript or JavaScript. Views written with JSX live in .tsx / .jsx files, and views written without JSX live in .ts / .js files. If you use TypeScript, your project needs version 5.4 or later (the core's type declarations use NoInfer ). @motifx/compiler brings its own TypeScript dependency (5.x/6.x) for type-aware checks ( motif-lint ) and for reading the plugin's tsconfig.json , and it works independently of the version in your project. @motifx/core — the core library. It ships as ESM ( dist/index.esm.js ), CommonJS ( dist/index.cjs ) and, for use without a bundler and without JSX, UMD ( dist/index.umd.min.js , the package's unpkg / jsdelivr entry; see Without a bundler ) @motifx/compiler — the build plugin. It compiles JSX into component calls, transforms decorators ( @Injectable ) in .ts / .js files and strips development-only code from production builds. Install it even in a project that does not use JSX. Node.js 18 or later — the @motifx/compiler plugin and its commands ( motif-lint , motif-explain ) run on Node; your bundler's own Node requirement applies as well. The two packages ( @motifx/compiler and @motifx/core ) are always published with the same version number, whether or not one of them changed, and they are installed at the same version. The surface that compiled code relies on in the runtime (the compiler contract) changes only in a major version. If the runtime does not support the contract number declared by the compiled code, development mode prints an MJX121 warning (the mismatch is noticed while modules load, but the warning appears when app.useDevelopment(true) is called).

title: Getting Started
heading: New project
text: pnpm create motifjs , yarn create motifjs , bun create motifjs and npx create-motifjs do the same thing. create-motifjs is the MotifJS community's project generator and needs Node 20.19 or later. It asks for the language (TypeScript or JavaScript), whether components are written with or without JSX, the AI agent docs and DevTools, and creates a Vite project with the compiler plugin and motif-lint already set up. Today the only template is starter , a complete notes application.

title: Getting Started
heading: Adding to an existing project
text: The core is a dependency of the application, and the compiler is a development dependency: With pnpm, yarn and bun the same two packages are installed with add , the compiler again as a development dependency. Then make the two settings in Build setup .

title: Getting Started
heading: Without a bundler
text: The core's UMD file is the package's unpkg / jsdelivr entry and exposes every export on the global motif object: main.js starts with const { Application, motifComponent, reactive } = motif; . JSX and decorator syntax need the compiler, so here the view is written without JSX , services are registered with builder.services , and code marked @DEV-ONLY is not stripped. In production, pin the address to a version: https://unpkg.com/@motifx/core@<version> .

title: Getting Started
heading: Build setup
text: MotifJS JSX is not handled by a standard jsxFactory but by its own compiler ( @motifx/compiler ). The compiler turns every JSX element into a motifComponent call, and the reactive expressions inside it (text, conditions, lists) into bindings.* calls. That is why two settings are needed: Add the @motifx/compiler plugin to the bundler. The plugin runs before Vite's own transform ( enforce: 'pre' ) and leaves no JSX behind, so Vite needs no separate JSX setting. Set "jsx": "preserve" in tsconfig.json : TypeScript checks the types of the JSX but does not compile it. A project without JSX does not need this line. Why jsx: "preserve" ? In MotifJS, JSX does not turn into a "render function call" but into compiled output that sets up reactive bindings. For example, the compiler turns the expression {model.count} into a sender.bindings.add("textContent", model, "count") call. Only @motifx/compiler knows this transform; TypeScript only checks the types, and @motifx/compiler is what compiles the JSX. The plugin compiles .jsx and .tsx files. In .ts / .js files it transforms decorators ( @Injectable ) (see Registering Services ), names module-level stores for DevTools during vite dev , and strips development-only code from production builds. In .ts / .mts / .cts files it adds a static elementTag from an element generic such as Component<HTMLUListElement> (see Root element ). In files under node_modules , only development-only code is stripped. In Vite 8 (Rolldown), if the application has not set optimizeDeps.rolldownOptions.transform.jsx for dependency scanning, the plugin sets it to 'preserve' , so .jsx files are read without looking for another JSX runtime. Rollup uses the same compiler() plugin; there is no separate Rollup or Babel plugin. Rollup has no mode of its own, so tell the plugin about production builds: compiler({ production: !process.env.ROLLUP_WATCH }) . The plugin also strips types from the .tsx and .jsx files it compiles. Stripping types from plain .ts files and resolving imports written without an extension or by package name is the job of the usual Rollup plugins: rollup-plugin-esbuild or @rollup/plugin-typescript , plus @rollup/plugin-node-resolve with the .tsx and .ts extensions added. The vite/client types and import.meta.env are specific to Vite.

title: Getting Started
heading: Development-only code
text: A production build strips code marked as development-only from application files and from packages under node_modules . MotifJS marks its own DevTools hooks this way, so this code never makes it into a production bundle, whatever app.useDevelopment() says. The app.useDevelopment(true) line is written with the same mark, so the production bundle contains neither that line nor the DevTools object. The single-line mark strips the statement or class member that follows it. To strip several statements or members in a row, use the @DEV-ONLY-BEGIN / @DEV-ONLY-END pair; the pair sits between statements and class members. @DEV-ONLY strips the single statement or class member (method, field, accessor) that comes right after it; everything between @DEV-ONLY-BEGIN and @DEV-ONLY-END , the marks included, is stripped. A mark is a block comment that contains only the mark; a // line that mentions the mark is not a mark. @DEV-ONLY works at any depth (inside a method, in front of an if or a const ). BEGIN and END sit in the same block, between statements, imports or class members. A BEGIN without END , an END without BEGIN , a nested BEGIN or a range mark inside an expression stops the build with an error at the mark, in vite dev as well. Production means vite build in Vite, and the production option or NODE_ENV=production in Rollup. In Vite the decision follows Vite's isProduction value, that is, NODE_ENV=production : if NODE_ENV=development is set in the environment, vite build does not strip the code either. Nothing is stripped during development.

title: Getting Started
heading: Plugin options
text: Option Description diagnostics With false , compile-time warnings ( MJX001 – MJX004 , MJX007 , MJX015 , MJX016 ) are not printed; on by default (see Compile-time warnings ). explain Prints what every JSX expression compiles to in the matching files: true means every file, a string matches paths that contain it, a RegExp uses test(id) (see What did this expression compile to? ). exclude Files the plugin keeps its hands off: a string matches paths that contain it ( includes ), a RegExp uses test(id) , or an (id) => boolean function. MotifJS does not compile the JSX in these files, which is left to Vite's own transform; in a production build the development-only code inside them is still stripped. storeNames Names module-level stores for DevTools; on by default in vite dev and off in production builds. In Rollup it is off and is turned on with storeNames: true . production Strips development-only code; the default is vite build in Vite and NODE_ENV=production elsewhere.

title: Getting Started
heading: HTML host
text: The application needs a root element to be mounted into, and a <script> tag loads the entry file:

title: Getting Started
heading: First component
text: A settings page: SettingsService holds the theme and density, writes them to <html> as data-theme / data-density and saves them to localStorage . SettingsPage shows the options as buttons, the selected one is marked with aria-pressed , and a summary line follows the choice. The class, function and Options API forms use the same core, and each is written both with and without JSX. In the example: aria-pressed={() => …} is a getter: it is recomputed on all three buttons on every choice, and the ones whose value changes are the previous and the new choice. A plain value ( type="button" ) is written once. {() => …} / bindings.text(() => …) is a live text binding. In JSX, a member expression such as {LABELS[option]} is a binding too, because the compiler turns it into a getter; in the form without JSX, setText(LABELS[option]) writes the text once. The service is registered in the main file with builder.services.addSingleton(SettingsService, { useClass: SettingsService, startup: true }) . A singleton given startup: true is created at the start of app.run() without waiting for a component to ask for it; if it was asked for earlier, it is not created again. In the example the class component gets the service with this.getService , and the function and Options components with FromService (the Options component can use this.getService too). Because the service is a singleton, the page sees the same settings every time it opens. Registering through @Injectable is covered in Registering Services . In JSX, .map compiles to a list binding. The options are fixed, so the form without JSX adds the buttons with a plain loop; for a list that changes, use bindings.list (see Conditional Rendering and Lists ). In the form without JSX, plain text is a "text" component: motifComponent("text", (node) => node.setText("…")) . The page class does not declare an element; view() returns the content, and motifComponent("main", …) is the single element of that content, not the component's own element (see Root element ). In the Options form the component's element is given with el , and view() returns the content.

title: Getting Started
heading: Mount the application
text: The Application class is the application's entry point. The usual flow: Create a builder with Application.CreateBuilder() . Register services on builder.services if needed (see Introduction to Dependency Injection ). Produce the Application instance with builder.build() . Optionally define routing with app.useRouter(...) . Mount the application on a DOM element with app.run(host, rootComponent) . A class component is passed as an instance; it can also be built with the <SettingsPage /> tag in JSX or with motifComponent(SettingsPage) when writing without JSX. Function and Options components are written as tags in JSX; without JSX, a function component is called and an Options component is built with motifComponent(SettingsPage) : The first argument of app.run accepts a CSS selector ( "#app" ), an HTMLElement or a Node ; if the selector matches nothing, an MJX406 error is thrown. The second argument is the root component . The host's existing content is kept, and the root component is appended after it. If the second argument is left out, MotifJS places a RouterView at the root by itself (for router-based applications; see below). Application.CreateBuilder() is called once per application; a second call throws MJX405 (it can be called again after app.dispose() ).

title: Getting Started
heading: Router-based startup
text: In multi-page applications, use routing instead of a root component. In that case do not pass a second argument to run ; MotifJS adds the root RouterView itself. When a second argument is given, the root is your component and you put the RouterView in its view yourself: useDevelopment turns on development mode: MJX warnings, route checks when it is called before useRouter , and DevTools. useLogging turns on console error logging (on by default). The mode values are 'history' | 'hash' | 'file' | 'shell' . Route definitions are covered in detail on the Route Table page, and placing a RouterView on the RouterView page. The module loaded through notFound must export the page as default ; for a named export, map it: notFound: () => import("./pages/NotFoundPage").then((m) => m.NotFoundPage) . A module without a default export is reported as MJX127 (the cause of MJX304 ), and the error view is shown instead of the 404 page (see Lazy loading ).

title: Getting Started
heading: Development helpers
text: Application has chainable configuration methods: Method Description app.useDevelopment(true) Turns on development mode: MJX warnings are written to the console ( console.warn ), and so are errors the framework catches internally and passes over quietly; when called before useRouter , route definitions are checked. MJX warnings are not buffered: warnings raised before development mode is turned on (other than MJX121 ) are not printed later, which is why useDevelopment is called before run . DevTools is turned on as well: the globalThis.__MOTIF_DEVTOOLS__ object is created ( The DevTools Contract ); useDevelopment(false) turns DevTools off and removes the object. Read it with app.isDevelopmentModeEnabled . In a production build the core's DevTools hooks are stripped from the code ( Development-only code ), so DevTools produces no data. app.useLogging(true) Turns writing errors to the console on or off (on by default). It does not turn off MJX warnings; those follow development mode ( useDevelopment ). app.useReactiveMonitor({ enabled: true, threshold: 200, name: 'app' }) Turns on tracking of reactive dependency leaks (recommended during development; when the threshold is exceeded an MJX507 warning is printed, and this warning only shows while useDevelopment(true) is on; see Leak tracking ). app.useTransitions({ mode: 'out-in' }) Picks the default mode for enter/leave transitions (see Enter/leave mode ). Errors thrown in hooks ( MJX122 ), event handlers ( MJX123 ), effect/binding functions ( MJX208 ) and using handlers ( MJX129 ) are reported regardless of development mode, in production too: they are written to console.error (unless useLogging(false) ) and passed to errorHandler.addListener(fn) listeners as a MotifError ( error.code , error.cause ; see Error Handling ). The application keeps running.

title: Getting Started
heading: Next step
text: To build the parts of the application, go on to Components .

title: Components
text: In MotifJS a component is an object that manages a DOM element and its child controls ( controls ). Every component derives from ComponentBase ; in everyday use you work with the concrete Component class. The view is written in JSX or built directly with the same calls, and every example on this page is given with and without JSX, in TypeScript and JavaScript. There are three styles for writing a component: class, function and Options API. All three use the same core, and which one you pick is a matter of preference. The examples come from a notes application, and this service is shared by all of them:

title: Components
heading: 1. Class components
text: You derive from Component and return the view from the view() method. NoteEmptyPage is the page shown when no note is open in a folder. It uses the usual parts of a class component: a field that gets a service ( this.getService ), access to the router ( useNavigation() ), a getter for a derived value, a method, the onConfig hook and view() . this.context.navigate navigates with the application's router. A class component that takes props and declares their type is on the Props and Children page. A class component is built with a tag in JSX ( <NoteEmptyPage /> ), and without JSX with new NoteEmptyPage() or motifComponent(NoteEmptyPage) .

title: Components
heading: Root element
text: The value you pass to super(...) decides the component's own element ( this.element ): super('div') → the component's element is a <div> . For an SVG element write super('svg', { options: { isSvg: true } }) ; the element is created in the SVG namespace. super(node) → a DOM node you already have ( document.createElement('canvas') , an existing element on the page) becomes the component's element; the component does not create it, it takes ownership of it (see Wrapping third-party libraries ). If you pass no argument ( super() ), the component has no element of its own (a fragment): this.element is a comment marker, and the content returned by view() sits between the opening and closing markers ( <!--[--> … <!--]--> ). In a component without an element, props can also be passed as the first argument: super(props) is the same as super(undefined, props) , and in a class that does not write a constructor, new MyComponent(props) works the same way. If you gave an element generic such as Component<HTMLDivElement> , @motifx/compiler adds static elementTag = 'div' to the class; then super() creates a real element of that type instead of a fragment (see Root element ). For SVG generics such as Component<SVGSVGElement> the compiler also adds static elementNamespace = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' , and the element is created in the SVG namespace. You can write the two static fields by hand as well; if they are already there, the compiler leaves them alone. The Vite plugin does this in .ts , .mts and .cts files too, so in a class without JSX the element type also comes from the generic. In a file the plugin does not process (for example in a library compiled only with tsc ), write static elementTag = 'ul' or call super('ul') . JavaScript has no generics, so there the element is always declared with static elementTag or super('ul') . If a ready component instance is passed to the constructor ( new Component(instance) ), no new component is created; that instance is returned. view() returns the content, not the component's element. In a class that declares no element, like NoteEmptyPage ( extends Component , no generic), the <div class="pane"> returned by view() is not the component's element but the first and only child of its content. So a class and id written on the tag, and this.class.add and this.attr.add inside the class, reach no element at all. An onclick written on the tag and this.motif.on inside the class, on the other hand, listen on the top-level elements of the content (see Events ), and x-display and this.motif.hide() hide the content between the markers. Classes and attributes are written straight onto the div . To give the component an element of its own, declare a concrete tag (the Component<HTMLUListElement> generic, static elementTag or super('ul') ): the common attributes written on the tag ( class , id , style , role , aria-* , data-* …; see common attributes ), DOM events ( onclick …) and this.class then apply to that element, while other props such as title stay in this.props only. view() returns only the content; ActivityLog below works like that. With Component<HTMLDivElement> , returning another <div> from view() produces two nested div s.

title: Components
heading: view() or controls directly?
text: Content arrives in two ways: Return it from view() : while the component is being built, view() is called once and its result is added as child controls. Call controls.add(...) : on a built component the child is built right away and put in place; on a component that is not built yet, it is built together with its owner. The two work together as well: view() builds the skeleton, and content that arrives later is added with controls.add . ActivityLog is a component whose element is a <ul> . It writes no view() ; on every noteSaved application event (whose data is the title of the saved note) it adds a row to the list. The this.context.on subscription is removed on its own when the component is disposed (see Context ):

title: Components
heading: Names of class members
text: Members of ComponentBase are not defined again under the same name in a class component; if they are, the member MotifJS uses is hidden. The reserved names: Methods and accessors: build , dispose , disposeAsync , style , setText , setState , reState , using , doWork , getService , useModel , $ , context , siblings , serviceProvider , isWait . Objects MotifJS sets up, and state fields: element , props , controls , class , attr , bindings , motif , parent , childs , isBuilt , isInitialized , isDisposed , isConfigured , isVisible . view() , the lifecycle hooks ( onBuilt , onDisposing …), initializeComponent and onElementCreating exist to be written in the class. If you need to extend a method such as build , dispose or style , the override calls super.build(...) , super.dispose(...) and so on. An overridden dispose() runs only when the component's own dispose() is called (by hand, or through controls.remove / clear ). For a component disposed together with a parent, the framework does not call the child's dispose() but uses its own internal path; in that case only the onDisposing / onDisposed hooks and the setDisposable registrations run. That is why work to do on disposal belongs in the hooks or in this.motif.setDisposable(...) . Framework operations ( show , hide , on , off , trigger , setDisposable …) live under this.motif , so these names are free to use in the class. TypeScript reports a clash whose type is plainly incompatible at compile time ( style = 'red' → TS2416). Defining a field with an accessor name — motif , controls , class , attr , bindings , context , siblings , serviceProvider , isWait and the state fields ( isVisible …) — gives a TS2610 error whatever its type (with any or declare as well). For method names, however, it does not report an any -typed field or a method with a compatible signature ( build() {} , a parameterless style() ). During compilation @motifx/compiler reports an override that does not reach super on every path with an MJX015 warning: a member that never calls it, or skips it on some path because of an early return , an if with one branch, a loop or a catch ( compile warnings ; motif-lint runs the same rule). In development mode ( app.useDevelopment() ), MotifJS reports these clashes once per class with an MJX128 warning while placing the component: an override that does not call super , an instance field that hides a method or an accessor, and another value put in place of controls / attr / class / bindings / motif / element / parent . The state fields ( isVisible …) and props are not checked at run time.

title: Components
heading: 2. Function components
text: A function returns a single component. State and event handlers are kept in a closure. NoteRow is a row in the list: it takes the note and the folder through props , and reads the open note from the router's parameter. A function component is used in JSX the same way as a class, as a tag; without JSX, the counterpart of the tag is motifComponent(NoteRow, props) . The function can also be called directly. That is an ordinary function call, and it gives the same result only for the props the function reads itself ( note , folder ): framework props such as ref , the common attributes ( class , id …) and options are applied to the root only by motifComponent (for directives and hooks written on the tag, see below ): In the function component, folder() is a local function that returns the folder.

title: Components
heading: Root component
text: A function component has no this . Whatever a class does with this.motif , this.context , this.class or this.bindings is done in a function component through the root component. The root component is the component of the root element the function returns, and it is a Component as well. You reach it through the first argument of a hook written on the root element ( onConfig={(root) => …} , initializeComponent , onBuilt ) or through a ref written on the root element; if the returned JSX expression is assigned to a variable ( const root = <section>…</section> ), that variable is the root component too. Without JSX, the root is the component returned by the motifComponent(tag, …) call, and the hooks are written in the object form of the same call.

title: Components
heading: Hooking into the lifecycle
text: In function components you can hook into the lifecycle by passing the hooks as props on the returned root element (see Lifecycle ). Without JSX, the hooks are written in the object form of motifComponent . SearchField takes focus once it enters the DOM; its oninput handler is written with two parameters, so the first one is the field's component:

title: Components
heading: Directives and hooks written on the tag
text: Framework props written on the tag of a function component — directives such as x-display and x-wait , lifecycle hooks such as onConfig / onBuilt / x-mounted / x-initializing (in both the x- and x: spellings), initializeComponent and ref — are applied to the root the function returns. Without JSX, the same keys go into the object passed to motifComponent ; instead of x-display and x-wait you can also use bindings.display / bindings.wait inside preconfig . These keys and ref are not part of the props passed to the function, nor of a class's this.props : The function does not have to do anything for this, and it does not have to pass the props on to its root either. (If the function already passes the props to its root — motifComponent('div', props) — the framework props are not applied a second time.) In class components the same props go to the constructor.

title: Components
heading: 3. Options API components
text: You return an object wrapped with motifOptions : el , data , view and an optional ctor . motifOptions returns the object as it is; it only tells TypeScript that this inside the methods is the component, so this.class , this.motif and this.props compile in strict mode and the editor can complete them. The function that returns the object is used like a component: in JSX ( <NoteFilter /> ), without JSX with motifComponent(NoteFilter, props) , as a route's control , and as the default loaded by Lazy . NoteFilter is a search box that takes its initial query from the factory's props parameter inside ctor . The factory's parameter also declares the tag's prop type ( <NoteFilter initial="…" /> ): Every field of the object except el is copied onto the component. ctor is not copied; it is called once , right after the component is created (before build() / view() ), with this as the component and the props written on the tag as its only argument. An error thrown inside it does not break the creation of the component; it is reported to the central error handler as MJX122 . The props written on the tag can also be reached as this.props . el can be a tag name ( 'div' ), a DOM node or another component (a class, a function, an Options object); when a component is given, its root is used. el is the component's own element, and view() returns the content: a fragment ( <>…</> ) in JSX, an array without JSX. To give the root a class, write this.class.add(...) inside view() (or in ctor / onConfigured ), and this.attr.add({ ... }) for attributes. Returning a wrapper with the same tag as el from view() produces two nested elements. get / set accessors on the object are carried over to the component as accessors: they do not run during copying, and they run again on every read with this as the component. You can write a derived value as an accessor ( get visible() { … } ) or as a method ( visible() { … } ). Of the lifecycle methods written on the object, onConfigured , onBuilding , initializeComponent , onBuilt , onMounted , onVisibilityChanged , onActivated , onDeactivated , onDisposing and onDisposed run. onInitializing and onInitialized do not run: those two phases end while el is being created, before the fields are copied from the object. An onConfig written on the object runs only when el is a class component (a class component's configuration phase is postponed to the start of build() , just before onConfigured ); when el is a tag name, a DOM node or a function that returns a plain element, this phase also ends while the element is being created, and the onConfig on the object does not run. An onConfig={…} prop written on the tag does run, but when el is a tag name it runs while the root is being created: at that moment the object's members ( data , view , methods) have not been copied yet, ctor has not run and parent is null . Put setup code that touches the members in ctor or onConfigured .

title: Components
heading: Next step
text: For the ways of creating a component in code, go on to Creating Components .

title: Creating Components
text: This page builds the row of the notes list, the NoteRow component, from start to finish. The code is shown according to the code choices on the page: the writing form, the component style and the language. Note , Folder and NotesService come from the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page.

title: Creating Components
heading: Writing the component
text: A component has four parts: Definition: a class that derives from Component , a function that returns a component, or a function that returns an object written with motifOptions . Element: the row's element is an <a> . In a class, the element is declared on the class: with the Component<HTMLAnchorElement> generic in TypeScript, and with static elementTag = "a" in JavaScript. In a function the element is the returned root, and in Options it is the el field. If no element is declared, the component has no element (see Root element ). Content: in a class and in Options, view() returns the content that goes inside the element. The element's own class and attributes are given in onConfigured with this.class and this.attr . A function builds the root together with its content itself. Data: the note and the folder arrive through props: this.props in a class, the parameter in a function, and the factory's parameter in Options. A read made inside a function such as () => note.title … is live; when the note changes, only that text or class is updated. The row reads the open note from the router's parameter and marks that row with the active class:

title: Creating Components
heading: Using the component
text: A component is created where it is used, together with its props. In JSX writing the tag is enough; the compiler turns the tag into a motifComponent(NoteRow, { note, folder }) call. Without JSX, a class is created with new , and function and Options components with motifComponent ; motifComponent accepts a class as well. In the function component, folder() is a local function that returns the folder. A created component becomes visible once it is placed somewhere: In JSX, where the tag is written. In code, through a parent's controls.add(...) call (see controls ). As the application's root, with app.run("#app", component) . In a route's control field: the router creates the page component itself when the address matches (see The Route Table ).

title: Creating Components
heading: Creation and building
text: Creating and building are separate steps. The component's element is prepared when it is created: in the constructor for a class, and when the function is called for function and Options components. The content arrives once, when the component is built ( build() ): view() , initializeComponent and the children run at that point. A component added to a parent that is already built is built right away, and a component added to a parent that is not built yet is built together with its parent. That is why this.element exists in a field initializer and in the constructor, but it is empty. Code that touches the content goes in onBuilt , and code that needs the element to be attached to the document (focus, measurements) goes in onMounted (see Lifecycle ). Every argument form that new Component and motifComponent accept without JSX, components without an element, and the keys of the props object are on the Views without JSX page.

title: Creating Components
heading: Next step
text: To give a component data and content, go on to Props and Children .

title: Props and Children
text: Data flow between components: `props`, prop types, live props and placing content with `childs`.

title: Props and Children
heading: props and data flow between components
text: The attributes you write on a component in JSX become that component's props . Without JSX, the same object is passed to the creating call: new MyComponent(props) for a class, and motifComponent(MyComponent, props) for function and Options components. The example is a row on the settings page: the setting's name on the left with a short description under it, and the control that changes the setting on the right. Setting takes the name and description through props, and the control as a child: Props are reached through this.props in a class, through the parameter in a function, and through the factory's parameter in Options. In TypeScript, the props type is the second generic argument of Component in a class ( Component<HTMLDivElement, SettingProps> ), and the parameter's type in a function and in Options. This type gives this.props its type and checks both the tag and the new Setting(…) call: if a required prop is missing or its type does not fit, compilation fails. The archive setting uses Setting like this. The description shows the number of notes in the archive, and the control is the button that empties the archive: In the function component, notes is the service the page gets with FromService(NotesService) .

title: Props and Children
heading: Plain values and live values
text: The props object is not reactive; it is given once, when the component is created. name="Archive" is a plain value: it is read and written once. A value that will change later is passed as a function. hint={() => …} is like that: as the number of notes in the archive changes, the description changes too. The receiving side types such a prop with Bind<T> and reads it inside a function with read(…) : () => read(props.hint) . read calls the value if it is a function and returns it as it is otherwise, so the same prop can also be given hint="Fixed text" . Because the read happens inside a function, the binding tracks the reactive values the function reads (see Reactivity ). An expression that is not passed as a function keeps the value it had at creation: hint={`${notes.count("archive")} archived notes`} is not updated when the count changes. The one exception is the conditional expression: the compiler wraps an a ? b : c expression on a component tag in a function itself, and the receiver reads that with read too (see Ternaries in attributes ).

title: Props and Children
heading: Callback props
text: Data travels from child to parent through a function the parent provides: the parent passes a prop such as onChoose={(theme) => settings.setTheme(theme)} , and the child calls props.onChoose(value) when a choice is made. This function is an ordinary prop too and stays in the child's props. If its name starts with on , it must not be the name of a DOM event the compiler recognizes (see the note below). In a subclass that extends an existing component, the props type is narrowed with declare : declare props: DialogProps; . That line is a type only and produces no code. props: DialogProps; or props!: DialogProps; , on the other hand, opens a new field on the class and overwrites the props value set up by the base class with undefined . Note: Lifecycle props ( onConfig , onBuilt , onMounted … and their x- forms) and initializeComponent are registered as hooks and taken out of the props dictionary. The same goes for the object passed with motifComponent(MyComponent, { … }) without JSX; in a function component the hooks are applied to the returned root and are not part of the props the function receives (see Directives and hooks written on the tag ). ref is applied to the component as well and is not part of this.props . On a component tag, a DOM event name the compiler recognizes ( onclick , onChange , oninput:once ) is attached to the component's element as a listener and never reaches props ; in a class without an element, this listener listens on the top-level elements of the content. The compiler does not recognize names such as onmouseenter , onpointerdown , onfocusin or ontransitionend : no listener is set up and the value stays in props without a warning. Listen to these events on a component tag with the on:mouseenter={…} spelling (see The on:name spelling ). Any other on... prop ( onSave , onChoose , onValueChange ) is an ordinary callback prop and stays in this.props ; its name must not clash with an event the compiler recognizes ( onSearch → the search event, an MJX002 warning).

title: Props and Children
heading: Child components ( childs )
text: JSX content written between a component's opening and closing tags reaches that component as childs ( ComponentBase[] ). Without JSX, the same array is passed under the childs key. That is how Setting receives the archive button. The component puts the children wherever its view wants them: with {this.childs} or {props.childs} in JSX, and without JSX with controls.add(...) or by adding them to the childs array of a part without an element. childs is a reserved name for the compiler: {this.childs} , {props.childs} and {childs} all compile to placing content ( controls.add ), not to text. The same holds for an array of components you have in hand: {[cardA, cardB]} . A few details: Placement is static : childs is a plain array that arrives once, during setup ( this.childs , or props.childs in a function component). Assigning a new array to this field later, adding an element to the array or calling setState() does not change the content in the slot. The same is true for {() => this.childs} : the getter produces a Frame , but it runs again only when a reactive value read inside it changes. The children's own bindings are live, though: a binding such as disabled={() => notes.count("archive") === 0} updates when the count changes, whatever form the slot takes. There is one rule: a class that writes view() places its children itself, and in a class that does not write view() the children are the content. In a class that gets no element in the constructor and writes no view() (a class that declares no element, or an element declared with Component<HTMLDivElement> / static elementTag ), childs are added to the root automatically. A class that writes view() gets no automatic adding: you place the children wherever and whenever you like with {this.childs} (or {() => this.childs} ) or with controls.add(...this.childs) , and the children are built only in the slot they are placed in. If the slot is behind x-wait / x-display or in a nested element, the children wait along with it; it makes no difference whether the call is in the view() body or in the slot's setup function. In classes given a concrete tag such as super("div", props) , and in a component created by tag name ( new Component("div", { childs }) ), you do the placing. An Options object follows the same rule: in an Options component that writes no view() , childs are added to the el element automatically, and an Options component that writes view() places them itself. Children that are never placed (because the slot never opened, or the component never placed them) are disposed when the component that received them is disposed. Only the exact name childs is special; names such as {childsCount} become ordinary text bindings.

title: Props and Children
heading: Next step
text: To manage a component's child controls, go on to controls and the Component Tree .

title: controls and the Component Tree
text: The child control collection `controls`, moving around the component tree, and moving content somewhere else.

title: controls and the Component Tree
heading: controls — the child control collection
text: Every component has a controls collection. It is a live list that manages the component's children, and every change to the list shows up in the DOM right away. Call What it does controls.add(a, b) Appends at the end and returns what was added as an array. controls.add(2, a) , controls.insert(2, a, b) Inserts at the given index. controls.remove(a) Removes the child and disposes it. await controls.detach(a) Plays the leave transition and takes the child out of the tree and the DOM; does not dispose it. controls.clear() Disposes every child. await controls.clearAsync() The same; resolves when every disposal is finished. controls.move(a, b) Moves a in front of b ; to the end if b is not given. controls.moveToIndex(a, 0) Moves a to the given index. The index is the resulting position; length - 1 and above moves it to the end. controls.items , controls.length The array of children and the number of children. controls.forEach(fn) , controls.map(fn) Walk over the children; map returns the results as an array. The activity log adds a row for every saved note. The newest row goes to the top, and the log keeps the last five rows; anything beyond that is disposed: At run time add / insert accept plain values too: strings, numbers, booleans and bigints are each wrapped in a text node. The TypeScript signature expects ComponentBase , so in typed code build the text node with motifComponent("text", …) . A child that already has a parent is first taken from there ( detach ) and then added. A disposed child is not added. A child added to a built component is built and put in place inside the add call; there is no render or flush to wait for. A child added to a component that is not built yet is built together with its owner. If the component is held with isWait , the child is recorded and built when the wait is lifted. If the container carries x-chunk , the first 100 of the children added together (the first n if a number is given) are built right away; the rest leave a marker and are built over the following frames, as far as the frame time allows (see Large lists ). detach takes the child out of the tree and the DOM but does not dispose it, so it can be added somewhere else with add . remove and clear do dispose. move works only between children of the same parent, and it moves them into the same order in the DOM (fragment-rooted children together with their range). If the position does not change, it does nothing. The onAdd / onRemove / onAddBeforeBuild callbacks belong to the framework and are not assigned by hand. To listen for a child being added, use motif.on('controladded', fn) . motif.on('controlremoved', fn) arrives only when the child leaves this component through detach (including when another component's controls.add takes the child from here); the event arrives after the leave transition and the removal from the DOM are finished. remove , clear , clearAsync and the child's own dispose() do not trigger this event. In both events e.control is the component that was added or that left.

title: controls and the Component Tree
heading: Moving around the component tree
text: Components form a live object tree, and from any component you can reach the tree in every direction. The element , props , public fields and methods of a component you find are used like those of any ordinary object. Member What it gives parent The parent component; null on a component that has not been added anywhere. controls.items The children. siblings.next() , siblings.prev() The next and previous sibling; undefined at the end and at the start. siblings.all() The parent's children, the component itself included. siblings.nextAll() , siblings.prevAll() The following and preceding siblings. $(selector).fromComponent() Descendant components that match the selector ( ComponentBase[] ). $(selector).fromDom() DOM nodes inside the element that match the selector ( NodeList ). A plain tag in JSX is a component too. The first parameter of a two-parameter event handler ( sender ) is that tag's component, and you can walk the tree from there: sender.parent , sender.siblings.all() . A one-parameter handler receives only the event (see Events ). siblings reads the parent's controls.items array; if there is no parent, every method returns undefined . The parent of the root component passed to app.run is not null : it is the application shell that run() builds around the host element ( app.getAppShell() ). The topmost component whose parent is null is this shell; for content moved into a window it is the window's host , and for content in the page layer it is app.layer (see Page layer ). fromComponent() walks the component tree depth-first starting from this component (it is in the result itself if it matches) and compares each component's element with the selector. In a component whose root is a fragment, the search starts from the nearest parent component that has a real element, so the result covers all of that parent's content: matching items of sibling components come back too, and in fromComponent() the parent itself if it matches. To search only your own content, search from an inner tag you hold through ref , or from a class that declares its element. fromDom() runs querySelectorAll inside the same element. On a disposed component it returns null / [] . A component obtained through ref is used the same way (see Element access inside a component ).

title: controls and the Component Tree
heading: Moving content somewhere else
text: There are two built-in pairs of components for showing a component's content outside its own tree, and each is covered on its own page: Transport and TransportTo — shows a sender's content in a named slot. When several senders come to the same slot, mode: 'replace' (the default) keeps only the content of the one built last, and 'merge' adds the content of all of them in the order they were built. The Transporter helper for moving content in code is there as well. ContentBody and ContentBlock — gathers the parts of several blocks in a single body.

title: controls and the Component Tree
heading: Page layer
text: Content such as notifications, dialogs and drop-down menus belongs to the component that opens it, but it has to appear above everything else on the page. app.layer is the component set aside for that: the first time it is read, it puts a plain <div> at the end of <body> , after the application's host element, and returns the component that wraps that element; later reads return the same component. If the host is <body> itself or contains the layer, the layer stays at the end of the host: the shell's root and every component added later go in front of the layer. It can be read before run() too; if <body> does not exist yet, the element is placed when the document loads, content added up to that point counts as placed at that moment, and onMounted runs then. If the element is later taken out of the page, for example because startup code emptied the body, the layer is put back at the end of the body together with its contents the first time content asks for a place, or in run() ; what was added until then is placed at that point. The core writes no styles or attributes on this element; positioning, z-index and markers such as aria-live are up to the application and are given the way they would be on any ordinary component: app.layer.class.add("overlays") , app.layer.attr.add({ "aria-live": "polite" }) . app.dispose() disposes the layer together with its contents and removes the element. When the application is started again with run() , the layer is built again on its first read; if a layer was read after dispose, run() moves it after the host and the next app.dispose() removes it. If the application will not be started again, call app.dispose() once more and the layer is removed right then. Content in the layer behaves like any other member of the tree: it goes in with controls.add ; it receives onMounted , onActivated and onDeactivated ; it sees the application's services and router through context ; remove disposes it and detach keeps it. The parent of an added component is the layer, and the layer itself, like the shell, is a root whose parent is null . app.layerOf(target?, ...components) puts content in the layer of the document the target is in. If the target is a component or a DOM node, its document is checked: if the document belongs to a window opened or connected through app.windows , that window's host is returned, otherwise app.layer ; if no target is given or it is null , app.layer is returned. The components that follow are added to the layer found with controls.add , and the layer is returned. If the first argument is a component that has no parent and whose element is not yet in any document, it counts as content rather than a target and is added to the page layer; a component without a parent whose element already sits in a document, such as a root wrapped with new Component(document.body) , is a target and stays where it is. So this.context.layerOf(this, new SaveToast()) puts the content in the window the component is in, and this.context.layerOf(new SaveToast()) puts it on the page. A target that is neither a component nor a node throws MJX424 . Content placed directly has the layer's lifetime; if it has to go away together with the component that opened it, put a Transport slot in the layer and write the content with TransportTo (see Transport and TransportTo ).

title: controls and the Component Tree
heading: Moving a component to another window
text: A component's element can also be moved into another document of the same origin: a window opened with window.open , an always-on-top Picture-in-Picture window or an <iframe> . The component is not rebuilt; its state, bindings and services stay on the page, and only the elements move. app.windows manages this: this.context.windows.open(editor, { width: 720, height: 560 }) opens the component in a window, puts it back in its old place when the window closes, and carries the style sheets and the theme over to the window. For the options, the closing rules and Electron, see the Windows page. If you want to open the window yourself and only introduce the document to the application, app.connectDocument(win.document) is there as the lower layer; then wrapping the body with new Component(win.document.body) , providing the content with controls.add and taking it back on close are up to you.

title: controls and the Component Tree
heading: Next step
text: To reach a component's element and its inner tags, go on to Element and Appearance .

title: Element and Appearance
text: Reaching a component's element and its inner tags: `element`, `ref`, `onRefCreated`; `class`, `attr`, `style` and `setText`.

title: Element and Appearance
heading: Element access inside a component ( element and ref )
text: Every component's real DOM node is reached through element , and the element is ready as soon as the component is created. To hold the component of one of the inner tags, write ref on that tag: in JSX ref={this.title} ( ref={title} in a function component) or ref={(c) => …} , and without JSX the ref key of the props object. The editing area of the note page holds its title and body fields through ref . When the page opens, it sizes the body field to the height of its content and, if the note is new, puts the cursor in the title; the body field grows as you type. onEdit is a callback prop called on every change: The note page places the fields with <NoteFields note={note} onEdit={() => this.edited(note)} /> . The note page places the fields with new NoteFields({ note, onEdit: () => this.edited(note) }) . The note page places the fields with motifComponent(NoteFields, { note, onEdit: () => this.edited(note) }) . ref={(s) => ...} — the callback form; s is the tag's component (on a plain DOM tag, the Component that wraps the element; on a component tag, the component instance; on a function component, the returned root). Without JSX this is the only form: motifComponent("input", { ref: (s) => (this.title = s), … }) ( (title = s) in a function component). ref={this.x} / ref={name} — the compiler resolves the target. If the target is a method, a field holding a function or a local function, it is called with the tag's component. If it is a declared field (without a value or with a plain value) or a variable without an initial value, the component is assigned to it. For targets that cannot be decided at compile time (a member that is not declared or comes from a base class, a parameter, props.x , a field typed as a function, a getter), the decision is made at run time: if the value is a function it is called, otherwise it is assigned. To pass an imported function as a ref, write the callback form: ref={(s) => registerField(s)} . With ref={registerField} the generated code also contains a branch that assigns to the imported name; that works on the development server, but vite build (Rollup) stops with an "Illegal reassignment of import" error. Both forms mean the same on a plain DOM tag and on a component tag; x-ref (and x:ref ) is the same as ref . ref is called exactly once, while the tag's component is being built (before build() ), and it is not written to the DOM as an attribute. On a class or Options component tag, by the time the ref is called, props , the tag's common attributes ( class , id …) and options have been applied. On a plain DOM tag, at the moment of the ref, options and the attributes that go to the constructor (those spread with {...p} , and without JSX those put directly in the object) have been applied; attributes written directly on the tag in JSX ( class , id , placeholder …) and, without JSX, those added inside initializeComponent are written during the build, after the ref. On a function component tag, the ref is called as soon as the function returns its root. In a class component the ref runs inside the base class's constructor; fields defined in the subclass body ( marker = 'ready' ) are set up after the constructor returns, as JavaScript requires, so they do not exist yet inside the ref. A ref is meant for assigning the component to a field in the parent component ( ref={(b) => (this.okButton = b)} ), not for writing to the class's own fields. If ref and x-ref are both written on the same tag, each runs once, in source order. ref is not a prop; it works only on the component it is given to: on a class component it applies to the component itself, and on a function component to the returned root. It is not part of the props passed to the function, nor of this.props , so spreading with {...props} / {...this.props} does not carry it to an inner component. It is the same when building without JSX: motifComponent(Setting, { ref: (c) => ... }) applies the ref to the component itself (to the returned root for a function component), and the ref does not stay in the props passed to the function or in this.props . In the class form, new Setting({ ref: (c) => ... }) is the same; in the function and Options forms you use motifComponent , not new . The rule is simple: if ref is a function, it is called with the component and removed from the props. On a class, an Options component or a plain tag, if it is an object, the component is assigned to that field ( props.ref ): for the class-style Setting , after const p = { name: "Archive", hint: "", ref: {} }; const s = new Setting(p); , p.ref === s . On a function component no assignment is made to an object-style ref; use the callback form. element exists before mounting too; its content arrives when the component is built. Work that needs the element to be attached to the document (focus, measurements) is done in onMounted . To expose an inner item to the outside, use a separate prop name (for example titleRef ) and call it from the inner tag's ref : <input ref={(c) => props.titleRef?.(c)} … /> . Outside, write <NoteFields note={note} titleRef={(c) => (this.title = c)} /> ( title = c in a function component). A ref written on a component tag, on the other hand, gives the component itself; in a function component that is the returned root div . Writing ref={props.titleRef} also works: if the value is a function, it is called with the inner component.

title: Element and Appearance
heading: onRefCreated — a shared hook for refs
text: If a class component defines an onRefCreated(sender) method, it is called right after each ref={this.x} / ref={name} inside view() has been applied to its target. sender is the component of the tag that got the ref; by then the target field has been assigned, or the target method called. It is not called for the callback form ref={(s) => ...} . Without JSX, ref is always a callback, so this hook only works in JSX. Instead of writing oninput on every field separately, the editing area can attach the listener in one place: In the form you picked this hook does not run; every ref is given in the callback form, and the shared work is done inside that callback. Each ref is applied the moment the tag's component is created, and onRefCreated runs once after each of them. Tags inside a plain tag are created while that tag is being built, that is, after its siblings have been created, so with nesting the order can differ from the order in the source: in <form><label><input ref={this.title} /></label><textarea ref={this.body} /></form> , body is applied first and title second. The hook is a member of the class that writes the JSX (the this of view() ), not of the component that got the ref. It is called for JSX in the class's methods and fields (arrow functions included); it is not called in function components, in module-level JSX, in function expressions inside a class method, or in object methods. An Options component's view() is an object method too: a ref={this.x} there is assigned, but an onRefCreated member written on the object is not called.

title: Element and Appearance
heading: Appearance: class , attr , style , setText
text: The class, attributes, inline style and text of a component's element are managed through the component. In the example above, these are this.class.add("editor") , field.attr.add({ … }) and this.body.style({ height: … }) . In the example above, these are class="editor" given on the root element (the class: "editor" key without JSX), field.attr.add({ … }) and body.style({ height: … }) . Call What it does class.add("a", "b") Adds classes. A function ( () => (note.pinned ? "pinned" : "") ) and an object such as { active: () => open() } are live; an array can be given too. class.remove("a") , class.remove("**") Removes a class; "**" removes every class and every live source. class.has("a") Whether the element has the class. attr.add({ type: "button", disabled: () => busy }) Writes attributes. A function value is live; false , null and undefined remove the attribute, and true writes it with an empty value. attr.remove("disabled") , attr.has("disabled") , attr.get("href") Removes an attribute, asks whether it exists, reads its value. style({ height: "120px" }) , style("color: red") Writes the inline style; an object changes only the properties it gives, and a string replaces the whole style. style(() => ({ opacity: … })) A live style, written again when a value the function reads changes. setText("Saved") Changes the element's text ( textContent ); the child nodes inside it are removed. For live text use bindings.text(() => …) . class , attr and style do nothing on a component without an element, because its root is a comment node (see Root element ). class.add keeps a count of the same class coming from several sources; the details and their JSX counterparts are on the Styling and Animation page.

title: Element and Appearance
heading: Next step
text: To show and hide a component, listen to events and release its resources, go on to The motif Namespace .

title: The motif Namespace
text: The operations MotifJS performs on a component are gathered in the motif namespace: this.motif in a class and in Options, and in a function component the motif of the root or of a component held through ref . These operations do not mix with the class's own members, so you can write your own method called show , on or clear in a class (see Names of class members ).

title: The motif Namespace
heading: Members
text: Member What it does show() , hide() , toggle() Show and hide the component without disposing it. A <!--h--> marker stays where the hidden element was, and when shown the element returns to the marker's place. show and hide return a promise that resolves when the transition ends (see Visibility ). on(name, fn) , off(name, fn) Listen to a DOM event or a component event, and stop listening. Modifiers such as "keydown:prevent" and "click:once" can be written. Listeners are removed when the component is disposed (see Component event API ). trigger(name, data) Calls the handlers registered under that name with data ; it does not dispatch an event to the DOM. addHandler(name, fn) The same as on(name, fn) , without a return value. setDisposable(fn) fn runs while the component is being disposed: for releasing a listener added to the document, a timer or a setup made by an external library (see Memory Management and Disposal ). register(object) Ties an object that has a dispose() method to the component's lifetime; it is disposed together with the component. clear() Disposes every child ( controls.clearAsync() ). Does nothing if options.disableDisposal is on. stopAnimations() Finishes a running CSS class transition and cancels WAAPI animations (see Styling and Animation ). options The component's settings; below .

title: The motif Namespace
heading: An example
text: The search box of the notes list does three things with motif . The / key focuses the search from anywhere on the page; because this listener is added to the document, it is released with setDisposable when the component goes away. Escape clears the search: the box's motif.on("keydown", …) listener catches the event bubbling up from the field. While the field has focus, the / hint is hidden with motif.hide() , and it comes back with motif.show() when focus leaves. The search itself lives in the parent's reactive state object: The notes list places the box with its own search state: <SearchBox state={this.state} /> . The notes list places the box with its own search state: new SearchBox({ state: this.state }) . The notes list places the box with its own search state: motifComponent(SearchBox, { state: this.state }) . A listener added with motif.on is released by the component itself. A listener added directly to the document or to window is unknown to the component, so setDisposable releases it. The same rule applies to timers, observers ( ResizeObserver , IntersectionObserver ) and setups made by external libraries.

title: The motif Namespace
heading: motif.options
text: Field Meaning hideStrategy How a hidden element stays in the DOM: "auto" (the default), "placeholder" or "detach" (see Hide strategy ). disableDisposal If true , motif.clear() does not dispose the children. transition The transition setting and the in / out animations with WAAPI (see Styling and Animation ). enableRouterClassing Write-only: gives the element a class based on the current address (see Route classes ). display Reading it gives isVisible ; writing true calls show() , writing false calls hide() . hasEvent(name) Whether a handler is registered under that name. getInstance() The component itself. hideStrategy and disableDisposal can also be given through the options prop when the component is created: options={{ hideStrategy: "detach" }} in JSX, and the options key of the props object without JSX.

title: The motif Namespace
heading: Next step
text: To get to know a component's bindings, go on to bindings .

title: bindings
text: A binding ties a reactive value to the component's element: to its text, an attribute, a field's value, its visibility or its content. When the value changes, only that binding runs again; the rest of the component is not rebuilt. Every component's bindings are in its bindings collection. Each live expression written in JSX becomes a binding on that tag's component; without JSX, the same binding is set up through bindings .

title: bindings
heading: The JSX counterparts
text: JSX Binding that is set up {() => note.title.trim() \|\| "Untitled"} bindings.method(fn) ; if the result is text it becomes a text node, if it is a component it becomes content. For text only, write bindings.text(fn) . {note.title} bindings.add("textContent", note, "title") : a one-way binding to a single field. x-text={() => …} bindings.text(fn) . value={() => state.query} , x-value={() => state.query} bindings.add("value", fn) and bindings.value(fn) ; both do the same job. x-model={() => state.query} bindings.model(() => state.query, (value) => (state.query = value)) : two-way. x-display={() => note.pinned} bindings.display(fn) , inside preconfig . x-wait={() => notes.loading} bindings.wait(fn) , inside preconfig . x-html={() => preview} bindings.html(fn) . {open && } bindings.when(fn, render) . {open ? : } bindings.ternary(fn, a, b) . {notes.map((note) => )} bindings.list(fn, render) . x-watch={() => …} bindings.watch(fn) , while the tag is being built. Attribute and class bindings ( class={() => …} , disabled={() => …} ) are not set up in bindings but with class.add and attr.add (see Appearance ).

title: bindings
heading: Members
text: Member What it does text(fn) , value(fn) Bind the element's text or value to the function's result. add(property, source, field?) Binds a property of the element or the component to a field of an object or to a function (see Binding a component property ). model(getter, setter) A two-way binding: the value is written to the element, and the user's input goes to setter . Works on input , select and textarea . display(fn) , wait(fn) display shows the component while the function is true ; wait holds the component without building it for as long as the function returns true (see x-wait ). html(fn) Binds the element's innerHTML ; the content must be trusted (see x-html ). when(fn, render) , ternary(fn, a, b) , switchCase(fn, cases, fallback?) Change the content based on a condition; nothing is rebuilt as long as the branch stays the same. list(fn, render) Turns an array into rows; rows are matched to the item object and moved when the order changes. loop is the same. method(fn) An expression whose result can be text or a component; this is what {() => …} in JSX becomes. watch(fn) A binding that writes nothing to the element: fn runs once right away, then again whenever the values it reads change (see A watcher tied to the component ). remove(binding) , clear() Stop and remove one binding, or every binding in the collection. watch , when , ternary , switchCase and method are not kept in the collection; they stop together with the component. items A copy of the bindings in the collection. The details of when , ternary , switchCase and list are on the Conditional Rendering and Lists page.

title: bindings
heading: An example
text: The info line of the note page shows when the note was edited, its address and its state. The edit time is live text; the address is written once because the note does not change. "Pinned", "Archived" and "Saved" are visibility bindings. The line also ties the browser tab's title to the note's title: bindings.watch writes nothing to the element, it only runs again when the title it reads changes, and it stops when the component is removed. saved comes from the parent as a live value: The note page places the line with <NoteMeta note={note} saved={() => this.state.saved} /> . The note page places the line with new NoteMeta({ note, saved: () => this.state.saved }) . The note page places the line with motifComponent(NoteMeta, { note, saved: () => this.state.saved }) .

title: bindings
heading: Binding a component property
text: add does not only write the value to the element. The names textContent , innerHTML , wait , display , visible , style and model do their own job; for any other name, the value is written to the first place found, in this order: If the name is value and the component has its own value property, to the component. If the element has a property with that name, to the element ( title , hidden , disabled , tabIndex , placeholder …). If the component has a property with that name, to the component: its setter is called or its field changes. Nothing is written for a name that is not found anywhere. A name that contains a dot is a path on the component and starts directly from the component; the special names and the element are not checked. bindings.add("options.locked", props.locked) writes the value to the locked field of the component's options object, and a setter along the path is called too. If a step of the path is missing or is not an object, nothing is written. This way a component can bind its own property to a function. A component that receives a prop as a function tracks the prop this way: if the data is reactive, the binding runs again on its own, and with plain data setState() or reState() makes the binding read it again. On the note page, the body of an archived note looks locked. The locked property of the NoteBody component follows the function passed as a prop; in onConfigured , the component binds the prop to its own setter with bindings.add("locked", props.locked) . The prop can also be given as a plain value, in which case it is written once: A function component has no property of its own; bindings.watch on the root element does the same tracking. watch also runs again with setState() and reState() . The note page places the body with <NoteBody note={note} locked={() => note.archived} /> . The note page places the body with new NoteBody({ note, locked: () => note.archived }) . The note page places the body with motifComponent(NoteBody, { note, locked: () => note.archived }) . If the note is a reactive object, archiving locks the body on its own. If the note is a plain object, the page calls its own reState() after changing the archived field; the call goes down to the children and the locked binding is read again. The limits of this path: A name that also exists on the element does not reach the component. A component property named title , hidden or disabled cannot be bound; the value is written to the element's property of the same name. A binding does not call a method; it writes the value in place of the method, so a binding set up on a method name breaks the method. If a method has to run whenever the value changes, call the method from bindings.watch , or define the property as a setter. Before writing, a binding calls a value that is a function, and if the result is again a function, it calls that too. A property whose value is itself a function (a formatter, a comparison) is not given through a binding; assign the function to the property directly. A value written from code to a bound property does not last: on the next run (a reactive change, setState() , reState() ) the binding writes its own value back. To leave the value to your code, first stop the binding with bindings.remove(binding) ; add returns the binding.
