title: bindings
heading: The lifetime of a binding
text: A binding set up with add , text , value , model , display , wait , html or list becomes active when the component is built if it is not built yet, and right away if it is. watch , when , ternary , switchCase and method run once the moment they are called, then again whenever the values they read change. Bindings belong to the component: when the component is disposed they all stop, and there is no need to remove them separately. What happens to the bindings of a hidden component is described in Visibility . To stop a binding before the component's lifetime ends, use bindings.remove(binding) ; add , model , display , wait , html and list return the binding. For tracking that is not tied to a component there is the core's effect function (see effect ); releasing it is up to you. Inside a component, use bindings.watch .

title: bindings
heading: Next step
text: To reach the application and services from a component, go on to State, Context and Services .

title: State, Context and Services
text: A component's state flags, its reactive state and `setState`; reaching the application (`context`) and services; `build` and `dispose`.

title: State, Context and Services
heading: State flags
text: A component reports where it is in its lifecycle through flags. MotifJS manages the flags; your code reads them and does not write them. Flag When it is true isInitialized Once the constructor has finished. isConfigured Once the configuration phase has passed: in the constructor for a plain Component , at the start of the build for a class component. isBuilt Once the component is built ( build() ). isVisible While it is visible. It turns false with motif.hide() . isWait While the component is waiting: while an x-wait or bindings.wait condition holds, and while an x-display condition is false . A waiting component is not built. isDisposed Once it has been disposed. From then on the component's methods do nothing. x-display and motif.hide() touch different flags: a component whose x-display condition is false is isWait and may not be built; a component hidden with motif.hide() is built, only its isVisible is false (see Visibility ).

title: State, Context and Services
heading: A component's state
text: A component's changing data is kept in a reactive object: a field in a class ( state = reactive({ … }) ), a local variable in a function component, and the data field in Options. Bindings that read this object update on their own when the object changes (see State in a component ). this.useModel(model) is the same as reactive(model) . If data that is not reactive has changed, the bindings do not notice it on their own. In that case you make the bindings read again by hand: setState() runs the children's bindings first, then the component's own. reState() runs the component's own bindings first, then its children's. Neither one rebuilds the component: view() is not called again and the childs slot does not change; only the bindings read their values again.

title: State, Context and Services
heading: Context ( context ) — reaching the application
text: Every component reaches the application through context by climbing its parent chain ( this.context in a class and in Options, and in a function component the context of the root component ); a component that has no parent yet (in the constructor, in onInitializing ) reaches the running application as well. context is a view of the running Application tied to the component, and its members are the application's: navigate , on , fire , onRouterChanged … The on and onRouterChanged subscriptions opened through context are tied to the component's lifetime and are removed on their own when the component is disposed. That does not hold for onLifecycle ; tie the returned cancel function to the component with its motif.setDisposable(off) ( this.motif in a class and in Options, the root component's motif in a function component). For application events, see Events . A function component has no this . The same work is done through the context of the root, or of the component a hook receives ( sender.context ), or with useNavigation() ; useNavigation().navigate(address) navigates the same way as context.navigate .

title: State, Context and Services
heading: Reaching services
text: Services registered with DI are reached in two ways. getService exists on every component: this.getService(T) in class and Options components, and in a function component sender.getService(T) through the sender that a hook written on the root (for example onConfig ) receives. FromService(T) works anywhere, the body of a function component included. For a singleton service both give the same instance; for a scoped service getService is tied to the component's own provider, while FromService resolves from the application's current provider (see Dependency Injection ). The header of the notes list shows the folder's name and the number of notes; the "New note" button creates a note through the service and takes the application to it: The notes list places the header with <NotesHead folder={this.folder} /> . The notes list places the header with new NotesHead({ folder: this.folder }) . The notes list places the header with motifComponent(NotesHead, { folder: this.folder }) .

title: State, Context and Services
heading: build and dispose
text: You do not need to build a component by hand: it is built when it is added to a built parent, together with a parent that is not built yet, or when it is made the root with app.run (see Creation and building ). build() runs once; on a component that is built, waiting or disposed it does nothing. dispose() takes the component out of the tree and disposes it together with its subtree, playing the leave transition first if there is one. It returns a promise that resolves when it is finished; a second call during a disposal that is still running gives the same promise. The way to remove a parent's child is controls.remove(child) , which disposes it as well. A disposed component's bindings, motif.on listeners, context subscriptions and setDisposable registrations are released on their own. To avoid using the result of a promise that arrives after disposal, there are using and doWork .

title: State, Context and Services
heading: Next step
text: To drop an async result that arrives after disposal, go on to Async Results with using .

title: Async Results with using
text: When a component asks the server for data, there is no telling when the response will arrive, and by then the component may have been disposed. A disposed component's bindings stop, and the fields of a component whose dispose() was called are cleared as well (see What is released on its own ). Code that writes a late response to that component shows nothing, and if the field has been cleared it throws a TypeError . using(promise, onfulfilled?, onrejected?) passes the promise's result to the handlers only if the component is still alive; if the component has been disposed, it drops the result.

title: Async Results with using
heading: Call form
text: Parameter What it takes promise A Promise , or any object with a then method. onfulfilled(value) Called when the promise resolves, if the component is alive. onrejected(reason) Called when the promise is rejected, if the component is alive. If the component has been disposed, neither handler is called; both the result and the rejection are dropped. If onrejected is not given, a rejection is swallowed quietly: it neither goes to errorHandler nor shows up as an unhandled promise rejection. If you want to see the error, write onrejected . using returns nothing. If you need to wait for the result, chain it or hand it back to the caller, use doWork . The value a handler returns is not used. If a handler throws, or the promise of an async handler is rejected, the error is reported to errorHandler with the code MJX129 , and the original error is in cause (see Error Handling ). The value's type comes from the promise: for a promise that gives Promise<SharedNote[]> , the parameter of onfulfilled is SharedNote[] . With a promise that returns any , such as r.json() , the type is lost; supply it with as Promise<SharedNote[]> as in the example below, or by writing a type on the parameter. Handlers can also be written with a body; they do not have to return a value.

title: Async Results with using
heading: An example
text: The "shared with me" section in the sidebar asks the server for the list while it is being built. When the response arrives the list fills in, and if the request fails a warning appears. If the user moves to another page before the response arrives and the section is disposed, neither handler runs: The request starts in onConfigured : the component's settings are ready, and the element does not need to be in the document. using is a method of the component and is called as this.using(…) . A function component has no this ; using is a method of the returned root. The body builds the root, ties the request to it with section.using(…) and returns the root. The body runs once, while the component is being built, so the request goes out once as well. The sidebar places the section with <SharedNotes /> . The sidebar places the section with new SharedNotes() . The sidebar places the section with motifComponent(SharedNotes) .

title: Async Results with using
heading: How it differs from doWork
text: using finishes the result in the handlers it is given; doWork hands the result back as a promise. All the details below follow from that difference: using doWork Returns Nothing; the work ends in the handlers given in the call. A promise; you add then , catch , finally , and it can be returned to the caller. Incoming value onfulfilled receives the value itself; no check is needed. then receives either the value or MJX108 ; an instanceof Error check is needed before using the value. After disposal No handler runs. then receives MJX108 , catch does not run, finally runs. Rejection while the component is alive Goes to onrejected ; without it, it is swallowed quietly. Goes to catch ; without a catch it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. An error thrown by a handler Reported to errorHandler with MJX129 . Goes to the next catch in the chain; without one it becomes an unhandled promise rejection.

title: Async Results with using
heading: Which one when
text: using is enough when: The result is only written to this component's state: loading a list on startup, refreshing in the background, fetching the content of a preview. Nobody outside the component needs to know when the work is done. One handler for success and one for failure are enough. Deliberately ignoring an error is also done by leaving onrejected out. doWork is needed when: Another piece of work follows the first; for example saving the note and then reloading the list. You wait for several requests to finish together: doWork(Promise.all([…])) . The method that starts the work is going to return the promise, so a parent component, a keyboard shortcut or a test can wait for the work to finish. You need finally , or an error carried along the chain.

title: Async Results with using
heading: When the check happens
text: using checks whether the component is alive at the moment the result arrives, through the isDisposed flag. This flag becomes true when disposal finishes, not at the moment dispose() is called. A result that arrives while disposal is in progress, such as the result of a promise that resolved just before dispose() , is still handled; nothing changes on screen, because the component's bindings have already stopped by then. A component that is hidden ( motif.hide() , x-display ), detached from the tree ( controls.detach ) or moved somewhere else does not count as disposed, and its result is handled.

title: Async Results with using
heading: The request keeps running
text: using does not stop the promise: even when the component is disposed, the request to the server keeps going and only its result is dropped. If the request has to stop too, set up an AbortController , pass its signal to fetch , and tie the abort() call to the component's lifetime with motif.setDisposable(() => controller.abort()) (see Resources tied by hand ). The setDisposable handler runs after isDisposed has become true . So using drops the cancelled request's AbortError rejection as well, and onrejected is not called. In the same situation doWork gives MJX108 , with the AbortError in its cause .

title: Async Results with using
heading: Next step
text: For work that waits for the result or chains it, go on to Async Results with doWork .

title: Async Results with doWork
text: doWork(promise) ties the given promise to the component's lifetime and returns a new promise. While the component is alive, this promise behaves like the one you gave it: the value goes to then and a rejection goes to catch . After the component is disposed the promise is not rejected; in place of the value or the rejection, a MotifError with the code MJX108 arrives. The difference from using is that it returns a promise: you can chain the result, add catch and finally , and hand it back to the caller.

title: Async Results with doWork
heading: The returned promise
text: The given promise If the component is alive If the component has been disposed resolves then receives the value. then receives a MotifError ( MJX108 ). is rejected catch receives the reason. then receives a MotifError ( MJX108 ), with the rejection in that error's cause ; catch does not run. MJX108 is a return value: it is not reported to errorHandler and not written to the console. Write an instanceof Error check before using the value; if the check holds, the component is gone and then returns without doing anything. finally runs in both cases. Code inside it that touches a field of the component writes to a cleared field if the component has been disposed; put that kind of work in then and catch . An error thrown inside then goes to the next catch in the chain; that is how promises normally behave. Any object with a then method can be given. Whether the component is alive is checked with isDisposed at the moment the result arrives; the flag becomes true when disposal finishes (see When the check happens ). The returned promise's type is Promise<T | MotifError> . After an instanceof Error (or instanceof MotifError ) check the value narrows to T ; using it without the check does not compile.

title: Async Results with doWork
heading: An example
text: The "Share" button on the note page asks the server for a share link. While the request is running the button is disabled; when the link arrives it becomes visible, and if the request fails a warning appears. If the user leaves the page before the response arrives, then receives MJX108 and returns without writing anything, and catch does not run: share() is a method of the component, and so is doWork , called as this.doWork(…) . A function component has no this ; doWork is a method of the returned root. share uses the root under the name box ; by the time the button is clicked, the root has long been built. The note page places the button with the open note: <ShareButton note={note} /> . The note page places the button with the open note: new ShareButton({ note }) . The note page places the button with the open note: motifComponent(ShareButton, { note }) .

title: Async Results with doWork
heading: How it differs from using
text: doWork hands the result back as a promise; using finishes the result in the handlers it is given and returns nothing. All the details below follow from that difference: doWork using Returns A promise; you add then , catch , finally , and it can be returned to the caller. Nothing; the work ends in the handlers given in the call. Incoming value then receives either the value or MJX108 ; an instanceof Error check is needed before using the value. onfulfilled receives the value itself; no check is needed. After disposal then receives MJX108 , catch does not run, finally runs. No handler runs. Rejection while the component is alive Goes to catch ; without a catch it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Goes to onrejected ; without it, it is swallowed quietly. An error thrown by a handler Goes to the next catch in the chain; without one it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Reported to errorHandler with MJX129 .

title: Async Results with doWork
heading: Which one when
text: Pick doWork when: Another piece of work follows the first; for example saving the note and then reloading the list. then starts the second request with doWork again and returns it; if MJX108 arrives at the first step, then returns early through the instanceof Error check and the second request never goes out. A single catch at the end of the chain catches the rejection of both steps. You wait for several requests to finish together: doWork(Promise.all([…])) gives the results as an array; if the component has been disposed, a single MJX108 arrives. The method that starts the work is going to return the promise, so a parent component, a keyboard shortcut or a test can wait for the work to finish. You need finally , or an error carried along the chain. finally runs after the component is disposed as well. If the result is only written to this component's state and nobody waits for the work to end, using is shorter: no instanceof Error check or catch is needed, and an error thrown by a handler goes to errorHandler on its own. doWork does not stop the request either; to cancel the request when the component is disposed, see The request keeps running .

title: Async Results with doWork
heading: Next step
text: For the details of writing a component's view, go on to JSX and Templates .

title: JSX and Templates
text: In MotifJS, JSX does not produce a virtual tree at run time. @motifx/compiler turns every JSX element into a live component object (a motifComponent call), and an expression inside curly braces becomes either a prop of that component or a call made on it ( attr.add , class.add , style , motif.on , bindings.* , controls.add ). Whether a live binding is set up depends on the form of the expression: in child position {note.title} and {() => …} set up a binding, while a plain call such as {fmt(note.updatedAt)} is evaluated once (see Text and reactive expressions ). This page covers what you can write inside JSX and which call each form comes down to. If Imperative is selected in the code choices, the examples show the same thing written without JSX (see Views without JSX ). The examples come from the notes application in the starter template. Note , Folder , FOLDERS and NotesService are in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page; note stands for the note in the list or the one that is open. In the examples, this.notes is this service and this.state is the component's reactive state. In the examples, notes is the service obtained with FromService , and state is the local state the component sets up with reactive .

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Every element is a component
text:
The compiler does not produce HTML. Every element becomes a component object through a motifComponent ( _mc ) call, and the tree is built by adding these objects to each other's controls collections in code. The placeholder of the empty folder page ( Components ): In the function component, notes is the service obtained with FromService and state is the local state set up with reactive ; folder() , visible() , create , archive and remove are local functions inside the component function. The JSX compiles to the following code, and the form without JSX is a readable version of it: What follows from this: The
, the

, the

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Elements and nesting
text: Standard HTML tags are written in lower case and components in upper case. If a component tag is a class it is built with new , if it is a function it is called, and if it is an Options API object it is turned into a component (see Creating Components ). Without JSX all three are built with motifComponent(MyComponent, props) , and the text and elements written inside the tag go into the childs array. The folder group in the sidebar:

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Fragment
text: To return several elements side by side, use a fragment. A fragment is a component without an element: in the DOM it sits between opening and closing comment markers ( <!--[--> … <!--]--> ), and no attributes or events can be written on the <> tag. The counterpart of <>…</> without JSX is motifFragment , which is also what the compiler produces. The note page returns the three buttons in its toolbar as a fragment: The same fragment can also be written as the value of a branch or a slot: motifFragment({ initializeComponent: (f) => f.controls.add(a, b) }) . The view() of an Options API component can return an array as well (see Options API components ). The note page itself declares no element, so it is a fragment too; the content returned by view() sits between its markers (see Root element ).

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Text and reactive expressions
text: Expressions are written inside curly braces {...} . The form of the expression decides whether it is reactive. The call each form comes down to, and its counterpart without JSX: Form Behaviour Without JSX {"Notes"} Static; written once. motifComponent("text", (node) => node.setText("Notes")) {count} (a local variable) A guarded getter: if it holds a string or number, it is written once; if it holds a function, it is called and stays live; if it holds a component (or an array of components), it is placed in controls ; null / undefined becomes empty text. Depending on the value's type, node.setText(String(count)) , span.bindings.text(fn) or controls.add(component) {fmt(note.updatedAt)} A plain call; evaluated once, during setup. node.setText(fmt(note.updatedAt)) {note.title} A one-way binding to that field; only that field is tracked. node.bindings.add("textContent", note, "title") {() => note.title.trim() \|\| "Untitled"} A getter; every reactive field read inside it is tracked, and it is recomputed when one of them changes. span.bindings.text(() => note.title.trim() \|\| "Untitled") {`${note.title} · ${fmt(note.updatedAt)}`} A template string is wrapped in a getter; it is live. span.bindings.text(() => `${note.title} · ${fmt(note.updatedAt)}`) {note.title ?? "Untitled"} , {a \|\| b} Live; the left side if it is there ( ?? : not null/undefined, \|\| : truthy), otherwise the right side. The right side can be JSX too. span.bindings.text(() => note.title ?? "Untitled") {this.badge(note)} (a member call) If the result is a component, a Frame slot (evaluated again on a reactive change); if it is a string, live text. li.bindings.method(() => this.badge(note)) {cond && <X/>} , {cond ? <A/> : <B/>} , {items.map(…)} Condition and list bindings; see Conditional Rendering and Lists . bindings.when , bindings.ternary , bindings.list {this.childs} , {props.childs} , {[a, b]} , {instance} Places component instances. controls.add(...)

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Fixed text
text: Literal text is written once. So is a plain local variable ( {count} , when count is a number): it contains no reactive read, so it is not updated.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: A reactive model field
text: If you write a field of a reactive object directly, a one-way binding is set up to that field. When the field changes, only that text node is updated:

title: JSX and Templates
heading: A reactive expression with a getter
text: To keep a computed value live, put the expression in an arrow function; the reactive reads inside the function are tracked, and the text is recomputed when one of them changes. The title and first line of a note row: Rule: If you want an expression's value to change over time and show up in the DOM, write either a reactive field directly ( note.title ) or a getter ( () => … ). With a path written directly, only the last field is tracked and the object in front of it is read once, during setup: {state.note.title} updates when that note's title changes, but when state.note is switched to another note it stays on the old one. To track the whole path, write a getter ( {() => state.note?.title} ); a path containing ?. ( {state.note?.title} ) is wrapped in a getter too and stays live. A plain local variable stays static: {label} written with const label = state.items.length + " notes" does not change even when a new note is added, while {() => state.items.length + " notes"} does.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Attributes
text: Attributes take a value or a function that returns a value. A function is a live binding, and a literal value is written once. In JSX the compiler wraps member access ( note.pinned ), operations ( !state.confirming , a + b ), template strings and ?. chains in a getter on its own, so these stay live as well (details below). From the note page: value , checked and selected are property bindings ( bindings.add("value", getter) ); the others are written with attr.add . On a plain DOM tag, literal values go to attr.add as they are: numbers, negative numbers, true / false and null (arrays and new X() also go through as values; for element methods they become arguments). false , null and undefined do not write the attribute (and remove it if present); true and the valueless form write the attribute with an empty value ( "" ); numbers are turned into strings: JSX On the element <button disabled={false} /> no disabled <button disabled /> , <li hidden={true} /> disabled="" , hidden="" <li tabindex={0} /> tabindex="0" <li title={null} /> no title On aria-* and data-* attributes a boolean value is written as text: aria-selected={false} → aria-selected="false" , data-pinned={true} → data-pinned="true" ; null / undefined still remove the attribute. An object or array value is turned into text as a single attribute value ( data-ids={[1, 2]} → data-ids="1,2" ). An expression that reads a variable ( a + b , !state.confirming , note.title ) is wrapped in a getter and stays live: aria-expanded={!state.confirming} updates when confirming changes. A lone variable ( attr={v} ) is passed as it is, and it is live only if it holds a function. A plain function call ( data-updated={fmt(note.updatedAt)} ) is evaluated once; to keep it live, write () => fmt(note.updatedAt) . Security: attributes written on a tag and attr.add values are written without filtering. If a value coming from the user is bound to a URL attribute such as href , src , action or formaction , a value starting with javascript: runs code on click. Before binding such values, check them against the allowed schemes ( https: , mailto: , a relative address) and turn anything that does not fit into # . attr.add({ innerHTML }) also writes HTML as it is, like x-html . Only spread skips innerHTML , srcdoc and javascript: URLs that come from outside on its own.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Element methods
text: On a plain DOM tag, a prop whose name is one of the element methods in the table below does not write an attribute; it calls that method. Method names that are not in the table ( setCustomValidity , stepUp …) are not called and are written as plain attributes. If the value is a getter (or a reactive field), it is applied again on every change, and the call is made one microtask later. Without JSX, the same name is given to attr.add , and the runtime is what turns it into a call. The delete confirmation opens and closes in a dialog , and when the confirmation opens, focus moves to the "Delete" button: Prop true false Any other value focus focus() blur() an object → focus(object) , anything else → focus() show , showModal calls it close() calls it without arguments on a truthy value showPopover calls it hidePopover() calls it without arguments on a truthy value togglePopover togglePopover(true) togglePopover(false) togglePopover() on a truthy value play play() pause() truthy → play() , falsy → pause() select select() clears the selection truthy → select() , falsy → clears the selection requestFullscreen , requestPointerLock calls it exits truthy → calls it, falsy → exits close , hidePopover , requestSubmit , checkValidity , reportValidity , showPicker , load calls it — method(value) on a truthy value — e.g. close('cancel') , requestSubmit(button) blur , click , pause , submit , reset , exitFullscreen , exitPointerLock , requestPictureInPicture , exitPictureInPicture calls it — calls it without arguments on a truthy value scrollIntoView scrollIntoView() scrollIntoView(false) null / undefined → scrollIntoView() , anything else scrollIntoView(value) scrollTo , scrollBy — — only an object or an array: method(value) setSelectionRange , setRangeText , setPointerCapture , releasePointerCapture , fastSeek method(true) — method(value) for anything except null / undefined An array value is spread into arguments ( setSelectionRange={[0, 5]} → setSelectionRange(0, 5) ), and an object value is passed as a single argument ( scrollTo={{ top: 0 }} , focus={{ preventScroll: true }} ); in neither case is an attribute written. focus calls blur() only for exactly false ; undefined , null , 0 and '' mean focus() too, so if you are going to write focus={() => state.confirming} , start the field at false . exitFullscreen , exitPointerLock and exitPictureInPicture are called on document . If the element does not have that method, the value is written as a plain attribute. On a component tag ( <NoteFields focus={…}/> ) these names are ordinary props.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Spread — `
text: An object spread onto a plain DOM element is applied as if its attributes had been written directly. The counterpart without JSX is to pass the object as the second argument of motifComponent ; the runtime is what applies the DOM props. TextField spreads everything it receives onto the input : The note page builds its title field with it: Key Applied as class / className class.add — combined with a class written directly style style() — a string, an object or a getter value / checked / selected a property binding ( bindings.add ) on* ( onclick , onClick , oninput:once ) a DOM event every other key ( id , title , aria-* , data-* , viewBox …) an attribute ( attr.add ) innerHTML / srcdoc not written (an MJX124 warning in development mode) href / src / action / formaction / xlink:href whose value starts with javascript: not written; for a getter, the current value is removed (an MJX125 warning in development mode) These two paths are closed because a spread object often carries data that comes from outside. For HTML you trust, use x-html or a srcdoc written directly on the tag ( <iframe srcdoc={html}> ), and for a javascript: link written on purpose, an attribute written directly on the tag ( <a href="javascript:void 0"> ); these are not filtered. Getter ( () => … ) values are live. Functions that expect a parameter ( renderItem: (x) => … ) do not count as attributes and are skipped. ref , key , options , transition , initializeComponent , childs , x-* and the lifecycle props go to the framework. Order: the spread is applied in the constructor, and the attributes written directly on the tag in the initializeComponent the compiler produces, so for the same attribute the one written directly wins ( <input {...p} id="title"/> ), while class is merged. This holds even if the value in the spread is a getter: the direct form becomes the owner of that attribute, the getter does not write to that attribute again, and the spread's other getters stay live. The same rule applies to value , checked and selected , and to the keys of style : a directly written style={{ color: "blue" }} takes over only the color key of the spread's style getter, and the getter's other keys stay live; a directly written style="…" string takes over the whole attribute. On a component tag, a known DOM event name ( oninput , onclick ) is attached to the component's element as a listener and never enters props . TextField above is a function, so the tag's oninput is attached to the input it returns. If a class without an element of its own writes <input {...this.props} /> in view() , props has no oninput ; a class with an element, and an Options component whose el is a tag name ( el: "input" ) or a ready DOM node, take only the common attributes and events below from the tag, and the others such as value stay in this.props . Do not spread plain values that do not belong to an element ( items: [...] ) onto a DOM element ; they are written as attributes.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: On a component tag: common attributes fall through to the component's element (attribute fallthrough)
text: When you write <CountBadge class="nav__count" id="count-notes" count={…}/> , only the common attributes — class / className (merged with the component's own class), style , id , tabindex , role , aria-* , data-* — are applied automatically to the component's own element , and getters are live. The same attribute written by the component itself in its own onConfigured / initializeComponent / view wins (the fallthrough happens in the constructor, before those). Data and callback props ( count , note , title , onSave , disabled …) are not written to the element — title is left off the list on purpose, because it is a common data prop name in components. All props, the ones that fall through included, stay readable in the component's props ( this.props in a class, the parameter in a function, the factory's parameter in Options). In TypeScript these attributes and the DOM event props are accepted on every component tag, also on a component whose constructor takes its own prop type; if the component defines a prop with the same name, its own type is used. The folder link in the sidebar shows the number of notes in a small badge: The result is the same in all three forms: <span class="nav__count badge" id="count-notes"> ( nav__count from the tag is added in the constructor, and the component's own badge during setup). In the class component the element comes from the generic ( Component<HTMLSpanElement> ), in the function from the returned root, and in Options from el . If the root of the function component is <span {...props}/> , the same value is not applied a second time. On a component without an element (a fragment) these attributes are quietly ignored, while DOM events listen on the top-level elements of the content (see Root element ).

title: JSX and Templates
heading: class and className
text: Both are supported. The value can be a string, an array, an object or a getter function. The classes of a note row: The first line is a fixed class, the second is a getter, and the template string in the third is wrapped in a getter and stays live. In an object the key is the class name and the value is the condition: if it is truthy the class is added, otherwise it is removed. On a plain DOM tag, constants such as true / false are applied once, and every other value is wrapped in a getter and is live. An object can also be written inside an array; each item in the array is handled as if it had been written on its own. In an object passed to class.add , on the other hand, a value that is not a function is read once, at the time of the call. The same is true on a component tag: there the compiler wraps only the ternary, and the class value is applied to the component's element with class.add , so the condition in <CountBadge class={{ empty: count === 0 }} /> , a template string and class={note.cls} are evaluated once, while the tag is being built. Without JSX and on a component tag, you pass a live condition as a function yourself ( { active: () => open() } , class={() => …} ): After setup, classes are managed with the component's class helper: class.add , class.remove , class.has ( this.class in a class and in Options, the class of the root component in a function component) (see Appearance ).

title: JSX and Templates
heading: style
text: style takes a string, an object or a getter: A getter is live : it is applied again when its dependencies change, and keys that are missing from the getter's new result are cleared (going from {color} to {opacity} removes color ). If the getter returns a string, cssText changes as a whole (the other inline styles on that element go too). x-style={...} is exactly the same as style . style(fn) keeps a single watcher; calling it again stops the previous one. Keys written with an object after the getter ( style({ color: "blue" }) ) are taken away from the getter, which does not write to them again; a string written after the getter stops the getter. CSS variables starting with -- are written in an object or a getter like any other key ( style={{ "--accent": note.color }} ); a variable whose value is null or an empty string is removed.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Placing ready components as children
text:
You can collect pieces of JSX in a variable and put it in child position; if the value is a component or an array of components, it is placed in controls without being turned into text. If the value is not a component (a string, a number…), the usual reactive text binding is set up, so you do not need to say separately whether a prop is a component or data . Without JSX you make this distinction yourself: a component is placed with controls.add , and text with a "text" component. JSX passed to a prop can also be written without curly braces: toolbar=
…
compiles the same as toolbar={
…
} . Pane , the frame shared by the pages, takes a toolbar component at the top and a title text under it:

title: JSX and Templates
heading: If the template will change later, write a getter
text:
The placement decision is made at setup time and only once : if the prop holds a component while it is being set up, it is placed, and the DOM is not updated even if it changes later (the placed component's own bindings are live as usual). Props are a plain object taken once, while the tag is being built: a plain expression such as toolbar={toolbar} does not carry a template assigned later to the child, and the getter {() => props.toolbar} does not track it either, because there is no reactive read inside it. If the template starts out null and arrives later, or is swapped while running, the parent passes it with a ternary or a getter ( toolbar={state.confirming ?
…
: null} ; a ternary in a prop is always wrapped in a getter). The child declares the prop as Bind and reads it with read() inside a getter; this sets up a slot ( Frame ) and places the getter's current result on every change: {() => props.toolbar} written without read() does not track the getter prop: it places only the first template, and if the template starts out null it shows nothing. If a component ends up in a text binding later even though you did not write a getter, the framework writes nothing to the DOM, and in development mode it suggests the getter form with an MJX204 warning.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Raw HTML — x-html
text: To set an element's innerHTML reactively, use x-html ; its counterpart without JSX is bindings.html . renderMarkdown in the example is a function from a Markdown library that sanitizes its output: Security: x-html injects HTML that has not been escaped. Use it only with content you trust, or with a converter that sanitizes its output.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Events
text: on... props are attached to DOM events; the counterpart without JSX is motif.on . A handler is written with the (sender, event) signature or with just (event) ; MotifJS looks at the number of parameters: An error thrown by a handler (including a rejected promise in an async handler) is reported to errorHandler with the code MJX123 . A ternary written in a handler position ( onclick={a ? b : c} ) does not work; see Ternaries in attributes . Event names are written in lower case ( onclick , onchange , oninput ). Modifiers ( :once , :prevent , :stop and so on) are supported; a JSX attribute name can take only one : , so on a tag you write one modifier per attribute, while motif.on("click:once:prevent", fn) chains them — see Events for details. The on:name / on-name / on_name spelling attaches the handler as it is to the tag's component with motif.on("name", fn) (only the prefix is dropped: on-note-saved → note-saved ). It is used for DOM events the compiler does not recognize ( mouseenter ) and for custom events ( motif.trigger ), and the same rule about the number of parameters applies: A handler given with on: on a component tag is attached to the component's element; in a function component that is the returned root (the <a> in NoteRow ).

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Special x- attributes
text: Helper props the compiler recognizes that are not DOM attributes, and the calls they come down to: Attribute What it does Without JSX x-ref={(s) => ...} / x-ref={this.field} / x-ref={field} Captures the tag's component instance; the same as the short ref , and both forms work on every tag. If ref and x-ref are both written on the same tag, both run in source order — see Element and Appearance for details. ref: (s) => … in the object form x-key={...} The same as key ( indexkey is accepted too); see Item identity with key . indexkey: () => … x-text={() => text} Sets the element's whole textContent reactively; if the element has other children, it removes them from the DOM on the first change. For live text that sits next to its siblings, write {() => text} in child position. bindings.text(fn) x-html={() => html} Sets innerHTML reactively. bindings.html(fn) x-value={() => value} Sets the element's value property one-way, reactively; for both directions use x-model . bindings.value(fn) x-model={() => state.query} A two-way binding; see Forms for details. bindings.model(() => state.query, (v) => (state.query = v)) x-watch={() => ...} Sets up a watcher tied to the tag's component: reactive reads inside the function are tracked and it runs again on change; it stops when the component is disposed. It writes nothing to the DOM. bindings.watch(fn) x-wait={() => bool} Holds/hides the component while the condition is true . The primary way to render conditionally. preconfig: (s) => s.bindings.wait(fn) x-display={() => bool} The reverse of x-wait : shows while the condition is true and hides while it is false . preconfig: (s) => s.bindings.display(fn) x-chunk / x-chunk={50} Builds the element's children in slices: the first 100 children added together (the first 50 if a number is given) are built right away, and the rest leave a marker and are built over the following frames. The framework decides how many to build in a frame by looking at the frame time; if a number is given, at least that many are built in each frame. {list.map(...)} rows under it are created when their turn comes. See Large lists . options: { chunk: true } / options: { chunk: 50 } x-style={...} The same as style (a getter is live). style(...) x-building , x-built , x-config , x-configured , x-mounted , x-activated , x-deactivated , x-disposing , x-disposed , x-initializing , x-initialized , x-visibilitychanged Lifecycle hooks (in prop form; the x: spelling works too). Several spellings on the same tag, such as onBuilt and x-built , are combined, and all of them run in source order. onBuilt: (s, e) => … in the object form, or s.motif.on("x:built", …) during setup x-text , x-html , x-value , x-model and x-watch want a getter, a method reference or an object; if a plain string or boolean is given, compilation stops with MJX011 . In every directive, x-wait and x-display included, a variable or member that holds a function is called as a getter: x-display={isAuthor} and x-wait={this.isLoading} (called with this ) work the same as x-display={() => isAuthor()} . x-chunk is the exception: it is written without a value or takes a number ( x-chunk , x-chunk={50} , x-chunk={this.minRows} ); if a string, an object or an arrow function is given, compilation stops with MJX012 . If a variable or member holding a function is given, the function is called once while the component is being built and the returned value is used; if the value changes later, that is not tracked. options: { chunk } follows the same rule. An x- name the compiler does not recognize gives an MJX007 warning; x-reload , x-bind , x-effect , x-focus , x-interrupt , x-to , x-list and x-loop are not supported and stop compilation with MJX006 (see Compile errors ). x-wait and x-display are evaluated before the component is built, which is why without JSX they are written in preconfig , not in initializeComponent . The notes list holds the row box until the first note arrives, and the empty list paragraph is shown only when there are no visible rows: If the condition is true on the first evaluation ( false for x-display ), the component is never built , and its subtree does not enter the DOM either. When it opens later it is built once, and when it closes again the instance is kept. {condition && <X/>} , on the other hand, builds a new instance every time it opens and disposes it every time it closes; for a detailed comparison see Conditional Rendering and Lists .

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Ternaries in attributes
text: A ternary operator written in an attribute or a component prop is always wrapped lazily : when <Setting name="Theme" hint={settings.state.theme === "system" ? "Follows the system." : "Chosen by hand."} /> is compiled, the prop becomes hint: () => settings.state.theme === "system" ? … : … . This is a deliberate design decision: without the wrapping, the expression would be evaluated once during view() and frozen. The other half of it is that the component receiving the prop declares it as Bind<T> and reads it with read() ; the hint prop of Setting works like that (see Plain values and live values ). A component that uses a plainly typed prop directly breaks this contract and receives a function at run time. Other expressions in a component prop ( {p.a} , {f()} , {a && b} ) are not wrapped and are passed as the value taken while the tag is being built; on a plain DOM tag, {p.a} and {a && b} are wrapped in a getter and stay live, while {f()} is evaluated once (see Attributes ). Without JSX there is no wrapping; you pass a prop you want to be live as a getter yourself: motifComponent(Setting, { name: "Theme", hint: () => (… ? "Follows the system." : "Chosen by hand.") }) . A ternary in an event attribute is wrapped too, but nothing reads this getter: onclick={note.pinned ? undefined : () => notes.archive(note)} registers the arrow function as the listener; on click the chosen handler is returned but not called, and there is no compile warning or motif-lint finding either. The same holds for on:click , onclick:once and an event on a component tag. Write the condition inside the handler: onclick={() => { if (!note.pinned) notes.archive(note); }} .

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Compile-time warnings
text: @motifx/compiler reports a few forms that quietly do the wrong thing to the terminal during compilation. Warnings do not stop the build; they appear next to the code, with the file, the line and a code frame. For MJX004 , MJX017 and MJX018 the check treats these roots as reactive: this.state and this.props ; fields set up in a class, in a field initializer or in the constructor, with reactive , useModel , createSignal , createComputed or createLazyComputed ; module stores set up with these factories in the same file; and aliases taken from these inside a getter ( const rows = this.state.rows , const { rows } = this.state ). It does not recognize a store imported from another file, a store created inside a function or returned from one, an injected service, or the props of a function component; the compiler does not see the same pattern there. Inside a getter, callbacks passed to synchronous array methods such as map , forEach , filter , reduce , flatMap , some , every and find count as part of the getter; event handlers, setTimeout and then callbacks do not. Code What it catches What to write instead MJX001 Declaring a local variable and returning a condition inside a block-bodied arrow function with parameters in JSX child position. The compiler moves the condition out of the closure, the variable is not visible in the branches, and you get a ReferenceError . (In an arrow without parameters, local variables are kept.) Use an expression-bodied arrow, or move the logic into a named method. MJX002 A camelCase spelling of a DOM event name the compiler recognizes on a component tag ( onChange , onClick ). It looks like a callback prop but becomes a DOM listener on the component's element, and props.onChange stays undefined. Names the compiler does not recognize ( onmouseenter , onpointer… , ontouch… , onfocusin , onanimation… , ontransition… ) set up no listener on a component tag: the value is passed as an ordinary prop, and no warning appears. Pick a name that does not clash ( onValueChange , onConfirm ). For a deliberate DOM listener on a recognized event, write it in lower case: <Button onclick={…}> — this produces no warning. To listen to an unrecognized event on the component's element, use the on: spelling: <NoteRow on:mouseenter={…}> (see The on:name spelling ). In a component without an element (a fragment), the listener listens on the top-level elements of the content. MJX003 A list item built with .map() / .forEach() has no key . Rows are matched to the item object (to the value for primitive items), so key does not change how the DOM is reused. Give the item's root a stable key: key={note.id} ; it identifies the item and is checked for duplicates ( MJX202 ). For how rows are matched, see key and item identity . MJX004 Inside a reactive getter (a JSX getter, an attribute getter, a directive, effect , createComputed , bindings.* ), a reactive list is scanned with find / findIndex / findLast / some / every and a predicate of the form x.field === value : every run reads that field of every element up to the match and subscribes to it, so if n components carry this getter, every change means n² reads. The list must be rooted at this. or be a store set up in the same file with reactive / useModel /a signal; includes , filter , map and predicates without a field comparison do not warn. Take the element from a keyed map or from a computed calculated once; if the list is only needed at that moment, read it with untracked(() => list.find(...)) . See The trap of every row scanning the list . MJX007 An x- name the compiler does not recognize ( x-checked ). The value is passed as an on<name> prop ( onchecked ) and usually does nothing. Use one of the supported directives, or a plain prop/attribute. MJX015 In a class component, a member that overrides a ComponentBase method ( build , dispose , style , setText …) or accessor ( context , isWait …) ends on some path without reaching super.<name> : it never calls it, or calls it inside an early return , an if with one branch, a loop, a catch or a callback. On that path, the work MotifJS does in that method does not run (a component left empty, a page not torn down on navigation, a lost style). The check also runs in .ts / .js files without JSX, and the base class is followed across files. Rename the member, or call super.<name>(…) on every path. An early return on this.isBuilt / this.isDisposed / this.isWait in build , and on this.isDisposed in dispose , is exempt; the base method does nothing in that case either. See Names of class members . MJX016 A switch or return a ? b : c getter in JSX child position could not be turned into switchCase / ternary : a case label that is not a literal, a return or a statement producing JSX before the switch , a break that leaves the switch . The getter runs as written, as bindings.method ; branches are not kept, and the content is rebuilt on every change. Make the label a literal or move the condition into the branches; if keeping branches is not needed, the warning is for information. MJX017 A reactive getter writes a reactive value it reads: ++ / -- , a compound assignment such as += , or a plain assignment to a field the getter reads elsewhere ( {() => this.state.n++} , effect(() => { stats.runs++; }) ). A getter that writes what it reads triggers itself and is stopped at run time with MJX203 . Reactive roots: this.state , this.props , fields set up in a class with reactive / useModel /a signal, and module stores in the same file. A plain assignment to a field the getter does not read ( this.state.query = seed ), writing to a plain class field ( this.loadedId = id ), writes in event handlers ( onclick={() => …} ) and writes inside untracked(...) to a value the getter does not read with tracking elsewhere do not warn. Move the write into an event handler or a method; if it has to stay, put the read of that value inside untracked so the getter does not subscribe to it (the whole expression for x++ and compound assignment, or the read in the condition for a lock flag). MJX018 A reactive list is changed in place inside a reactive getter: sort / reverse always (they read and write the list: {() => this.state.items.sort(cmp)} ), and push / pop / shift / unshift / splice when the getter also reads that list (such as stats.log.length ). A getter that reads the list triggers itself. Working on a copy ( [...list].sort() , list.slice().sort() ), an effect(() => { log.push(x); }) that only writes, and event handlers do not warn. Sort a copy, or keep the sorted list in a field or a computed. To turn the warnings off, pass diagnostics: false to the Vite plugin:

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Compile errors
text: The forms below cannot be brought down to working code; the compiler stops the build and gives the error with the file, the line and a code frame. The code field of the error object is the code. Code What it catches What to write instead MJX006 An unsupported directive: x-reload , x-bind , x-effect , x-focus , x-interrupt , x-to , x-list , x-loop . x-wait / x-display for conditions, {items.map(i => <X key={i.id}/>)} for lists, effect(...) or x-watch for effects, and the focus={() => …} element method or ref for focus. MJX008 A function () { … } expression in child position. Write an arrow function: {() => …} . MJX009 A string or boolean value on a DOM event ( onclick="go()" ). Give a handler function: onclick={() => go()} . MJX010 A value that is not a function on a lifecycle hook ( onBuilt="x" ). Give a function, a list of functions or a reference to a function. MJX011 A value that cannot be turned into a getter on the x-text , x-html , x-value , x-model or x-watch directive ( x-text="plain" ). Give a getter or a reference: x-text={() => note.title} . MJX012 An object literal on the x-wait / x-display directive; a value that cannot be a number (a string, an object, an arrow function) on the x-chunk directive. Give an expression or a getter that returns a boolean; write x-chunk without a value or give it a number: x-chunk={50} . MJX013 A JSX form the compiler does not support: a namespaced tag name ( <svg:rect> ) or a spread in child position ( {...items} ). A lower-case name without a hyphen that is not an HTML tag ( <card> ) does not give this error; it resolves to the identifier of the same name in scope, and if there is no such identifier, the error arrives not at compile time but at run time, as a ReferenceError . Remove the namespace prefix ( <rect> ). Place a ready array of components with {items} , and build a list from data with {items.map(…)} .

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Type-aware checking: motif-lint (MJX005, MJX015)
text: The compiler cannot see prop types . A ternary in an attribute is always wrapped with () => … (see Ternaries in attributes ), so with <NoteRow folder={note.archived ? "archive" : "notes"}/> , if folder is declared as a plain Folder , the component receives a function at run time; TypeScript sees no problem either, because the type of the ternary is that union. A separate check that runs over the TypeScript program closes this gap: Code What it catches What to write instead MJX005 A ternary is written on a component prop, but the prop's declared type does not accept a function ( folder: Folder ). Declare the prop as Bind<T> in the component and read it with read() / toGetter() . If the value really is static, compute the ternary outside JSX and pass the variable. MJX015 The same rule as the compile warning (an override that does not reach super ). motif-lint resolves the base class with the TypeScript type checker and scans every file in the tsconfig, so files the Vite plugin does not see (tests, for example) are checked as well. See MJX015 above. The rule stays silent on DOM tags, on props typed as Bind<T> / any / unknown /a function, on the key / x-* / on:* names and on generic ( value: T ) props. If there are findings, the exit code is 1; you can put "lint:jsx": "motif-lint" in package.json and hook it into CI. If tsconfig cannot be read, the command stops with an MJX014 error.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: What did this expression compile to? — explain
text:
In MotifJS, JSX is not a view language but a short way of writing the binding API ( bindings.add , bindings.when , controls.add …), and the compiler is not a transformer but a lowering stage in the classic sense. Looking for a resemblance between the source and the output is pointless, but the question "what will happen when this runs" is not left to guesswork. explain , which works like a compiler's -S flag, prints for each JSX expression the real call it comes down to (taken from the generated code, not guessed), its reactivity class and its dependency surface: For this file: The listing: Reactivity classes: Class Meaning LIVE An effect is set up; the DOM is updated when the dependencies change. STATIC No binding is set up: literal values (string, number, negative number, boolean, null ), a valueless attribute, a prop whose value is JSX, fixed forms such as transition / options , and the element itself (

, ); the element is built once, and the expressions inside it appear on their own lines. ONCE The expression is evaluated once at setup and never read again ( attr={f(x)} , prop={object} ). With prop={object} the receiver gets the object itself: if it reads the fields of a reactive object inside a binding, it sees changes made in place, but it does not see the object being replaced by another one at the source. RECEIVER The expression is passed as a function; whether it is live depends on the receiving component's Bind contract. RUNTIME The value's type is known only at run time: live if it is a function, once otherwise ( attr={variable} ). To see the same listing on the development server, give explain to the Vite plugin; a string or a RegExp lists only the matching files, and the output code does not change: Programmatic use: import { explain } from '@motifx/compiler' → explain(source, fileName) returns a MotifExplanation[] ( site , shape , source , lowered , reactive , deps , note ).

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Item identity with key
text: Give list items a key ; rows are matched by the item object, not by key . The counterpart without JSX is indexkey . In development mode a duplicate key is reported with MJX202 . For details see Conditional Rendering and Lists :

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Transitions — the transition prop
text: To give a component an enter/leave animation, use the transition prop. If you pass a string, it becomes a CSS class transition whose class names are derived from that prefix; if you pass an object, you can specify custom class names. Without JSX it is a key of the object form: This applies the CSS classes fade-enter-from/active/to and fade-leave-from/active/to . For details and WAAPI (keyframe) based animation, see Styling and Animation . transition does not write an attribute on a plain DOM tag; it goes to the transition engine. The options prop is the same: hideStrategy and disableDisposal in <li options={{ hideStrategy: 'detach', disableDisposal: true }}/> are copied into that tag's motif.options , and no attribute is written to the DOM; without JSX, options is also a key of the object form.

title: JSX and Templates
heading: Next step
text: To write the same view without JSX, with component calls, go on to Views without JSX ; the details of reactive state are in Reactivity .

title: Views without JSX
text: The compiler turns every JSX element into a motifComponent(tag, setup) call, and the tree is built with sender.controls.add(...) . A project that does not use JSX ( .ts / .js ) writes the same calls by hand: the hand-written version of the code the compiler produces. The runtime, the bindings, the lifecycle and the rules are the same; only the way of writing changes. This page is for projects without JSX, for libraries that should not depend on the compiler, for views generated in code, and for reading compiled output. Which call each JSX form comes down to is given next to every example on the JSX and Templates page; here the calls themselves are explained. The examples are slices of the version without JSX of the notes application in the starter template: the sidebar ( MainLayout ), the notes list ( NotesLayout ), the list row ( NoteRow ) and the editor ( NotePage ). Note , Folder and NotesService are the ones in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page. In TypeScript the parameter of a setup function is written as ComponentBase ; motifComponent returns any , so you declare the types yourself (see Pitfalls ).

title: Views without JSX
heading: motifComponent(element, props?)
text: motifComponent("div", fn) : fn is the component's initializeComponent . It runs once while the component is being built ( build() ), just before the children are built, and never again; this is not bound, so use the parameter. motifComponent("div", { … }) : the object form. The framework keys are initializeComponent , preconfig , ref , childs , options ( isSvg , hideStrategy , disableDisposal ), transition , key / indexkey and the lifecycle hooks ( onConfig , onConfigured , onBuilt , onMounted , …). On a plain tag the other keys are applied like a spread: { type: "button", class: "row", onclick: fn, "aria-pressed": () => note.pinned } go to attributes, classes and events, and getters stay live. The compiler writes attributes with attr.add in the setup function, and that is also the readable choice when writing by hand. motifComponent(SomeClass, props) : new SomeClass(props) . The framework keys of the object form ( preconfig , initializeComponent , onMounted , childs , ref …) are applied to a class component too. motifComponent(functionPart, props) : the function is called with props , and the framework keys of the object form are applied to the root it returns, as with a class: ref , the common attributes ( class , id , style , role , aria-* , data-* ; see attribute fallthrough ), options , transition , key / indexkey , preconfig , initializeComponent , the lifecycle hooks and the x- keys. The hook and x- keys are not part of the props the function receives, nor of a class's this.props ; callback props such as onSave stay. motifComponent(instance) : returns a ready component instance as it is. motifComponent({ initializeComponent: (holder) => … }) (an object without a tag): a component without an element . In the DOM it sits between <!--[--> … <!--]--> markers, and its children land inside the parent. This is the holder the compiler uses for lists. new Component("div", { initializeComponent }) is the same as the string form; you can also build with new Component("div") and call controls.add later. motifFragment({ initializeComponent: (f) => f.controls.add(a, b) }) : a fragment for a branch or a slot with several roots; in the DOM there are only comment markers, and no attributes or events can be written (see Fragment ). Timing: on a plain tag the configuration phase ( preconfig , onConfig ) ends inside the motifComponent call, while the component is being created; onConfigured , initializeComponent and onBuilt run when the component is added to a built parent ( build() ), and onMounted when it is attached to the document. In a class component the configuration phase is postponed to the start of build() (see Lifecycle ). The third argument seen in the compiler output ( , 1 ) and the __childExpr and __isSvgElement keys are compiler markers; hand-written code does not write them and does not call motifCompiled / motifReport (see Reading the compiled output ).

title: Views without JSX
heading: new Component(element, props?)
text: The constructor's first argument decides the component's element, and the second is the props object: First argument Result A tag name: new Component("li", props) A new element with that tag is created. "text" produces a text node. For an SVG element, write options: { isSvg: true } in the props. A DOM node: new Component(node, props) The existing node becomes the component's element, and no new element is created. app.run("#app") wraps the #app element on the page this way. A props object, or nothing: new Component({ … }) No element is created, and the component's root is a comment node. In a subclass that declares static elementTag , an element with that tag is created. An array: new Component([title, body]) A component without an element. Each item in the array is turned into a component by the same rules and added as a child. A class or a function: new Component(NoteRow, props) A class is built with props and a function is called with props ; the new expression gives the returned component. The framework keys of the props are applied to the root the function returns, as with motifComponent (see the function part item above). If the function returns an Options object, the component is built from that object. A ready component: new Component(row) The same component is returned; no new one is created. How it differs from motifComponent : The second argument is read only as a props object. new Component("li", (li) => …) does not run the function; setup code goes under the initializeComponent key. motifComponent is the one that takes an Options object directly ( motifComponent({ el: "section", … }) ). new Component treats the object as props and you end up with a component without an element; it does recognize a function that returns an Options object, though. On a plain Component , the keys in the props object that are not framework keys are written to the element: class , style , events ( onclick …) and attributes; value , checked and selected are set up as bindings, and a function value without parameters becomes a live getter; on action and formaction , the function returned by the getter is the form's submit handler. In a subclass these keys stay in this.props , and only the common attributes fall through to the element. innerHTML and srcdoc are not written this way ( MJX124 ); a javascript: address in an href , src , action or formaction value is blocked ( MJX125 ). motifFragment(props) is the same as new FragmentNode(props) : while being built, it adds the components in the childs and nodes arrays of the props as children. FNComponent(view) turns a view function into a function component; when the returned function is called with props, it builds a component without an element, gives it the props and adds the component returned by view(props) as a child. That is the _mfc import in the compiler output; function components written in JSX are not wrapped in it.

title: Views without JSX
heading: Keys of the props object
text: MotifJS handles these keys itself; they are not written to the element as attributes. Key What it does initializeComponent The component's setup code. Runs once while the component is being built, before its children; its parameter is the component itself. oninitializeComponent Runs right after initializeComponent (see Lifecycle ). preconfig Runs in the configuration phase, before onConfig (see preconfig ). onConfig , onConfigured , onInitializing , onInitialized , onBuilding , onBuilt , onMounted , onVisibilityChanged , onActivated , onDeactivated , onDisposing , onDisposed Lifecycle hooks: a function or an array of functions, with the signature (sender, e) (see Hooks and run order ). x-wait , x-display Registered as bindings.wait and bindings.display . Other x- keys such as x-mounted are attached to the hook of the same name. childs Child components; nested arrays are flattened. A component without an element, and a class created without an element that writes no view() , add them as content; a class that writes view() places them itself. A component created by tag name does not add childs : new Component("ul", { childs }) gives an empty <ul> , and the children are added with controls.add inside initializeComponent . ref A function called with the component itself once the component is created. options isSvg (an SVG element), hideStrategy (see Hide strategy ) and disableDisposal . transition An enter and leave transition with CSS classes (see The transition prop ). onElementCreating A function that returns an element; the component uses it instead of the element from the first argument. key , indexkey The identity of a list row; the compiler writes key from JSX as indexkey . It is not written to the element and is used only in the MJX202 warning, which reports the same identity arriving twice. In a function component row, indexkey is written to the props object of the root the function returns. If the function builds its root with the same props object on every call (a module-level constant: motifComponent("li", ROW_PROPS) ), every row reads the key written to that object last. Even if the keys are unique, an MJX202 warning arrives the first time the list updates; the rendering is not affected. Give the root's props as a new object on every call: motifComponent("li", { class: "row" }) . In JSX this does not happen, because the compiler produces a new object on every call.

title: Views without JSX
heading: Text nodes
text: "text" is a real tag: motifComponent("text", (node: ComponentBase) => node.setText("…")) produces a text node, and text next to an element becomes one more child in the same controls.add call. A binding can be set up on a text node too: node.bindings.text(() => …) for live text through a getter, and node.bindings.add("textContent", note, "title") for a one-way binding to a single field. On an element whose only content is text, write span.setText("…") or span.bindings.text(fn) without creating a node. The runtime also turns strings and numbers given to controls.add into text nodes, but the TypeScript signature of controls.add takes components ( ComponentBase[] ), so in a TypeScript project write the "text" call. The folder link in the sidebar shows the number of notes in the folder next to its name. The name is a text node and the number is a badge bound with bindings.text ; both are given to RouterLink as childs : In the function component, notes is the service obtained with FromService and state is the local state set up with reactive ; visible() , folder() , confirmation , actions and remove are local functions inside the component function.

title: Views without JSX
heading: preconfig
text: preconfig: (c) => … runs while the component is being configured, before onConfig and build() ; on a plain tag this is inside the motifComponent call. A bindings.display / bindings.wait registered there keeps an element that starts out hidden unbuilt : its subtree, initializeComponent , onBuilt and onMounted wait until the condition holds. That is what x-wait / x-display are in JSX. wait holds the component for as long as the function returns true , and display shows it while it is true . If the same binding is registered inside initializeComponent , the element is built first and hidden afterwards. The pin mark on a list row is visible only on a note that is pinned and not archived; the empty list message in the list pane appears when no visible notes are left: Neither is built when it starts out hidden; initializeComponent runs the first time it is shown. When the condition turns false again, the element stays built and is hidden. wait is the reverse of the same binding: it holds the component for as long as the function returns true and shows it when it turns false . It is given to a component with the same key, and it is the same for class and function components: motifComponent(NoteRow, { note, folder, preconfig: (row: ComponentBase) => row.bindings.display(() => !note.archived) }) . The difference between display and wait , and the hide strategy, are on the Conditional Rendering and Lists and Lifecycle pages.

title: Views without JSX
heading: Fragments for branches and lists
text: If a branch has a single root, give a component; if it has several roots, a motifFragment ; if it is only text, a "text" component; frame.flush() empties the spot. The editor's toolbar asks for confirmation before deleting a note. The confirmation is a question and two buttons, and since it has several roots it is given with motifFragment ; actions(note) returns the pin, archive and delete buttons the same way: For a list that changes, use a holder without an element and bindings.list ; the row component declares its identity with indexkey (that is how the compiler writes key ). When the order changes the nodes are moved, not rebuilt. For fixed options a plain for loop is enough. The list pane lists the visible notes like this: The behaviour of when , ternary , list and switchCase is described on the Conditional Rendering and Lists page.

title: Views without JSX
heading: Class components in files without JSX
text: The Vite plugin processes .ts , .mts and .cts files too: it adds static elementTag = "div" to a class that writes extends Component<HTMLDivElement> , and the component gets an element of its own. In a .js file no generic is written, so static elementTag = "div" is written by hand. In a file the plugin does not process (a library compiled only with tsc , a package in node_modules ), write static elementTag = "div" or call super("div") as well. A class that declares no element type is a fragment : this.element is a comment marker; this.class and this.attr reach no element at all, this.motif.on listens on the top-level elements of the content, and x-display and this.motif.hide() hide the children. Returning a wrapper from view() does not give the component an element: the wrapper is the first child of the content, so write classes and attributes on it (see Root element ). The layout of the notes list is a class without an element; view() returns the content: NotesLayout has no element of its own; <div class="notes"> is the first child of the content. The form with an element of its own is the PinnedNotes class below: its element is <aside class="pinned"> , and view() returns only the children. A class's view() returns a single component (of type ComponentBase ); for several roots write motifFragment . The view() of an Options API component can return an array as well. The reading order stays as it is in JSX: the children as const s, a single controls.add at the end, and private methods that each return a component for the parts. PinnedNotes , added to the sidebar, lists the pinned notes, and each row has a button that unpins it; it is the same component in all three forms: The component is built the way it would be written as a tag: motifComponent(PinnedNotes) ; in all three forms the common attributes fall through to the root ( motifComponent(PinnedNotes, { class: "sidebar__pinned" }) ). In a file without JSX, @Injectable and the other decorators, DI, the router, useNavigation() , transitions and Virtualization work just the same; an override that does not reach super ( MJX015 ) is reported during the Vite plugin's build, while motif-lint only looks at JSX files.

title: Views without JSX
heading: Reading the compiled output
text: npx motif-explain file.tsx prints which call an expression comes down to (see What did this expression compile to? ). For the whole file, use the Compiler class in the @motifx/compiler package: new Compiler().motifCompile(code, "NoteRow.tsx")?.code returns the compiled code. This JSX: compiles to this code: The hand-written version: A key for reading the output: In the output When writing by hand _mc( motifComponent( _mf( motifFragment( _mfc FNComponent ; the compiler's import, not used by hand-written code _mv(1) motifCompiled ; the contract mark between the compiler and the runtime, absent from hand-written code try { … } catch (__e) { _mr(__e); } motifReport ; this is how the compiler reports the error of a child expression. A hand-written getter does not need try / catch : the runtime reports the error with MJX208 preconfig: sender => { sender.bindings.display(…) } x-display / x-wait ; written the same way indexkey: () => n.id key __isSvgElement: true options: { isSvg: true } __childExpr: () => note.title , childs: [] , the third argument , 1 compiler markers; drop them bindings.method(fn) bindings.text(fn) , or method as it is sender any parameter name you like ( (li: ComponentBase) )

title: Views without JSX
heading: Pitfalls of hand-written views
text: An accidental fragment. A class that declares no element type is a fragment, and so is a Component<HTMLDivElement> class in a file the Vite plugin does not process. Write static elementTag or call super("div") . Returning a wrapper from view() does not give the component an element. An error inside initializeComponent is swallowed. If the setup function throws, the element stays empty; the only trace is the entry that lands in console.error with MJX122 . A common cause: a const that calls a function with the same name in its own setup. Setup runs in build() , so at that moment the name holds the component: in const title = motifComponent("p", (p: ComponentBase) => p.controls.add(title("…"))) , title("…") tries to call the component. motifComponent returns any , so type checking does not catch it; check the rendered text in a test, or watch console.error . display / wait in the wrong hook. If registered inside initializeComponent , the hidden element is built once; register it inside preconfig . No compiler, no diagnostics. MJX001 – MJX005 and MJX016 are only for JSX; there is no warning for a list without indexkey or for a plain value that should have been a getter. A plain value is a snapshot, as in JSX: for CountBadge , motifComponent(CountBadge, { count: notes.count("pinned") }) reads the count once; to keep it live, write count: () => notes.count("pinned") . The types are yours. You write the setup parameter ( (c: ComponentBase) ), the ref field ( search!: Component<HTMLInputElement> ) and the motif.on handler ( (_sender: ComponentBase, e: KeyboardEvent) ) yourself. controls.add is immediate , so there is nothing to wait for; reactive updates , on the other hand, are applied on a microtask, as in JSX ( await Promise.resolve() in a test).

title: Views without JSX
heading: Next step
text: Reactivity : reactive , createSignal and effect , which bindings track. Conditional Rendering and Lists : the behaviour of wait / display , when , ternary , list and switchCase . Events : motif.on signatures, modifiers and application events. Lifecycle : initializeComponent and the order of the hooks.

title: Reactivity
text: MotifJS's reactivity system is fine-grained . When a field of a model changes, only the bindings and effects that read that field run again; the component is not re-rendered. There are several tools for holding state, and each one is designed for its own job; what decides the choice is the shape of the thing being held.
