A note, with its title, body, flags and the lists inside it, is a model: reactive wraps it as it is, tracks each field separately and makes nested objects and arrays reactive as well, and a changed field wakes only the binding that reads it. If the state is a single value, such as the id of the selected note or a scroll position, there is no need to wrap it in an object: createSignal holds that value, the value is written as a whole and, if you like, compared with its own equality rule. If hundreds of rows compare this id with their own id, createSelection wakes only the previously selected row and the newly selected one when the selection changes (see The selected row ). Instead of keeping a value derived from other values up to date by hand, createComputed calculates it; if the calculation is expensive and the value is read rarely, createLazyComputed does not calculate until it is read. When a change has to be answered with work outside the screen, you write an effect . They all run on the same tracking mechanism, can read one another and reach the screen through the same bindings; a reactive model and a signal can sit side by side in the same component. Tool What it is for reactive(model) A model with fields: nested objects, arrays, Map and Set . Each field is tracked separately; a component's or a service's state is usually this. useModel does the same job. createSignal(value) A single value: a number, a string, a selected id. The value is written as a whole through .value ; changing an object inside it in place does not notify, so you notify with mutate() . An equality comparer can be given. createComputed(getter) A value derived from other values and read constantly. It is kept ready and recomputed on the next microtask when a dependency changes. createLazyComputed(getter) An expensive derived value that is read less often than it is written. It is not computed until it is read. effect(fn) Answering a change with a side effect: the document title, localStorage . Inside a component use bindings.watch , which stops together with the component. The examples are slices of the notes application in the starter template. Note and NotesService are in src/services/notes.ts on the Components page, and SettingsService is in src/services/settings.ts on the Getting Started page; notes and settings are instances of these services.

title: Reactivity
heading: reactive(model)
text: Turns an object (or an array) into a reactive proxy. You read and write the fields as you would on a normal object; reads are tracked and writes trigger dependents. If a primitive value (a number, a string, a boolean) is given, it is wrapped in an object of the form { value } : reactive("") returns a { value: "" } proxy, and the value is read and written through .value . NotesService keeps the notes in a state.items array like this; create() adds a new note to the front with unshift . A write that does not change the value wakes nobody: writing the same value to a field, replacing an array element with itself or setting the length to the same number triggers nothing; the comparison uses Object.is . If a reactive object is put into another reactive field or array, its raw object is stored ( state.current = state.items[0] ); when read, the same reactive object comes back, and the raw data does not carry proxies. The array's read methods ( find , findIndex , some , every , filter , map , forEach , reduce , join , slice , includes , indexOf ), for...of and spreading ( [...state.items] ) subscribe to the array through a single key rather than index by index: an index write that changes a value, a change of length, or a structural method such as push , splice or sort wakes them once. A search that stops at a match ( find , findIndex , some , every , indexOf , includes ) is tied only to the prefix it walked: a write beyond the index where it stopped, an insertion in between or a push at the end does not wake it; a search that completes without a match, and findLast / findLastIndex , are tied to the whole list. The fields the callback reads on the elements ( note.title ) subscribe to those elements as well; the elements returned by find and filter are reactive too. A direct index read ( state.items[3] ) tracks only that index. The proxy is set up on top of the original object; no copy is taken. The same proxy comes back for the same object ( reactive(a) === reactive(a) ), and if the proxy itself is given, it is returned. clearModel(a) drops this record; after that, reactive(a) gives a new proxy (see Helpers ). Plain objects, arrays, class instances ( [object Object] ) and Map , Set , WeakMap and WeakSet become reactive ( collections ). In getters and methods called through the proxy, this is the proxy, so a getter or method that touches a class's private field written with # throws a TypeError , whether the instance is wrapped directly or read from inside a reactive object. Keep the reactive state of such a class in a reactive({ … }) field inside the class; a field written with TypeScript's private keyword is an ordinary field, works through the proxy and is reactive. Component, Application and ServiceProvider instances and app.router are returned as they are; they are not wrapped even if they are put in a field of a reactive object. Objects such as Date and RegExp , and non-extensible ( Object.freeze ) objects, are returned as they are , and changes inside them do not trigger bindings. RegExp is not proxied: inside a reactive object, test , exec and replace work as usual. The pattern does not change in place; a new pattern is written to the field as a new RegExp ( highlight.pattern = /new/ ), and that write triggers bindings. When a Date changes, write the field with a new reference ( reminder.due = new Date(reminder.due.getTime() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) ).

title: Reactivity
heading: State in a component
text: State is a field in a class, a closure variable in a function, and the data field in the Options API; all three are the same reactive object, and the getters in the view read it. FilterBar holds a search box and a "pinned only" option, and the number of matching notes is derived from the two fields: matches() is an ordinary method; when the getter inside <small> calls it, it reads state.query , state.onlyPinned and the archived , title and pinned fields of the notes in the service. Whichever of these fields changes, only that text is recomputed.

title: Reactivity
heading: Changing state only through methods
text: When you want to know where a piece of state changes from, validate a change or keep a record of it, do not hand the reactive object out. The state stays inside a module or a service, and the outside world gets getters for reading and methods for changing it. Since the getter reads the reactive object, bindings and effect s track it. Since every change goes through a method, the rule, the validation or the record lives in one place. The notes selected for a bulk action in the notes list are state of this kind. Without DI, in a module: state never leaves the module; only selection 's methods write to it. The component imports selection and uses it: With DI, in a service: The component gets the service with this.getService(SelectionService)! in a class, and with FromService(SelectionService)! in function and Options components; the usage is the same as above. The service route also brings DI's scope: if the selection should reset when the page changes, register the service with addScoped , and every navigation gets its own instance (see scoped ). On both routes, selection.count = 3 and selection.ids.push(…) do not compile in TypeScript; the getter's return type is readonly number[] , so the array cannot be changed from outside either. The service's state field is private , so access from outside does not compile. Assigning to a field that has a getter also gives a TypeError at run time in an ES module. TypeScript's readonly and private protections are compile-time ones; the state in the module, on the other hand, is invisible from outside at run time as well. Even when a method writes several fields, the bindings that track it run once. To close it off at run time too, hand out a view made with asReadonly . The view reads the same data and tracks its changes; writing to it, deleting from it or calling a changing method such as push throws an MJX212 error: selection.ids.push(4) is now rejected at run time as well; the getter's return type is read-only by itself, and there is no need to write readonly number[] separately.

title: Reactivity
heading: asReadonly(obj) — a read-only view
text: Gives a live, read-only view of a reactive object, array, Map or Set . It is not a copy: it looks at the same data, every change made through the original object shows up in the view as well, and the bindings that read the view wake up. Nested objects, array elements, Map values and Set elements read from the view are read-only too. The array's read methods ( map , filter , find , for...of ) work and are tracked. Writing, delete , methods that change the array ( push , splice , sort , reverse ) and Map / Set changes ( set , add , delete , clear ) throw MJX212 , and the data does not change. The error is the same in strict mode and outside it. The same view is always returned for the same object. reactive(view) gives the view itself; you cannot get a writable proxy from a view. isReadonly(x) is true only for views obtained through asReadonly . A frozen object ( Object.freeze ) cannot be changed anyway, so it is returned as it is. The return type is DeepReadonly<T> , so assignments and changing methods are caught at compile time as well.

title: Reactivity
heading: useModel(model)
text: An alias that does the same job as reactive . Every component also has a useModel(model) method that does the same thing.

title: Reactivity
heading: Map , Set , WeakMap , WeakSet
text: Collections inside a reactive model are reactive too. You call their methods as usual, and the bindings and effects that read them run again only on the relevant change: The list and the selection are drawn like an array: Read Writes that run it again get(k) , has(k) Only a set , add , delete or clear that changes that key size , forEach , values() , entries() , for…of , [...x] Every write that changes the content keys() on a Map Only adding or deleting a key; changing the value of an existing key does not trigger it Writes where nothing actually changes trigger nothing: a set with the same value ( Object.is ), an add of an existing element, a delete of a missing key, a clear of an empty collection. Objects inside: Map values and Set elements come back as reactive proxies when read, and changes to their fields are tracked. Map keys come back raw during iteration. Raw storage: proxies written to a collection are stored in their raw form. It makes no difference whether you give an object key raw or reactive; both reach the same entry. Identity: reactive(new Map()) can be used directly too. The same proxy always comes back for the same collection; instanceof Map , chaining ( map.set(a, 1).set(b, 2) ) and Object.prototype.toString keep their native behaviour. WeakMap / WeakSet : they have only their own methods ( get , set , has , add , delete ), which are tracked by the same rules.

title: Reactivity
heading: Derived (computed) fields — a function inside the object
text: If you define a function field inside a reactive object, it behaves like a derived reactive value: A template slot calls the function value without arguments ( {filters.label} , x-text={filters.label} , title={filters.label} ) and calls it again whenever the fields it reads change. {filters.label} and title={filters.label} call the function without this , while x-text={filters.label} calls it through filters ; that is why the derived field reads filters instead of this . A method that uses this is passed to a slot as {() => filters.method()} . A function that must not run when the binding is set up and whenever the fields it reads change (a Promise resolver, for example) is not given to a template slot; call it from your own code.

title: Reactivity
heading: Signal and Computed
text: These are the finest-grained primitives, each wrapping a single value. They suit holding reactive state that is independent of the component tree.

title: Reactivity
heading: createSignal(initialValue)
text: A summary of the Signal class: Member Description get value / set value A tracked read / a triggering write. peek() Read without tracking. update(fn) Update based on the previous value. mutate(fn) Notify after an inner mutation (when the reference stays the same). notify() Manual notification. asReadonly() A ReadonlySignal<T> view ( value , peek() ). dispose() Makes later operations a no-op. valueOf() / toString() A tracked read; gives the value in a template string ( `${draft}` ) or in string concatenation. The equality comparer can be customized (the default is Object.is ); for that, construct the Signal class directly or call Signal.create(value, equals) :

title: Reactivity
heading: createComputed(getter)
text: A cached value derived automatically from its dependencies. It is computed right away at setup; when one of its dependencies changes, it is recomputed on the next microtask even if nobody reads it, and if the value changed it triggers the effects that depend on it. .value gives the cached value and does no computation while being read, so a synchronous read right after a write can give the previous value:

title: Reactivity
heading: createLazyComputed(getter) — no computation until it is read
text: The lazy counterpart of createComputed . It does no computation at setup; when a dependency changes, it is only marked dirty and the effects that depend on it are woken. The computation happens when .value is first read and on every dirty read; a value that is never read is never computed. The marking is synchronous at the time of the write: right after the line items.value = … , index.value gives the fresh value. Which one when: if the value is read on screen all the time, createComputed (ready after every change); if it is expensive and read less often than it is written, createLazyComputed (N writes between two reads → 1 computation). Writes in the same synchronous block come down to a single computation with createComputed too (see Consecutive writes ). The trade-off: dependent effects wake even when the lazy value does not change, because no computation is done while marking it dirty and equality cannot be known. Synchronous freshness holds when the whole chain consists of reactive / Signal / LazyComputed . If there is a createComputed in the chain, its refresh happens on a microtask, so a lazy value fed by it is refreshed after the flush, not right after the write.

title: Reactivity
heading: createSelection(source) — the selected row
text: If every row of a list compares the selected id with its own id ( () => state.selected === note.id ), every row's binding wakes and redoes its comparison when the selection changes, even though only two rows have actually changed. createSelection keeps the comparison by key: isSelected(key) subscribes the binding that calls it only to that key, and when the source changes, only the bindings of the old and the new value wake up. The row gets its selected class through this function: The comparison uses Object.is . Reactive objects are reduced to their raw object before comparing, so isSelected(note) matches the selected object whatever form it reaches the row in. Called outside a binding, it only compares and sets up no subscription. It is for equality only; a comparison such as state.selected > note.id cannot be split by key, and in that case a plain getter stays. dispose() stops tracking the source; a selection created in a module next to the data lives along with the data. Measured on a 60,000-row list: a selection change drops from 49 ms to 0.2 ms, and memory per row stays the same.

title: Reactivity
heading: effect(fn) — side effects and watchers
text: An effect runs once, synchronously, the moment it is set up, subscribes to the reactive values read inside it, and runs again whenever they change. effect returns a stop function : The second argument is an optional result callback : effect(getter, onValue) passes the return value of getter to onValue after every run, and reads inside onValue are not tracked . The first onValue call runs synchronously inside the effect(...) call; if the effect is set up while another effect is running, the reads in that first call are recorded on that outer effect. It is used to limit the dependency surface to getter alone; the framework's when / ternary / switchCase bindings are set up this way. If getter throws, that run has no value: onValue is not called, the error is reported as MJX208 and the effect keeps tracking; the next healthy value still reaches onValue (which is why a when / ternary / switchCase branch stays as it is when an error happens): When setting up an effect inside a component, use bindings.watch (see below ): the effect stops when the component is disposed, with no manual stop() needed.

title: Reactivity
heading: Reads after await
text: Tracking is limited to the synchronous part of an effect: in an async getter/effect, reactive fields read after the first await are not recorded as dependencies. For state that has to update based on the result of async work, write the result to a reactive field and show it with a separate binding that reads that field. The only exception is the dataRequest prop of Virtualization : the compiler wraps the await s of an async function written inline on a <Virtualization> tag, and reads after await are tracked there too; a function passed by name ( dataRequest={loadPage} ) or one that is not async is not wrapped (see Virtual Lists ). The run-time half of this wrapping is the asyncTracking export; it is not called by hand.

title: Reactivity
heading: Reading without tracking — untracked
text: When you want to read a value inside an effect but not subscribe to it, use untracked(fn) ; it gives the return value of fn . effect s set up inside it track their own dependencies as usual. The core uses this in the list binding ( bindings.list ): row components are produced inside the list effect, but the reads in the row template and in the row's setup are recorded on the row's own bindings, not on the list; rows added after the first render are set up the same way. That way, when a value a row reads changes, the list binding does not run again for nothing. Rule: an effect should not write a value it reads. stats.runs++ is both a read and a write; the effect triggers itself again and loops. Put side records such as counters and logs inside untracked : untracked only turns off the tracking of reads; writes inside it still trigger their dependents: a binding that shows stats.runs is updated. The framework catches this: if an effect runs 50 times in a single flush, it is skipped for the rest of that flush and an MJX203 warning is printed in development mode. The other effects in the queue are not affected. The array mutators ( push , pop , shift , unshift , splice , reverse ) are an exception to this rule: the call's own internal reads ( length , indices) are not tracked, so writing stats.log.push(x) inside an effect does not subscribe the effect to the array. If the effect also reads the array (such as stats.log.length ), the subscription is still set up. sort is not part of this exception: it reads the array and writes it in place, so if it is called inside an effect, the effect triggers itself; do the sorting inside untracked or on a copy ( [...stats.log].sort() ). If an effect collects more than 1000 dependencies in a single run, it prints an MJX209 warning in development mode; once per effect, and at most ten times per session. With DevTools open, the warning names the owning component and the binding ( StoreRow at [0, 2, 5] (binding:textContent) ). This is usually a reactive list being scanned from start to end in every row: find the element by key, or read the list with untracked . The threshold is changed with app.useReactiveMonitor({ dependencies: 2000 }) , and 0 turns it off. The second signal is MJX210 : if two or more instances of the same component type scan the same reactive list with a search method such as find / some , and the list has at least as many items as there are instances (like the list of rows itself), development mode warns once per list, even if the list comes from props or from another file. A hundred rows scanning a three-item settings list does not warn; for effects without an owner ( createComputed , a plain effect ) the threshold is eight; with DevTools closed the owner is unknown, so the check does not run. scans: false turns it off.

title: Reactivity
heading: Chained (derived) state
text: An effect can read state written by another effect. The whole chain settles in the same microtask ; the final value does not depend on the order in which the effects were set up, and there is no need to wait for the intermediate steps: If an effect (or a binding's getter) throws, only that effect is affected; the others in the same flush keep running. The error is reported to the central error handler as a MotifError with the code MJX208 , carrying the original error in its cause field: it is written to the console and reaches the errorHandler.addListener(fn) listeners. A binding whose getter throws leaves the last value in the DOM (text, attribute, class, style) as it is.

title: Reactivity
heading: A watcher tied to the component — bindings.watch / x-watch
text: The watcher is registered on the component and stops on its own when the component is disposed. The first run happens at registration time, synchronously: a watcher set up in a class's onConfig or in Options' onConfigured runs before onBuilding , while an x-watch on a tag and a bindings.watch in a setup function run for the first time while that tag is being built (inside initializeComponent ). QueryField is a search box; it reads the last query from localStorage on startup and writes it there on every change. In the class it is this.bindings.watch inside onConfig , in the function an x-watch on the tag, and in Options this.bindings.watch inside onConfigured ; without JSX, all of them are a bindings.watch call:

title: Reactivity
heading: The trap of every row scanning the list
text: Trap: a getter that scans a reactive list in every row. If a row component holds only an id and looks up its element with a getter such as notes.items.find((n) => n.id === this.props.id) , that getter reads the id field of every element up to the match and subscribes to all of them. In a single row that is n subscriptions; in n rows it is n² subscriptions. When one id changes, every row that walked past it runs again, and when the list is replaced with a new one, every row runs again, each scanning the list from the start: n² reads and n² new subscriptions; appending at the end wakes only the rows that had not found their match. Measured with 2000 rows and a 2000-element list: 2 million subscriptions, 1.2 s for the first build, 0.8 s for changing one id , 4 s for replacing the list. The reason is that reactivity is fine-grained: every field read is a subscription, and every scanned element is a field read. The scan itself is cheap; what is expensive is every row subscribing to every element. includes and indexOf do not read element fields, so they do not fall into this trap, while a "full walk" such as filter(...).length makes it bigger. The framework points this out in four places: the compiler warns with MJX004 when it sees find / findIndex / some / every with a predicate of the form x.field === value inside a reactive getter; at run time, if two or more instances of the same component type scan the same list with a search method and the list has at least as many items as there are instances, it is reported with MJX210 , even when the list comes from props or from another file; an effect that collects more than 1000 dependencies in a single run is reported with MJX209 , together with the owning component and binding when DevTools is open; and in DevTools the component's effect list shows the dependency count of every binding. Ways to avoid it, in order of preference: Give the row the element, not the id. The list binding already does this: {notes.items.map((note) => <NoteRow note={note} />)} ; the row reads this.props.note.title and subscribes only to that field of that object (see Showing lists ). If you only have the id, keep a keyed index. The store that holds the list also keeps the elements in a Map ; the row reads notes.byId(id) and subscribes only to that key, and when the list changes only the reader of that key wakes up: If the list changes rarely, the index can also be a computed: const index = createComputed(() => new Map(state.items.map((n) => [n.id, n]))) . The scan happens once and the rows read index.value.get(id) ; every time the list changes, all rows run again once, but each run is a single read. 3. untracked if no subscription is needed. A getter that only wants the current value reads the list with untracked(() => notes.items.find((n) => n.id === id)) ; when the list changes this getter is not refreshed, and some other dependency of it makes it run again.

title: Reactivity
heading: Consecutive writes are batched on their own
text: Writes made in the same synchronous block need no separate batching call. Writes add effects to a queue; the queue is emptied on the next microtask, and each effect runs once . No effect sees the intermediate states: The flush happens in rounds: if an effect also reads a value written in the same flush by another effect or by a createComputed , it runs again one round later, in the same microtask. Depending on the order things were set up, its first run may see the old version of that value; its last run sees the current values.

title: Reactivity
heading: Helpers
text: Function Description deepClone(value) Produces a non-reactive deep copy of the value; if a proxy is given, its raw form is copied. Plain objects, arrays, Map and Set are copied recursively; Date and RegExp become new instances; a class instance keeps its prototype, and its getters and methods work on the copy; circular references set up the same cycle in the copy. Functions, WeakMap and WeakSet are passed by the same reference, and a DOM node is copied with cloneNode(true) . The objects' own enumerable fields are copied. clearModel(model) Deletes the proxy record of the object and of the nested objects whose proxies have been created; it does not reset the values and does not stop the bindings and effects that are set up. After the call, reactive(model) gives a new proxy, and writing through it still updates the existing bindings. Writing to the fields of a proxy obtained before the call changes the value but does not notify; nested objects read later from that proxy come back as new proxies and do notify. read(value) / toGetter(value) Read a value of type Bind<T> (a value, or a getter that returns it): read calls the value and gives the result if it is a function, and gives the value itself otherwise; toGetter gives a getter in every case. Used in components that can also take a prop as a getter (see If the template will change later, write a getter ). configureReactivityLeakMonitor({ enabled, threshold, name }) Prints an MJX507 warning when the number of effects tracking a single field reaches threshold (200 by default when enabled); in an application, app.useReactiveMonitor(...) is the same call (see Leak tracking ).

title: Reactivity
heading: Where reactivity meets the DOM
text: Reactive fields show up in the DOM through bindings . When you write JSX the compiler sets them up; without JSX you write the same calls yourself: setState() / reState() re-evaluate the bindings of a component and all of its children: text and attribute paths, class and style getters, x-text , x-html , value / checked / x-model , x-display / x-wait , {() => …} , template string and member call slots, && /ternary/ switch branches and x-watch / bindings.watch watchers run again; lists match their rows to the items again, just as on a reactive update: the row of an item that stays in the list stays in place and reads its own bindings again, a row is built for a new item, the row of an item that left is disposed, and if the order changed the rows swap places. Only the order differs: setState() handles the children first and then the component itself, while reState() handles the component itself first and then the children. In a function component these calls are made on the component itself ( list in the example): in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. When working with reactive there is no need for setState ; fine-grained reactivity does the update itself. setState is for cases where you update plain, non-reactive data by hand; for example, making every slot read again when the fields of a plain language dictionary are changed in place. If you replace the dictionary object with another object, a path written directly ( {i18n.dict.title} ) stays on the old object read during setup, while a getter slot ( {() => i18n.dict.title} ) reads the new object.

title: Reactivity
heading: Next step
text: To learn conditional and list-based rendering, go on to Conditional Rendering and Lists .

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
text: In MotifJS the primary way to render conditionally is the x-wait directive, and lists are written with .map inside JSX. @motifx/compiler turns these into reactive bindings: bindings.wait , bindings.display , bindings.when , bindings.ternary , bindings.list , bindings.switchCase , bindings.method . Next to every JSX form, this page shows its counterpart without JSX, that is, the binding call underneath it. The examples are slices of the notes application in the starter template: the notes list ( NotesLayout ), the editor ( NotePage ) and the sidebar ( MainLayout ). Note and NotesService are the ones in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page; visible is the notes visible in the list layout ( this.visible in a class and in Options, visible() in a function), and state is the component's own state ( this.state in a class and in Options, a local state in a function).

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: x-wait — the primary method
text: The natural way in MotifJS to show an element based on a condition is the x-wait directive. As long as the function returns true , the element waits , and when it turns false the element becomes visible. It reads as "wait until this condition is met". x-display is the same mechanism turned around: it shows while true . Without JSX both are written in preconfig , because they are evaluated before the component is built: In the function component, notes and settings are the services obtained with FromService , and state is the local state set up with reactive ; visible() and folder() are local functions inside the component function. Both work on every kind of tag: a plain DOM element, a class component (a class without an element included), a function and an Options component. The pinned badge in the sidebar is not built until the first pinned note arrives; CountBadge behaves the same whichever form it is written in:

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Why x-wait ?
text: Lazy building. If the condition is true on the first evaluation, the element is never build() -ed. Neither it nor its subtree enters the DOM, and a placeholder is left in its place. The component object is still created: in a class the constructor and onInitializing , onInitialized , onConfig and onConfigured run, and in a function component the function body runs; view() , onBuilding / onBuilt / onMounted and the setup inside do not run until it is first shown. The view of a heavy panel that is closed at startup is not built until it is first shown. The instance is kept. Once it has been built, opening and closing it only shows and hides it. The component is not disposed, and its internal state (scroll position, form input, a third-party plugin) stays as it is. Synchronous first render. Both are in place by the time build() returns. The same holds for && , the ternary and a {part()} that returns JSX: the first content lands in an empty Frame synchronously. Later branch changes are asynchronous. In both modes a hidden element leaves the DOM; onDeactivated runs on the hidden component and the ones in its subtree, and onActivated when it is shown. Bindings keep running while it is hidden, and the element comes back with the current value when shown. hideStrategy makes the difference: the default 'auto' and 'placeholder' leave a comment node in place of the element and swap it back when showing, while 'detach' removes the element without a trace and puts it back according to its order in the parent when showing. The default also applies to list rows: a hidden or waiting row leaves a marker in its place, and when the list is sorted the marker moves together with the row. An element that starts out waiting puts a marker in its place before it is built, too. See Visibility .

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: && — build and dispose
text: {condition && <X/>} is supported too, and it compiles to a bindings.when(conditionFn, buildFn) call. The difference is in its behaviour: every time the condition becomes true a new instance is built , and every time it becomes false that instance is disposed . The branch is rebuilt only when the condition's value changes ( Object.is ; two falsy values count as the same). As long as the value stays the same, the branch keeps the component instance and its state: {notes.count("pinned") > 0 && <PinnedNotes />} keeps the same PinnedNotes while the pinned count goes 1 → 2 → 3. If the condition's value is an object ( {state.selected && <NoteFields note={state.selected} />} ), the branch is rebuilt when it is replaced with another object: a new NoteFields on every selection. So choose && only when you want the building and disposing itself: when a third-party plugin really has to be destroyed, or when the content is so heavy that it should not be kept in memory. In every other case x-wait is cheaper and more predictable. The condition is evaluated by JS truthiness : for false , null , undefined , 0 , '' and NaN , nothing is rendered. So {state.selected && <NoteFields … />} (an object or null ) and {notes.count("pinned") && <PinnedNotes />} (a number) behave as expected; 0 is not written to the screen. With a numeric condition, the branch is rebuilt every time the number changes (the value rule above); to keep the instance, write {notes.count("pinned") > 0 && <PinnedNotes />} . This rule holds both inside a real element and as a direct child of a fragment ( <>…</> ) root.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Which one to choose?
text: Situation Method Show/hide, state must be kept x-wait / x-display Closed at startup, heavy content x-wait (never built) Must really be disposed on every close {condition && <X/>} One of two branches the ternary operator Only the text changes a getter

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: The ternary operator — one of two branches
text:
Each branch gets a Frame and places its content with frame.navigate(...) . As the condition changes, the matching branch is shown and the other is disposed; if the old branch has a leave transition it is played, and the order follows the transition.mode of the nearest element ancestor (see Styling and Animation ). If both branches are light, this is the most readable form; if they are heavy, putting the two elements side by side with x-wait / x-display keeps the instances. If a branch has several roots, give <>… in JSX and motifFragment without JSX; the confirmation in the editor's toolbar works like that (see Fragments for branches and lists ). The branch is rebuilt only when the condition's value changes ( Object.is ); in a nested ternary, the inner branch is kept as well, as long as the outer condition's value stays the same. {notes.count("pinned") > 0 ? :

No pinned notes.

} does not rebuild PinnedNotes while the pinned count goes 1 → 2.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Component props inside a branch
text: A prop given to a component inside a branch with a plain expression is, just as outside a condition, the value at the moment the branch was built . <CountBadge count={notes.count("pinned")} /> does not see a note pinned later; the branch is not rebuilt as long as the condition's value does not change. To keep the prop live, pass a getter and read it on the receiving side with the Bind<T> contract (see Ternaries in attributes ). Without JSX you write the getter yourself anyway: CountBadge takes the prop as count: Bind<number> and reads it with read(props.count) ( read(this.props.count) in a class); either a value or a getter can be given (see Common attributes ).

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Conditional text inside a getter
text: For simple text a getter is enough, and the element does not even change: The getter in JSX compiles to bindings.ternary , and the two branches are text nodes. Without JSX a single binding writes the same text: bindings.text changes the element's textContent , and if the element has other children they are removed as well.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: A block-bodied getter
text: A getter in child position can also be written with a block body; the statements before return run in the condition's getter on every evaluation, and the branches see those variables: The condition function can also prepare the value the branches will use: the function runs on every evaluation, and the branches read the same variable: The branch reads the variable at the moment it is built: when note.pinned changes, the branch changes and takes the current value of label , but as long as the condition stays the same, a change to the title does not show up in the branch that is already built. A value that has to stay live inside the branch is written there as a binding. Write a getter in the branch: {() => note.title.trim() || "Untitled"} . If there is an expression that produces JSX or a class declaration among the statements, the compiler cannot turn the getter into bindings.ternary ; it warns with MJX016 , and the getter runs as bindings.method , so the content is rebuilt on every change. In a block-bodied function that takes a parameter ( {(x) => { const label = …; return … ? … : …; }} ), the condition is moved out of the closure, the local variables are not visible in the branches and a ReferenceError is thrown; the compiler warns about this with MJX001 (see Compile-time warnings ). Write bindings.text(() => note.title.trim() || "Untitled") in the branch.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Showing lists — .map
text: Turning an array into items with .map sets up a reactive list binding ; it compiles to bindings.list(itemsFn, buildFn) . Without JSX the list is set up on a holder component that has no element ( motifComponent({ initializeComponent }) ), and each row carries its key through indexkey : When the array changes (adding, removing, sorting), MotifJS applies only the difference to the DOM; it does not recreate the whole list. notes.list("notes") filters out archived notes, so archive(note) drops the row from the list; togglePin updates that row's class and box; and since the list puts pinned notes first, the row moves to the top without being rebuilt.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: key and item identity
text: Rows are matched by the identity of the item object : if the same object (the raw object of the reactive proxy) is still in the new array, its row is reused and moved in the DOM if needed, and the row of an object that is no longer in the array is disposed. If new objects are put into the array (for example a fresh list from the server), the rows are rebuilt even if they carry the same id . The same object can appear in the array more than once ( push(items[0]) , splice(i, 0, items[j]) ); each occurrence gets its own row, all of them show the same object, and a change to the object shows up in all of them. Array methods do not copy items; if you need an independent copy, copy it explicitly: items.splice(i, 0, { ...items[j] }) . In arrays of primitive values ( string[] ), the same value at the same position keeps its row; if the template function does not take the second argument ( index ), the same value that changes position keeps its row too. For object items the row is reused when it moves, so the index the template receives is the position at the moment the row was built; it is not updated after sorting. key takes no part in this matching and does not change how the DOM is reused; it identifies the item. Still, give it a stable, unique value (usually note.id ): if the same key is seen on two items, development mode prints an MJX202 warning, and for a .map with no key the compiler warns with MJX003 . The names x-key and indexkey are the same as key ; without JSX, use indexkey: () => note.id . In a function component row, indexkey is written to the props object of the root the function returns. If the function builds its root with the same props object on every call (a module-level constant), every row reads the key written last, and MJX202 arrives for no reason when the list updates. Give the root's props as a new object on every call (see Keys of the props object ).

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Reactivity inside items
text: List items are reactive too. In the row in NoteList , when note.title changes only that row's text is updated. When note.pinned changes, the row's class and checkbox are updated; since the list also reads its sort order from this field, it leaves the row built in place and moves it to its new position. The row template has to return a component (an instance, a class or a factory); any other value throws MJX201 , and in that update the list places no rows at all. To skip a row based on a condition, do not return null ; filter the array first (see Filtering ). The second argument of .map works as in JS: inside items.map(function (i) { … }, ctx) , this is ctx . An arrow function keeps its own this . The row receives the element as a prop. Giving a row only an id and looking up the element in every row with items.find((n) => n.id === id) subscribes every row to every element, n² subscriptions for n rows (see The trap of every row scanning the list ).

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Filtering
text: A .filter().map() chain is supported; if the condition depends on reactive sources, the filter is reactive too:

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: A switch -like multi-branch
text: To show different content depending on a discriminant value, there is the switchCase binding. In JSX it is written as a switch inside a block-bodied getter; the compiler turns the branch that each case return s into switchCase : The settings page shows the name of the selected theme, and writes nothing for the system theme: Each branch gets a Frame , and you place that branch's content with frame.navigate(...) . The discriminant's value is turned into a key with String(...) ; if the same value comes in a row, the branch is not rebuilt, and when going from one unmatched value to another, the default branch stays in place as well. If no case matches (like system ), the spot is emptied and the previous branch is disposed. The spot is also emptied when a branch returns null or undefined ( default: return null , return saving ? … : null ). Without JSX, the default branch is the third argument; frame.navigate(null) places nothing and the previous content stays in place, so to empty the spot use (frame) => frame.flush() . case labels must be string, number or boolean literals . Statements written in the block body before the switch run in the discriminant's getter on every evaluation, and the branches see those variables; a branch reads a variable at the moment it is built, and as long as the discriminant stays the same, a change to the variable does not show up in the branch; statements before return inside a case run while the branch is being built; with case "a": case "b": return ; , "a" shows X as well; a branch that leaves with break and the statements after the switch run on the default path. If there is no default branch, a return that comes after the switch becomes the default branch, and that content is shown when no case matches ( return null empties the spot). A shape the compiler cannot turn into switchCase runs as written, as bindings.method , and the compiler warns with MJX016 : a case label that is not a literal or is written twice, a second default or switch , a return before the switch , a statement that produces JSX or a class declaration, a break / continue inside a case that is not the last statement or that carries a label. With such code branches are not kept, and the content is rebuilt on every change.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Using the binding API directly
text: JSX is a short way of writing these calls; the same API can be written without JSX and called directly inside initializeComponent / onConfig or in tests. Rather than guessing which JSX form comes down to which call, print it: npx motif-explain file.tsx (see What did this expression compile to? ). Method What it does bindings.add(prop, source, member?, format?, formatInfo?) Sets up a one-way binding to a DOM property/attribute. bindings.text(fn) Binds textContent reactively ( x-text ). bindings.value(fn) Binds value reactively ( x-value ). bindings.html(fn) Binds innerHTML reactively ( x-html ). bindings.when(condFn, renderFn) Conditional content ( && ) — a new instance when the condition's value changes and is truthy. bindings.ternary(condFn, trueFn, falseFn) A two-branch condition; a branch is rebuilt when the condition's value changes. bindings.list(itemsFn, renderFn) Showing a list ( .map ); rows are matched to the item object. bindings.loop(itemsFn, renderFn) The same as list ; an alternative name. bindings.switchCase(discFn, cases, defaultFn?) Multiple branches. bindings.method(fn) Reactive text or a single piece of reactive content; fn is called once per run. Strings, numbers, booleans and bigints are written as text; a component is placed in a Frame . The result can switch between text and a component, and the new content is drawn in the same spot. If null / undefined arrives, the spot is emptied: previous content that was a component is disposed, and previous text is cleared; content that comes later fills the spot again. bindings.watch(fn) A side-effect watcher ( x-watch ; stops automatically on disposal). bindings.model(source, member?, format?, formatInfo?) / bindings.model(getter, setter) A two-way binding (see Forms ). bindings.writeModel(value) Writes the value back to the model / x-model bindings on the component; returns true if it wrote (see Forms ). bindings.wait(fn) / bindings.display(fn) Waiting / visibility ( x-wait / x-display ) — the instance is kept; called inside preconfig . bindings.remove(binding) / bindings.clear() Remove one binding (or all of them) from the collection and turn it off; with the binding returned by the add / html / list / model / wait / display calls. when , ternary , switchCase , method and watch are not registered bindings; they stop together with the component. bindings.items A copy of the registered bindings (those set up with add / html / list / model / wait / display ).

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: A bindings.add example
text: bindings.add signatures: Call Value read add(propertyName, dataSource) dataSource itself; if it is a getter, the value it returns add(propertyName, dataSource, dataMember) The dataMember field on dataSource (it can be a dotted path) add(propertyName, dataSource, dataMember, formatString) The same field, formatted with formatString add(propertyName, dataSource, dataMember, formatString, formatInfo) The same field; locale and currency come from formatInfo ( { locale, currency } ) add(binding) A ready binding object Every form returns the added binding ( IBaseBinding ); propertyName is the name of the property to write ( "textContent" , "value" …). dataSource can also be a getter on its own ( add("textContent", () => note.title) ); when dataMember is given, that field is read, and it can be a dotted path ( "author.name" ). The formatString codes: for numbers C currency, P percent ( 0.25 → 25% in en-US ), N / N2 fixed decimals (2 by default), and the number codes can be written in lower case too; for Date values d date and t time. A value of any other type, or an unrecognized code, is written with toString() . Locale and currency come from formatInfo : bindings.add("textContent", order, "total", "C", { locale: "en-US", currency: "USD" }) → $1,234.50 . Without locale , the runtime's default locale is used; without currency , C writes the amount with two decimals and no symbol.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: A bindings.list example
text: The first argument is the item source: a function that returns an array or an iterable. The second is the row template, and it returns a component. In the function component, visible() and folder() are local functions inside the component function.

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Large lists
text: When thousands of rows enter a page at once, the browser cannot respond until all of them have been built and laid out. MotifJS has two tools for this: Chunked building — x-chunk . All the rows enter the DOM, but spread over frames: the first 100 children added together are built right away, and the rest leave a marker ( <!--h--> ) in their place and are built over the following frames. The framework decides how many children to build in a frame by measuring time. As much DOM is still created as there are rows; the gain is that one long task is split across frames. This is the way to go if the whole content has to be in the DOM, for in-page search, printing or the real length of the scrollbar. Virtual scrolling — Virtualization . Only the visible rows are in the DOM, so the DOM stays small even with tens of thousands of items — see Virtual Lists .

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Chunked building — x-chunk
text: The directive is written without a value on the element that receives the rows. The archive page lists all archived notes in a single table: the first 100 rows arrive with the page, and the rest are spread over the following frames. In every frame the framework measures two durations: the time to build the children, and the time the browser takes to lay them out and paint them. In the next frame it builds as many children as keep the sum of the two at about 50 ms. A small list finishes in a few frames; as the container grows, more children are built per frame. If you want a lower bound on the number built, give a value: x-chunk={50} builds exactly 50 children in the first round and at least 50 in every following frame, more if the frame's time allows. The browser lays out the container that children are added to again in every frame, and that work grows with the size of the container. It is most expensive for a table: as rows are added, the table measures its columns again. Once laying out the container alone takes more than 50 ms, frames get longer. At that point the framework builds more children per frame and spreads the cost over fewer frames, but it cannot make the frames shorter. In a desktop browser this limit is around 10–30 thousand rows for table rows and a few tens of thousands for plain rows; on slow devices it comes earlier. For lists of this size, use virtual scrolling. The count is kept for every child that goes into the element: tags written directly, .map rows, and children coming from a condition or a fragment all share the same budget. .map rows are not created until their turn comes: the row function is not called and the component is not built. This applies to a list written with {notes.list("archive").map(...)} as in the example. If the rows are written inside a getter, as {() => notes.list("archive").map(...)} , all row components are created up front and only their building is chunked. No row is ever built for an item that leaves the array in the meantime; if the array is re-sorted, the row is built at its new position and index is the current position. A child with its own x-wait follows its own condition and is not part of the chunking. A child whose turn comes follows the usual lifecycle ( onConfigured , onBuilt , onMounted ). Chunks keep flowing while the tab is in the background. If building a child throws, it is reported with MJX130 , and the other children of the chunk keep being built. A marker stays in place of the .map row that failed, and the row is created again on the list's next update. The first chunk belongs to the element: children added together (in the same run, up to an await ) share the first 100, and rows that arrive later with push start with a new first chunk. If there are several chunked elements on the same page, each gets its share in every frame, and the frame time is measured for all of them together. Without JSX, give options: { chunk: true } or a number, or set motif.options.chunk before setup; 0 or false turns chunking off. If a function is given instead of a value, it is called once during setup and not tracked afterwards. On a chunked page, scroll memory retries the position in every frame while rows arrive, until it reaches the target or settleMs runs out — see Scroll memory .

title: Conditional Rendering and Lists
heading: Next step
text: To learn about event handling, go on to Events .

title: Events
text: MotifJS has three layers of events: DOM events — attached to an element with props such as onclick and oninput , and without JSX with motif.on . Component events — communication between components with component.motif.on/trigger/off . Application events — application-wide broadcasts with context.on/fire . The examples are slices of the notes application in the starter template: the notes list ( NotesLayout ) and the editor ( NotePage ). Note and NotesService are the ones in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page. this.state is the component's own state; this.remove and this.close are methods of the component. state is the local state the component sets up with reactive ; remove and close are local functions inside the component function.

title: Events
heading: DOM events
text: In JSX, on... props are attached to DOM events, and event names are written in lower case. Without JSX the same binding is a motif.on(name, handler) call: On a plain tag every DOM event is attached this way ( onpointerdown , onmouseenter and onanimationend included); a camelCase spelling such as onClick attaches the same event. On a component tag, a prop carrying a DOM event name ( onchange / onChange , onCopy , onResize , onSelect , onReset , onContextMenu …) is attached to the component's element as a DOM listener and does not reach the component's props; for the camelCase spelling the compiler prints an MJX002 warning. For a callback prop, pick a name that does not clash with a DOM event ( onValueChange , onConfirm ). In a component without an element (a fragment) there is no element for such a listener to be attached to (see Root element ).

title: Events
heading: Handler signatures
text: A handler is written in one of two forms, and MotifJS calls the right one based on the number of parameters. The rule is the same for motif.on : a one-parameter handler receives the event, not the sender: sender — the ComponentBase instance that triggered the event; you can reach members such as sender.element , sender.context and sender.motif . If the handler returns { cancel: true } , MotifJS calls preventDefault() and stopPropagation() . Other return values, false included, are ignored, which is why the short body of onkeydown above does not cancel other keys. These methods are called only if they exist on the event object; when a plain data object is passed with motif.trigger("name", { … }) , neither is called and no error occurs. The :prevent / :stop modifiers follow the same rule. The number of parameters is the function's length : if the declared parameter count is ≤ 1, fn(event) is called, and if it is 2 or more, fn(sender, event) . A parameter with a default value or a rest parameter, and anything after it, is not counted; so (...a) => … counts as 0 and receives only event , and (s = null, e) => … counts as 0 too. In TypeScript both forms, on a plain tag and on a component tag, are typed from the element's event: with onkeydown={(e) => e.key} , e is a KeyboardEvent , and in the (s, e) => … form e gets the same type. Since the meaning of the first parameter depends on the number of parameters, the event and the component are typed together ( KeyboardEvent & ComponentBase ); use the event's members inside (e) => … and the component's members inside (s, e) => … . The type of motif.on is the (sender, e) signature; if you are going to use the event, write two parameters.

title: Events
heading: Handler errors
text: If a handler throws, or the promise returned by an async handler is rejected, the error is reported to errorHandler as a MotifError with the code MJX123 ( The '<event>' event handler threw. ), with the original error in the cause field. The report is written to the console in production mode too ( app.useLogging(false) turns it off) and reaches the errorHandler.addListener(fn) listeners. The other listeners of the same event keep running.

title: Events
heading: The on:name / on-name / on_name spelling
text: This spelling attaches the handler as it is to the tag's component: <X on:saved={fn}/> means sender.motif.on("saved", fn) . The event name is everything left after the prefix ( on: , on- , on_ ) is dropped: on-my-event → my-event , on_my_event → my_event . It is used both for DOM events and for custom events triggered with motif.trigger , and the parameter count rule above applies just the same: When the "Delete" button is pressed, the delete confirmation DeleteConfirm calls motif.trigger("confirm", note) on its own component ( this.motif.trigger in a class and in Options, the motif.trigger of the root it returns in a function component), and the first handler receives the note. Without JSX the listener is set up in the initializeComponent key, the same for class, function and Options components. Since the event name is free, the parameters of on: / on- / on_ props are typed any ; you give the data its own type in the parameter ( (target: Note) => … ). The type of motif.on is (sender, e) , so without JSX the data is the second parameter.

title: Events
heading: Event modifiers
text: Modifiers added to the event name with a colon adjust the behaviour. They are defined in the component.motif.on API and in the type system: Modifier Effect :once Runs once, then removes itself. :passive passive: true for addEventListener . :capture Listens in the capture phase. :prevent preventDefault() after the handler. :stop stopPropagation() after the handler. :self Runs only if the event target is the element itself. :trusted Runs only for isTrusted events. In JSX an attribute name can take only one : , so on a tag you write one modifier per attribute; with motif.on they chain. A prop with a modifier gets the same type as the one without; inside onkeydown:once={(e) => e.key} , e is a KeyboardEvent :

title: Events
heading: The component event API: motif.on / motif.off / motif.trigger
text: Programmatic event handling on every component lives in the motif namespace. In the example, when the row is clicked the component triggers its own saved event; that event's handler is registered internally only: In a function component these calls are made on the component itself ( row in the example): in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. Listeners added with motif.on are cleaned up automatically when the component is disposed. The third argument of motif.on is domEvent ( true by default). If you pass false , no addEventListener is done on the DOM; it is kept only as an internal (custom) event and is triggered with motif.trigger . On a component without an element (a fragment), a DOM listener listens on the component's content : each of its top-level element children, nested fragments included. A child added later is covered and a child that leaves is released; :self means the target is one of these elements; :once and motif.off act on all of them at once. motif.trigger("name", data) calls only the handlers registered under exactly that name (without modifiers, case-insensitive); a handler registered with "click:once" is not called by trigger("click") . Handlers receive data as the event object; no event is sent to the DOM. A :once handler is used up by whichever path reaches it first: trigger("click:once", data) runs it once and removes it, just like a DOM click; after that, motif.options.hasEvent("click:once") returns false . For DOM events, motif.off(name, fn) removes one registration of the same handler; if the same handler was added several times, call it once for each. The event name is given with the spelling used at registration (modifiers included). motif.addHandler(name, fn) is the same as motif.on(name, fn) (no return value). motif.toggle() hides the component if it is visible and shows it otherwise.

title: Events
heading: x:mounted — the moment of attaching to the DOM
text: A hook that runs when the element is actually added to the DOM; for work such as giving focus to the title field: In the function component, title is the component of the title field: obtained with ref in JSX, and the variable built with motifComponent without JSX. Each subscription runs once , in the task after the element is attached to document ; if the element is already in document , in the task after the subscription. When the component is detached and placed again (moving, motif.hide / motif.show , keepAlive), x:mounted does not fire again; use x:activated for that moment ( Lifecycle ). motif.off("x:mounted", handler) cancels a subscription that has not run yet. An error thrown by the handler is reported as MJX122 .

title: Events
heading: Lifecycle events
text: You can also listen to component lifecycle events with motif.on . The x: prefix attaches these events not to the DOM but to the component's own emitter; the handler is called with the (sender, e) signature ( e : { cancel } ), and a one-parameter handler receives only e : Recognized names: x:initializing , x:initialized , x:config , x:configured , x:building , x:built , x:mounted , x:visibilityChanged , x:activated , x:deactivated , x:disposing , x:disposed . The subscription is cleaned up together with the component, and it can also be removed by hand with motif.off . If the same handler subscribed several times, motif.off removes all of them. x:initializing and x:initialized end in the component's constructor; if you subscribe to a built component later, the handler runs once at the moment of subscribing. If one of these listeners throws, the error is reported to errorHandler with the code MJX122 (e.g. The component x:built hook threw. ), as if the hook had been written as a class method or a prop; the component keeps being built. A note on timing: on plain new Component("div", …) instances x:config fires in the constructor, so subscribing after the constructor returns is too late. In subclasses ( class X extends Component ) onConfig runs at the start of build() , so subscribing after the constructor is enough. Details: Lifecycle .

title: Events
heading: Application events — context.on / context.fire
text: To communicate between components (without a parent-child relationship), use the application event bus. A component's context is the running Application ( this.context in a class and in Options, the context of the root component in a function component); when the listening component is disposed, the subscription goes away on its own. ArchiveCounter counts archived notes: in the class it is this.context.on inside onConfig , in the function an onConfig prop written on the root, and in Options onConfigured ; without JSX all of them are the same context.on call: The publisher broadcasts through the context of the component sending the event; the second argument of fire goes to the listeners as data: The Application event API: Method Description app.on(event, handler) Listens; returns a function for unsubscribing. The handler's parameter is the data given to fire ( (note?: Note) => … ). app.fire(event, args?) Triggers the event. app.off(event, handler) Removes the listener. app.onRouterChanged(handler) A hook that runs on every navigation (startup and 404 included); returns a function for unsubscribing. app.onLifecycle(handler) Tab/application visibility and connectivity changes; see Application lifecycle . An event name can be a string or a Symbol ; fire calls the listeners synchronously, in the order they were added. An error thrown by an application event listener is reported with the code MJX123 ( The '<event>' event handler threw. ), and the event's other listeners run. The same goes for onRouterChanged handlers ( The 'motifjs-router-navigated' event handler threw. ); the navigation still completes. A component's context is a view of the application tied to the component: the on and onRouterChanged subscriptions opened through it are removed on their own when the component is disposed ( onLifecycle is not covered by this). Subscriptions opened through Application.main , an app instance you hold, or useApplication().application are not tied to any component; call the returned function yourself, or register it on a component with motif.setDisposable ( Memory Management and Disposal ):

title: Events
heading: Service events — Emitter<T>
text: Application events work by name and are open to the whole application. For a service to broadcast its own event together with its type, use Emitter<T> ; it is a small emitter that carries a single type and is independent of components. The service in the example announces the deleted note: A component ties the subscription to its own lifetime with motif.register ; when the component is disposed, the subscription goes away: In the function component, list is the component that carries the subscription: in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. event(listener, thisArgs?, disposables?) subscribes and returns an IDisposable ; if disposables is a DisposableStore or an IDisposable[] , the subscription is added there too ( notes.onRemoved(fn, undefined, store) ). fire(value) calls the listeners synchronously, in the order they were added. A listener added during dispatch does not receive that dispatch; a removed listener is never called again. An error thrown by a listener does not stop the others; it goes down the unexpected error path (see Unexpected errors ). dispose() invalidates every subscription; later event(...) calls return an empty IDisposable . The provider calls the service's dispose() method; for a singleton that is the moment of app.dispose() (see Disposing Services ).

title: Events
heading: Next step
text: To learn about form input and two-way binding, go on to Forms and Two-Way Binding .

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
text: MotifJS handles form input in two ways: Reactive read + event write (one-way, explicit): value={() => note.title} + oninput . A two-way binding ( bindings.model , x-model in JSX): the input and the model stay in sync automatically. For a one-way binding to a specific DOM property, use bindings.add . The examples are slices of the notes application. Note and NotesService are the ones in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page, and SettingsService and THEMES come from the src/services/settings.ts file on the Getting Started page; note is the note being edited.

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: The one-way (explicit) approach
text: You read the value reactively and write the change to the model with an event. This is the route to take when a change involves extra work (conversion, validation, a side effect): value and checked are property bindings: a value={() => …} written on a tag in JSX compiles to a bindings.add("value", getter) call, and no attribute is written.

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Two-way binding — bindings.model
text: bindings.model picks the right DOM property automatically based on the type of the element and binds it to the model in both directions: Element Bound property , checked (boolean) (others) value

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: The x-model shorthand
text: x-model compiles to a bindings.model(getter, setter) call and is two-way; without JSX you write the getter and the setter yourself: The setter the compiler produces reads the object that owns the member again on every write ( note for note.title , row.note for row.note.title , state.selected for state.selected.title ). That way the binding does not break when the object is replaced as a whole ( state.selected = otherNote ) or when list rows change places: The write is skipped while the owner is null / undefined ( x-model={() => state.selected?.title} ) and while the member holds a function (a getter prop). An expression without member access ( () => a + b , () => fn(x) ) is only read and stays one-way; motif-explain shows which case applies.

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: x-model on your own component
text: A component whose element is not a form element can also be used with x-model . The bound value is written to the component's value property; if the component defines its own value property, the value goes to the component even when its element is something with a value field of its own, such as a <button> . The component writes the new value back to the model with bindings.writeModel(value) ( this.bindings in a class and in Options, the bindings of the root component in a function component). PinSwitch is a button that turns pinning a note on and off: in the class and in Options, value is an accessor ( get / set ), and in the function the accessor is set up with Object.defineProperty in the root's initializeComponent hook: writeModel writes to every binding set up on the component with bindings.model or x-model ; converterBack is applied if there is one, and the write path is the same as on form elements. If there is no binding, it writes nothing and returns false , so the component can be used without x-model too. It does not touch bindings set up with bindings.add .

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Binding a specific property with bindings.add
text: If you want to specify which DOM property to bind yourself, use bindings.add . This binding is one-way (model → DOM); to write the user's change to the model, add an event handler: When checked , selected , muted , indeterminate and srcObject are written as attributes, they are assigned as element properties ( !!value ), not as HTML attributes: <input type="checkbox" indeterminate={() => selection.partial} /> .

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Text input and value
text: For <input> and <textarea> the value prop is recognized specially; it takes a reactive value or a getter:

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: A <select> example
text: The theme choice is written to the settings service. The change goes through setTheme , because the service applies the theme to <html> and saves it: <select x-model={() => settings.state.theme}> binds both ways too, but it writes to the field directly and skips the applying and saving that setTheme does.

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Form submission
text: NoteForm binds the fields of a new note to a draft with x-model and writes it to the service on submit. onsubmit:prevent keeps the page from reloading; without JSX the same modifier is given with motif.on("submit:prevent", …) : onsubmit={(sender, e) => { e.preventDefault(); save(); }} does the same job with a block body. When element methods are written as JSX props, no attribute is written and the method is called: <form requestSubmit={() => draft.send}> , <input focus={() => draft.editing} /> ( false → blur() ), <input setSelectionRange={[0, 5]} /> . reportValidity , checkValidity , select , reset and submit are in this group as well; for the full list and the value rules, see Element methods .

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Submitting with a function action
text: When a function is given to the action attribute instead of a URL, that function is called when the form is submitted and the page does not navigate. The search box is a form: on submit, search receives the query, and the "Clear" button empties the query with its own formAction : In the function component, search and refresh are local functions inside the component function, and state is the local state set up with reactive . As with every attribute, the value is read inside a getter. If the result is a function, no attribute is written and the function becomes the submit handler; if it is a string, it is written as the URL and stays live ( action="/search" , action={state.url} ). That is why, without JSX, the value is given with a getter: attr.add({ action: () => search }) attaches the handler, while attr.add({ action: search }) treats search as the getter and writes its result. motif-explain shows this attribute as attr.action . On submit, the form's own onsubmit handlers run first; if one of them called preventDefault() ( onsubmit:prevent included), the function is not called. Otherwise the framework calls preventDefault() , builds new FormData(form, submitter) and calls the function by the rules of event handlers: one parameter (data) , two parameters (sender, data) ; sender is the component that carries the attribute, the form for action and the button for formaction . The name / value pair of the submitting button is inside data . If the submitter's formaction is a function, it takes precedence over the form's action ; if it is a string, the browser does the submitting. form.requestSubmit() runs the function; form.submit() produces no event, so it does not. If the function throws, or the promise it returns is rejected, the error is reported with MJX123 (see Error Handling ). The form is not reset after submission; the function empties any field that needs emptying itself. The function can be async. The waiting state is kept in the operation itself: refresh pulls the notes from SyncService ( src/services/sync.ts on the Lifecycle page), raises a flag at the start and lowers it at the end, and the button is bound to that flag: In the function component, state is the local state the component sets up with reactive , and notes and sync are the services obtained with FromService .

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: A validation pattern
text: MotifJS does not impose a special validation API; you build it with reactive fields. A derived get field holds the rule, and x-wait holds the error text back until the rule is satisfied:

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Comparing the methods
text: Method When One-way ( value + oninput ) When you will run extra logic on change (conversion, validation, a side effect). bindings.model / x-model When two-way sync is enough; the least code. bindings.add("checked"/"value", ...) + an event When you want to pick the bound property by hand (one-way; writing back through an event). onsubmit:prevent When the fields are bound to the model; the submission only triggers the operation. action={fn} When the fields are not bound and you want their values in one go as FormData ; different operations per button with formaction .

title: Forms and Two-Way Binding
heading: Next step
text: To learn about the lifecycle of components in detail, go on to Lifecycle .

title: Lifecycle
text: Every MotifJS component goes through a set lifecycle, from its creation to being attached to the DOM and being disposed. You define the hooks that run at these stages as a class method , a JSX prop , or, without JSX, a key in the object form of motifComponent . The examples are slices of a notes application. Note and NotesService are the ones in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page; this is the service that pulls notes from the server:

title: Lifecycle
heading: Hooks and run order
text: Order Hook When it runs 1 onInitializing In the constructor, after the element has been assigned and the props processed ( this.props is ready; fields of the subclass such as state = reactive(...) have not been initialized yet). 2 onInitialized In the constructor, right after onInitializing . 3 onConfig The configuration stage; props are ready, not attached to the DOM yet . A good place to fetch data. In subclasses it runs at the start of build() (after the class fields are initialized). 4 onConfigured When configuration is complete (the start of the build). 5 onBuilding As DOM construction starts. 6 initializeComponent Right before view() is called; the component's setup code (the compiler produces it from JSX, and without JSX you write it). 7 oninitializeComponent Right after all initializeComponent code (the class method, the value on the tag, the one the compiler produced) has run, before view() . 8 onBuilt After the component and its children have been built. At this moment the element may still be inside a detached fragment (ternary/list branches). 9 onMounted Once , in the task after the component has been placed in a tree attached to a root on the page; the screen may have been painted by then. The root is the target of app.run or a component wrapping an element already in the document, and every component along the way must be visible. It is only for work that needs the element to really be on the page and visible: focus() , measurements, libraries that want the element in the document. Other setup work goes in onBuilt . — onActivated / onDeactivated When the component is detached from the DOM (without being disposed) and placed again: returning to a keepAlive route, controls.add after controls.detach / silentDetach (moving included), motif.hide() / motif.show() ( x-wait / x-display included), a Virtualization row leaving the window and coming back. onDeactivated on leaving, onActivated on coming back. It does not run on the first show.
