It is passed on to the visible subtree too (parent first); a hidden child is not activated together with its parent, it is activated by its own motif.show() . — onVisibilityChanged When motif.show() / motif.hide() / motif.toggle() ( x-wait / x-display included) change visibility; it runs before isVisible is updated (when hiding, after the leave animation finishes; with hideStrategy: "detach" , before the animation), so inside the hook isVisible shows the previous value and e.visible the new one. — onDisposing As disposal starts. — onDisposed When disposal is complete. onInitializing and onInitialized run while the component is being created (in the constructor flow). onConfig runs in the constructor for plain new Component(tag, { onConfig }) instances; in subclasses ( class X extends Component ) it runs after class fields such as state = reactive(...) have been initialized, at the start of build() , right before onConfigured (a subclass instance that is never built does not get onConfig ). onConfigured , onBuilding , initializeComponent , oninitializeComponent and onBuilt run during build() ; onMounted runs in the task after the component has been placed in a tree attached to the root (also in the next task if the tree is already attached at the moment it is placed). isInitialized is false during onInitializing and true from onInitialized on (it is set when the initialization in the constructor finishes). onMounted hooks are queued and run after the task that did the setup, in the order they were registered. The queue is processed in 8 ms slices: when the time is up, the remaining hooks are left for the next task, and in between the browser paints the screen and handles user input. That way, setting up many components that wrap a chart or table library does not lock up the page. A child component's hook runs before its parent's, and the hook of a component disposed before its turn does not run. The core follows the placing: controls.add , the end of an x-wait , motif.show() and Transporter put the hook in the queue; if you put an element into the document yourself with appendChild , the hook does not run. To give content to an element that already exists, wrap the element with new Component(element) and add the children with controls.add ; the body of a window opened with window.open is wrapped the same way, and the components given to that window are attached there. The queue runs on the timer of the window the root is in. State flags: isInitialized , isConfigured , isBuilt , isVisible , isWait and isDisposed are updated when the corresponding phase has passed, and are read from the component. onInitializing , onInitialized and onConfig written on an Options API object do not run (these phases end before the fields are copied from the object); for setup use ctor or onConfigured (see Options API ).

title: Lifecycle
heading: Defining hooks
text: In a class a hook is a method; in a function component it is a prop written on the returned root, and in the Options API it is a member of the object. Without JSX the class method stays the same, and for functions and plain tags the hook is a key in the object form of motifComponent . NoteBoard fetches the notes while it is being configured ( onConfig ), focuses the search box once it enters the DOM ( onMounted ) and refreshes once a minute; the timer is tied to the component with motif.setDisposable and stops on its own during disposal: Every hook is called with the (sender, e) signature: sender is the component itself and e is EventArgs ( { cancel: boolean } ). In a function component sender is the returned root; the NoteBoard written as a function ties the timer to this root's motif.setDisposable . An error thrown in a hook, or the rejection of a Promise returned by a hook ( async hooks included), is reported as MotifError MJX122 : it is written to console.error (unless app.useLogging(false) ) and passed to the errorHandler.addListener(fn) listeners; development mode is not required, it works in production too. The component keeps being built. This rule also applies to initializeComponent , oninitializeComponent , the ctor of an Options API object, the ref callback (on a plain tag and on a class component tag; the component is still created) and lifecycle listeners added in code with motif.on("x:built", fn) ( x:mounted included).

title: Lifecycle
heading: Hooks on a tag
text: A hook can be written as a prop on any tag, and it is attached to that tag's component. Without JSX the same names are keys of the object form. In the example, onMounted is given to a plain tag and onDisposing to a component tag ( TitleSync , described below): The x- and x: forms are accepted too: <ul x-config={…} x:built={…}> . In an object without JSX the x- form works as a key ( { "x-config": … } ); only JSX recognizes the x: form. Important: lifecycle handlers you give as props do not replace the class methods; both run (prop handlers are collected and called in addition to the class method). Several spellings of a hook on the same tag ( on<hook> , x-<hook> , x:<hook> ; differences in case included, e.g. onBuilt and onbuilt ) are combined: each runs once, in source order. Without JSX a key can also be given an array of functions ( onBuilt: [a, b] ); they run in the order of the array. This is the same on a plain DOM tag and on a component tag; on a function component tag the hooks, whether written once or combined, are applied to the root the function returns. The initializing / initialized hooks on a function component tag run as soon as the root is built, in the same order as on a class component tag: ref → initializing → initialized → config → … → building → initializeComponent → built . This rule holds for all of the built , building , mounted , config , configured , initializing , initialized , disposing , disposed , visibilitychanged , activated and deactivated hooks:

title: Lifecycle
heading: initializeComponent — the component's setup code
text: initializeComponent runs once per component, right before view() . The compiler passes the setup code it produces from JSX (the attributes written on the tag, events, directives, placing the children) under this name; without JSX, the second argument of the motifComponent(tag, setup) call is exactly this. In a component that uses JSX it is also used to add a binding or to prepare children in code. TitleSync keeps the tab title in step with the number of notes: initializeComponent can also be written as a prop on a tag; the tag's component is given as sender , and it is called once during setup. On a plain DOM tag, on a class component tag and on a function component tag (on the root the function returns), its meaning and timing are the same: Both the one the user gives and the one the compiler produces run; the order is: the component's initializeComponent method, the one given on the tag, the one the compiler produced.

title: Lifecycle
heading: oninitializeComponent — right after the setup code
text: In a component that uses JSX, the initializeComponent stage is filled by the compiler's setup code. oninitializeComponent is the hook that runs in the same stage, right after that code finishes. At this moment the attributes, events, bindings and children have been defined, and view() has not been called yet. This is the place for code that wants to add its own setup on top of the setup the compiler produced. The order inside build() : The class's initializeComponent method. The initializeComponent values from the tag or from the compiler. The class's oninitializeComponent method. The oninitializeComponent values from the tag. view() . As a class method (a member with the same name on an Options API object runs at the same point): As a prop on a tag (a plain DOM tag, a class component tag and a function component tag; on a function component it is applied to the root the function returns). When this hook runs, the children written on the tag have been added to controls ; without JSX it is a key of the object form, and it runs after the children added by the setup function or given with childs :

title: Lifecycle
heading: Visibility — motif.show / motif.hide / motif.toggle
text: You can hide and show a component without disposing it: In a function component these calls are made on the component itself ( panel in the example): in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. When visibility changes, onVisibilityChanged(sender, e) runs; the hook is called before isVisible is updated. The new state is in the event argument: e.visible is true while showing and false while hiding, while isVisible gives the previous state at that moment. The same argument also reaches the onVisibilityChanged prop and a motif.on("x:visibilityChanged", …) listener. A hidden component and its subtree get onDeactivated , and onActivated when shown again. Bindings keep running while it is hidden, and the component appears with the current value when shown. The same order applies to a component without an element (a fragment): the children's elements swap places with their own markers ( <!--h--> ) and play their own leave/enter transitions, and the notification goes to the fragment first and then to the visible children; the children's own isVisible does not change, a child hidden separately stays hidden when the fragment is shown, and a child added while the fragment is hidden (new, built earlier or moved from another parent) stays hidden as well; its place is set by its order in controls , and it takes that place when the fragment is shown.

title: Lifecycle
heading: Hide strategy — hideStrategy
text: hideStrategy decides how a hidden component is handled in the DOM: Value Behaviour 'placeholder' The element leaves the DOM and a <!--h--> comment marker is put in its place; when showing, it swaps with the marker. controls.move and list sorting move the marker together with the component. 'detach' Removed from the DOM without leaving a trace; when shown, it is added again according to its order in the parent. 'auto' (default) Behaves like placeholder ; every component, .map rows and items given a key included, leaves a marker in its place. The strategy is given with options ; it is a prop in JSX and a key of the object form without JSX. In code, write it to the motif.options.hideStrategy field: In the function component, state is the local state the component sets up with reactive . options is the component's own settings object, and the keys the framework recognizes are read: hideStrategy and disableDisposal are copied into motif.options , and isSvg decides the element's namespace (see Root element ); other keys are ignored. Do not use this name as a data prop. An options written on a function component tag is applied to the returned root.

title: Lifecycle
heading: Waiting — isWait / x-wait
text: The x-wait directive makes adding a component to the DOM depend on a condition; its programmatic counterpart is the isWait property ( isWait is not a JSX prop). While the condition is true the component is held (hidden/not added), and when it turns false it is added. This is the primary method for conditional rendering — see Conditional Rendering and Lists . In the example, the component tag is not built for as long as the x-wait condition is true : A child chunked with x-chunk also waits with isWait until its turn comes and leaves its marker; when its turn comes, the framework lifts the wait. If you write isWait = false earlier yourself, the child is built right away and leaves the chunk queue — see Large lists . In code: Two points that matter for the lifecycle: If the condition is true at the start , build() does not run until the condition turns false . onConfig / onConfigured run, but the onBuilding / onBuilt / onMounted hooks do not fire until then, and the component's subtree is not built and does not enter the DOM. Only a <!--h--> marker sits in its place; when the condition turns false , the component is built and takes the marker's place. Going back to the waiting state does not dispose . onDisposing / onDisposed do not run and the internal state is kept; the component is hidden and gets onDeactivated . If you really want disposal, use {condition && <X/>} ( bindings.when(conditionFn, buildFn) without JSX) or call dispose() .

title: Lifecycle
heading: Disposal (dispose)
text: A component that is no longer needed is disposed. This removes its event listeners, deactivates its bindings, disposes its children recursively and takes it out of the DOM: deep ( true by default) also does reference cleanup in the child components ( element , props , childs , the event maps); the root component is always cleaned up. disposeAsync is the path the framework uses for the children while a parent is being disposed; called from outside, the component goes away without waiting for the leave transition. While a disposal is in progress, a second dispose / disposeAsync call does not start a new one; it returns the same Promise. controls.remove(child) or controls.clear() dispose the children concerned as well. Everything you set up with JSX or with motifComponent (listeners, bindings, children, context.on subscriptions) is cleaned up on its own; external resources such as timers, observers and sockets you register with motif.setDisposable (like the setInterval in NoteBoard ). For details, see Memory Management and Disposal .

title: Lifecycle
heading: The application lifecycle — app.onLifecycle
text: Separate from component hooks, the application as a whole has a lifecycle too: the tab goes to the background, a mobile operating system freezes the page, the connection drops. For pausing and resuming polling, websockets and timers, and for refreshing stale data on return: app.isVisible and app.isOnline give the current state. The browser listeners are set up only on the first subscription (if unused, they cost nothing) and are removed with app.dispose() . The subscription is not tied to a component's lifetime; if you open it from inside a component, register off with the component's motif.setDisposable(off) ( this.motif in a class and in Options, the motif of the root component in a function component).

title: Lifecycle
heading: Next step
text: To learn about the styling and animation system, go on to Styling and Animation .

title: Styling and Animation
text: The class/style/attr helpers, inline <style>, the CSS class based transition prop, WAAPI keyframe transitions, visibility and the enter/leave mode.

title: Styling and Animation
heading: class
text: An element's class is given with the class (or className ) attribute in JSX, and with the element's class.add call without JSX. The value can be a string, an array, an object or a getter: In an object the key is the class name and the value is the condition: if it is truthy the class is added, otherwise it is removed. On a plain tag, constants such as true / false are applied once, and other values are wrapped in a getter and stay live. On a component tag the compiler wraps only the ternary; there, pass a live condition as a function (see JSX: class ). In an object passed to class.add , a value that is not a function is read once, at the time of the call; for a live condition, pass a function (see JSX: class ).

title: Styling and Animation
heading: style
text: Inline style is given with the style attribute in JSX, and with the element's style call without JSX. The value can be a string, an object or a getter; when a value the getter reads changes, the style is written again (see JSX: style ):

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Inline <style>
text: You can give CSS directly inside view() with a <style> block; without JSX, this is a "style" element whose text is the CSS. The rules are not limited to the component; they apply to the whole document:

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Classes and styles in code
text: After setup, classes and styles change through the component's class and style helpers: In a function component these calls are made on the component itself ( row in the example): in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. class.remove("**") removes every class and every live source, and class.has tells whether the element has the class. class.add keeps reference counting: if the same class is added from several sources, the class stays until all of them are removed. In an object passed to class.add , a value that is not a function is read once, at the time of the call; for a live condition, pass a function. The object form of style changes only the properties it gives, while the string form replaces the whole inline style.

title: Styling and Animation
heading: The attribute helper — attr
text: Attributes are written in code with the component's attr helper: Attributes written on a tag in JSX are also attr.add calls in the compiler output; the value rules below are the same for both. The RouterLink component adds its href this way too (unless showHref: false is given). attr.add values: false , null and undefined remove the attribute, true writes it with an empty value ( "" ), and strings and numbers are written as they are. On aria-* and data-* attributes true / false are written as text ( "true" / "false" ). If a key in the object is null , only that attribute is removed and the other keys are written ( attr.add({ title: null, role: "tab" }) ). Attribute names are only the object's own keys passed to attr.add ; the value is not looked into. An object or array value is turned into text and written as a single attribute value: { title: { a: 1 } } → title="[object Object]" , { 'data-ids': [1, 2] } → data-ids="1,2" . Objects and arrays returned by a getter are written the same way. For a key whose name is the same as an element method, the value is that method's argument (see Element methods ).

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Tailwind, Bootstrap and external CSS
text: MotifJS is not tied to any CSS solution; the classes of a CSS library are given like any other class: For Tailwind, add the @tailwindcss/vite plugin to vite.config.ts .

title: Styling and Animation
heading: The transition system
text: MotifJS supports two kinds of enter/leave animation: CSS class based transitions — with the transition prop. WAAPI (Web Animations API) keyframes — in code, with motif.options.transition.in/out . Transitions play automatically when a component is added to the DOM (enter) and when it is removed or hidden (leave).

title: Styling and Animation
heading: CSS class based transitions — the transition prop
text: The transition is given a name: the transition attribute in JSX, and the transition key of the props object without JSX. The pin mark in the example is shown and hidden as the note is pinned and unpinned, and the transition plays both ways: This applies the following CSS classes at the right stages: Stage Classes applied Enter fade-enter-from → fade-enter-active → fade-enter-to Leave fade-leave-from → fade-leave-active → fade-leave-to You write the matching CSS: transition works the same way on a plain element, a class component and a function component; on a function component it is applied to the returned root, and a value given from outside takes precedence over the value the function writes on its own root. The value can also be a getter: it is tracked for as long as the component lives, and if the getter returns null or an empty string the transition is turned off. In JSX, a ternary written on a tag compiles to a getter on its own; without JSX you pass the getter yourself: In the function component, settings is the service the component gets with FromService(SettingsService) .

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Custom class names and duration — the object form
text: Class names and the duration are customized by giving transition a TransitionProps object:

title: Styling and Animation
heading: WAAPI keyframe animation — motif.options.transition.in/out
text: For keyframe animations defined in code, the enter and leave animations are given with motif.options.transition.in / out , in the component's onConfig or initializeComponent stage: In a class component and in an Options object, the same calls are written in the component's own onConfigured hook as this.motif.options.transition.in(...) and out(...) . in / out use the standard WAAPI element.animate(keyframes, options) signature: keyframes : Keyframe[] or PropertyIndexedKeyframes options : a duration (number) or KeyframeAnimationOptions The in / out definition belongs to the component and is used on every later enter/leave; calling it again replaces the previous one. Running animations are kept in the motif.options.transition.activeAnimations array. When a new keyframe animation starts on the component, the running one is cancelled: if motif.hide() is called while the enter is running, the enter is cut off and the leave plays; if motif.show() is called while the leave is running, the leave is cut off and the enter plays. Precedence: if both WAAPI ( motif.options.transition.in/out ) and a CSS class transition are defined on a component, the WAAPI keyframes take precedence.

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Transitions and visibility
text: When motif.hide() / motif.show() is called, the matching leave/enter transition plays automatically. On leave, removal from the DOM happens after the leave animation finishes. If two calls come one after the other, the last one wins: if motif.hide() comes while the enter is running, the enter is cut off and the leave plays; if motif.show() comes while the leave is running, the leave is cut off, the element is not removed from its place and the enter transition plays from the start. The await motif.hide() promise of the interrupted leave resolves at that moment, and the component has stayed visible. The x-display and x-wait conditions follow the same rule: if the condition flips back before the leave finishes, the element is not removed. If the root is a fragment, the same goes for its children. To make the next leave happen without animation, turn on the component's skipNextLeave flag: In the function component, panel is the component to hide: the component held through ref or received by the onConfig hook, and without JSX the component returned by motifComponent . The flag affects only the next leave and is reset once used. If the root is a fragment, the visible children are hidden without animation as well. A route page's transitions play during navigation too: the page that leaves finishes its leave transition, and then the incoming page enters. When the router is in stack mode ( useRouter({ stack }) ) and stack.animation is not given (or is 'none' ), these transitions are used as the stack transition, and the page element carries data-nav-direction for the duration of the enter transition. When stack.animation is given, the stack animation plays on push , back and forward navigations instead of the page's own enter transition; see Stack Navigation .

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Enter and leave order — mode
text: When one child leaves a container while another enters, there are two modes: Mode Behaviour 'concurrent' (default) The incoming child is placed right away and plays its enter, while the outgoing child's leave runs at the same time. 'out-in' The incoming child is not placed in the DOM until the leaves running in that container finish; when they finish, it is placed and plays its enter. 'in-out' The incoming child is placed right away and plays its enter; the outgoing child stays in place meanwhile and plays its leave once the incoming one's enter is finished. The mode is given in three places, and the narrower one overrides the wider one. For the whole application, without needing the router: Per container, with the container's transition value: or through the container's settings, in code: A transition value that carries only mode sets the mode and adds no animation to the container itself; it can also be given together with name and class names. The mode applies to every child that comes to the container with controls.add : when /ternary/ switch branches, Frame and Lazy content, list rows, components added by hand. The mode is read from the nearest element container: containers with a comment node, such as Frame and fragments, use their parent's mode if they have none of their own, so it also works when a conditional branch changes inside an element that carries the mode (see Frame timing ). When switching between siblings with motif.hide() / motif.show() , show waits for the sibling's leave too. If a child that arrives while waiting is removed or hidden again, it is never placed. If no leave is running, out-in does not wait. A cancelled leave ( Animation.cancel ) releases the one waiting. In in-out mode the outgoing child's leave waits one microtask to see the enters starting in the same operation; if the incoming child has no enter transition, or nothing comes in at all, the leave plays right away. If the outgoing child is being disposed, the dispose() Promise resolves when the leave finishes; the same goes for motif.hide() . A cancelled enter releases the leave waiting on it.

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Stopping active animations
text: A running CSS class transition is finished right away, running WAAPI animations are cancelled, and activeAnimations is emptied. If the interrupted transition was a leave, the hiding completes at that moment: the element leaves the document and its marker stays in its place. The running animations of a component being disposed are cancelled the same way.

title: Styling and Animation
heading: Next step
text: To manage the lifetime of components and resources, go on to Memory Management and Disposal .

title: Memory Management and Disposal
text: In MotifJS every element is a live component: it holds its own event listeners, bindings, reactive subscriptions and children. When the component is disposed, these are released together with it. Resources opened outside the component (a timer, a listener added to the document, an observer, a connection), on the other hand, you tie to the component yourself.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: What is released on its own
text: While a component is being disposed, MotifJS does the following itself: Removes the DOM listeners attached with motif.on . Stops the bindings ( bindings : text, attributes, watch , method …). Releases the context.on and context.onRouterChanged subscriptions. Runs the functions registered with motif.setDisposable and disposes the objects tied with motif.register . Disposes the child components the same way. Takes the element out of the document; if a leave transition is defined, after the transition finishes. Clears the component's fields: element , props , class , attr and the fields you added to the component become undefined . For children this step is skipped with dispose({ deep: false }) . No manual cleanup is needed for the events, bindings and children the component sets up itself.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Resources tied by hand
text: The component does not know about a resource opened outside it: setInterval , a document or window listener, ResizeObserver , WebSocket . These are tied to the component's lifetime through the motif namespace; this.motif in a class and in Options, and the root's motif in a function component.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: motif.setDisposable(fn) and motif.register(object)
text: A note row's date is written with formatDay(note.updatedAt, now) : the time for today, "Yesterday" for yesterday, and the day for anything older. The component in the example refreshes now once a minute so the text changes when the day turns over; the timer stops when the component is disposed: The row places the date with <NoteTime note={note} /> . The row places the date with new NoteTime({ note }) . The row places the date with motifComponent(NoteTime, { note }) . motif.setDisposable(fn) : fn runs once, while the component is being disposed. motif.register(object) : ties an object that has a dispose() method ( IDisposable ) to the component's lifetime; the object is disposed together with the component. disposableCore.toDisposable(fn) turns a function into such an object: motif.register(disposableCore.toDisposable(() => clearInterval(timer))) does the same job as setDisposable .

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Application event subscriptions
text: A subscription the component opens with context.on(...) is tied to the component's lifetime on its own and goes away when the component is disposed. To release it earlier, call the function it returns: In a function component the calls on this page are made on the component itself ( list in the examples): in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. A subscription opened outside the component, through the application ( app.on(...) , Application.main.on(...) ), is not tied to any component; give the function it returns to a component with motif.setDisposable , or call it yourself.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Cleaning up an effect
text: effect(...) is not tied to any component; to stop it, call the function it returns. For a watcher that belongs to a component, bindings.watch does the same job and stops together with the component: The two forms give the same result: in the first, the component releases the watcher, and in the second, you hand the stop function to the component yourself.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: The dispose methods
text: For details of the options, see Disposal . isDisposed tells whether the component has been disposed; calling dispose() again on a disposed component does nothing, and motif calls do not throw. Children are disposed through controls as well: motif.clear() does nothing if motif.options.disableDisposal is on; controls.clear() ignores this setting.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Moving without disposing
text: remove() and clear() dispose the child: its bindings, watchers, listeners and DOM go away. To move a component somewhere else without disposing it, or to reuse it later, use one of these three: Method Collection Leave animation DOM Notification detach(child) removes plays it : the element's own leave if the root is an element; if the root is a fragment, the leaves of its visible element children (nested fragments included) together removes it when the leave finishes (for a fragment root, the whole range from opening to closing; if hidden, the placeholder); synchronous if no transition is defined controlremoved on the parent after the leave finishes and the DOM is removed silentDetach(child) removes does not play removes synchronously none silentUnlink(child) removes does not play does not touch none All three leave the component and its children alive. detach and silentDetach send onDeactivated to the component and its visible subtree when the DOM is removed, and onActivated when the component is placed again with controls.add ; silentUnlink does not touch the DOM, so it sends no notification ( Lifecycle ). detach returns a Promise ; if there is a transition it resolves when the removal is finished, otherwise it comes back already resolved: Writing other.controls.add(child) without waiting is safe too: detach from the old parent happens on its own, the collection and parent are updated right away, and the DOM is attached to the new parent when the leave finishes. The other ways of removing with animation are motif.hide() and dispose() .

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: DisposableStore — cleaning up a group
text: Several resources are collected in a DisposableStore and disposed together: If you add to a store that has been closed, the added object does not enter the store and is not disposed (it leaks); in development mode an MJX504 warning is written. If several items throw during clear / dispose , all of them are gathered in an AggregateError in the cause of a single MJX503 error; a single error is thrown as it is. A store is tied to a component with motif.register(store) .

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Safety after disposal: using and doWork
text: When an async job finishes, the component may have been disposed and its fields cleared. using(promise, onfulfilled?, onrejected?) passes the result to the handlers only if the component is alive, and returns nothing (see Async Results with using ). doWork(promise) returns a promise; if the component has been disposed, a MotifError with the code MJX108 arrives in place of the value or the rejection (see Async Results with doWork ).

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Leak tracking
text: When the number of effects tracking a single field of a reactive object reaches threshold (200 if not given), an MJX507 warning is written; the warning also shows the most frequent setup stack. This usually means that the bindings of components that were never disposed are piling up. The warning is written only in development mode. Tracking is off by default; turn it on during development.

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Counting live components — disposableCore.disposableTracker
text: Every component is a Disposable : its constructor calls trackDisposable , and the disposal chain calls markAsDisposed . By attaching a tracker to disposableCore.disposableTracker , the number of live components is measured; it is used in round-trip tests ("after building and tearing down N times, did the counter go back to where it started?"): Next to components, the tracker also receives stores and toDisposable objects; the instanceof check in the example counts components only. markAsDisposed arrives once per object; it is not reported again even if dispose() is called again. To inspect the dependency maps of reactive objects, use debugGetDeps(target) and debugGetDepMap() from the @motifx/core/devtools subpath ( import { debugGetDeps } from "@motifx/core/devtools" ). In development mode, __MOTIF_DEVTOOLS__.getCounters().components.notInTree counts components that are alive but not in the tree; if it does not drop after leaving a page, those components are being held somewhere ( The DevTools Contract ).

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Best practices
text: The events, bindings and children a component sets up itself are released on their own; no cleanup is written for them. Every resource opened outside the component (a timer, a document or window listener, an observer, a connection) is tied to the component with motif.setDisposable or motif.register . For a reactive watcher that belongs to a component, use bindings.watch instead of effect . Handle async results with using or doWork . A component added by hand with controls.add is disposed together with its container; to remove it earlier, use controls.remove .

title: Memory Management and Disposal
heading: Next step
text: To learn how errors are thrown, reported and caught, go on to Error Handling .

title: Error Handling
text: MotifJS does not swallow errors coming from user code, but it does not bring the application down either. Every situation the framework throws, reports or writes as a warning has an MJX code , and these situations go down one of three paths. This section covers those paths, the places to listen for errors, and the framework's own error-safe call helpers. The full list of codes is in the Error and Warning Codes table.

title: Error Handling
heading: Three paths
text: Path When Where it goes Throw Misuse the caller has to fix right away: the named route does not exist ( MJX302 ), the service is not registered ( MJX401 ), a second ApplicationBuilder ( MJX405 ), Query.first() on an empty array ( MJX601 ) … A MotifError is thrown; catch it with try/catch . Report A user code error that should not stop the flow: a component hook ( MJX122 ), an event handler ( MJX123 ), an effect/binding ( MJX208 ), a route hook and guard ( MJX306 ), disposal and data loading errors … errorHandler.report(MotifError) : to the console with console.error ( app.useLogging(false) turns it off), to the errorHandler.addListener(fn) listeners, and to the devtools bus if there is one. The original error is in cause . Works in production too. Warning A situation that keeps running but is most likely unwanted: a duplicate key ( MJX202 ), an effect that triggers itself ( MJX203 ), route definition checks ( MJX310 – MJX316 ) … Only in development mode ( app.useDevelopment(true) ): console.warn and the devtools warning list. It does not go to listeners.

title: Error Handling
heading: MotifError
text: Every error the framework throws or reports is a MotifError : Field Description code MotifErrorCode (such as 'MJX302' ). Branch on this, not on the message text; the texts are in English and may change. message An English message of the form [motifjs] MJX302: … . cause For reported errors, the original error (the value the user code threw). name 'MotifError' ( 'TimeoutError' for a Resilience timeout). The MotifErrorCode type is the union of all codes; it gives completion when you write switch (e.code) .

title: Error Handling
heading: Listening for reports — errorHandler
text: A listener receives every reported MotifError ( MJX122 , MJX123 , MJX208 , MJX306 …). Errors without a code that go to setUnexpectedErrorHandler (below) reach the listeners as they are too. Thrown errors do not go to the listener (they already return to the caller), and neither do warnings. A listener is not tied to any component; it is removed with the function returned by addListener ( off() ). Listeners are called in the order they were added. An error thrown by one listener does not stop the other listeners or the flow that made the report; the error is rethrown with setTimeout(…, 0) and shows up in the browser at the window.onerror level. safeCall still returns the fallback value in that case. You can put your own error on the same path with errorHandler.report(err) ; err must be an Error , it does not have to be a MotifError . The other members of the ErrorHandler class: setDevelopmentMode(b) / isDevelopment() ( app.useDevelopment uses these), setConsoleLogging(b) ( app.useLogging ), reportSuppressed(context, err) (writes to the console only in development mode and does not go to listeners; the framework uses it for errors it swallows internally), getUnexpectedErrorHandler() .

title: Error Handling
heading: Unexpected errors — setUnexpectedErrorHandler
text: Errors caught inside safeCall / safeCallAsync and errors thrown by Emitter listeners have no code ; they go down the errorHandler.onUnexpectedError(err) path: The handler given with setUnexpectedErrorHandler(fn) is called. The default handler rethrows the error with setTimeout(…, 0) : it shows up in the browser at the window.onerror / unhandledrejection level, and the calling flow is not interrupted. Then the addListener listeners receive the error as it is. Reports with a code ( MJX122 …) do not go to this handler; use addListener for them.

title: Error Handling
heading: Error-safe call helpers
text: The helpers the framework uses to wrap its own code are public: Function Behaviour safeCall(fn, context, fallback?) Calls fn() ; if it throws, writes [motifjs Error - context] in development mode, passes the error to onUnexpectedError and returns fallback (or undefined ). safeCallAsync(fn, context, fallback?) The same; fn returns a Promise , and the rejection is caught. safeCallSilent(fn, context) If it throws, writes to the console only in development mode; it does not go to onUnexpectedError or the listeners. errorHandler.safeCallSilentAsync , errorHandler.wrapSafe(fn, context) , errorHandler.wrapSafeAsync(fn, context) An async silent call; return a new function that wraps fn with the same behaviour (reports like safeCall ). context is a free label that only appears in the log.

title: Error Handling
heading: Where is an error in user code caught?
text: Place Result A lifecycle hook ( onConfig , onBuilt , onMounted …), initializeComponent , a ref callback, an Options API ctor , a motif.on('x:…') listener An MJX122 report; the component keeps being built. The rejected promise of an async hook is the same. A DOM/component event handler ( onclick , motif.on , on:name ) An MJX123 report; the other handlers of the same event run. An application event listener ( app.on , onRouterChanged ) An MJX123 report; the other listeners run and the navigation completes. effect , bindings.watch , a binding getter, a createComputed getter An MJX208 report; the other effects in the same flush run, and the effect that failed keeps tracking. That run has no value: onValue in effect(getter, onValue) is not called, and bindings ( text / attr / class , a when / ternary / switchCase branch) keep their last healthy state. A route hook ( onEntering , onEnter , onLeave , onUpdate , onShow ) An MJX306 report; the navigation continues. A useGuard guard An MJX306 report, and the navigation is cancelled ( { ok: false, cancelled: true, reason: 'guard' } ). A route component's constructor / an import() failure An MJX304 report and the fallbacks.error page ( params.error ). Virtualization dataRequest First load/refresh: errorTemplate or MJX207 ; a later page: MJX207 + getState().error . Lazy caller onError , then Fallbackview ; if there is no Fallbackview , MJX126 is reported ( cause = the original error). Cancellation ( signal ) is not reported. Several errors inside DisposableStore.clear/dispose MJX503 is thrown; the cause.errors array. An Emitter listener onUnexpectedError (default: rethrow) + the listeners.

title: Error Handling
heading: Development and production
text: Development ( app.useDevelopment(true) ) Production Reports ( MJX122 …) console + listeners console + listeners Warnings ( MJX2xx , the MJX3xx checks …) console.warn none safeCallSilent / reportSuppressed console none Compiler contract mismatch ( MJX121 ) console.warn none app.useLogging(false) turns off only the console output; the listeners keep working.

title: Error Handling
heading: Next step
text: To wrap network and external resource calls with retries, timeouts and a circuit breaker, see Resilience .

title: Resilience
text: Network requests and external resources fail, slow down and get overloaded. Resilience offers six policies for these situations and combines them in a single chain. It is independent of the rest of the framework, and can be used in services, in the data layer or inside a dataRequest .

title: Resilience
heading: The chain and its order
text: Resilience.create gives a new, empty chain; each policy method adds to the chain and returns the same object. execute(action, ctx?) wraps the added policies from the outside in, in the order they were added , and runs action : timeout and fallback require an options object (the timeoutMs and fallback fields are mandatory); for the other policies the options are optional. action can be synchronous or return a Promise ; execute always returns a Promise . ctx is a free-form object ( ResilienceContext ), passed as it is to action(ctx) and to the callbacks. The types are exported: RetryOptions , TimeoutOptions , CircuitBreakerOptions , BulkheadOptions , RateLimiterOptions and FallbackOptions<T> for the options; CircuitState for the circuit state; ResiliencePolicy for the execute signature and ResilienceAction<T> for action . The Resilience class implements ResiliencePolicy ; type a function that takes a chain as (policy: ResiliencePolicy) => … . State lives in the chain. circuitBreaker , bulkhead and rateLimiter keep counters between calls, and every Resilience.create opens new counters. For these policies to be of any use, build the chain once (a service field, a module constant) and use the execute of the same object on every call. retry , timeout and fallback are stateless. In this order each attempt runs with its own 8-second timeout. By default a timeout is neither retried nor counted as a failure for the circuit; if you want the circuit to open for a server that does not respond, give circuitBreaker shouldHandle: () => true .

title: Resilience
heading: retry(options?)
text: Waits and retries a failed action . Option Default Description retries 3 The number of retries; total attempts are retries + 1 . backoff 'exponential' 'exponential' : delay × 2^(attempt−1) ; 'fixed' : delay every time; 'none' : no waiting. delay 100 The base wait (ms). jitter 0.1 The share of randomness added to the wait (0–1): the wait varies within ± jitter × wait . shouldHandle every error except a timeout (error) => boolean ; if it returns false , there is no retry and the error is thrown right away. The default does not retry a TimeoutError (the timeout policy's error) or a rejection with undefined / null . onRetry — (attempt, error, waitMs, ctx) ; called before each wait, and awaited if it returns a Promise . If the last attempt also fails, the last error is thrown. To retry a request that timed out as well, give shouldHandle: () => true .

title: Resilience
heading: `timeout(
text: If action does not finish within timeoutMs , a MotifError with the code MJX605 and the name 'TimeoutError' is thrown. The running operation is not cancelled (wire up an AbortController yourself for fetch ); its result is just not waited for. The timer is cleared in both cases.

title: Resilience
heading: circuitBreaker(options?)
text: After failures in a row, it rejects calls for a while without making them at all, giving the resource room to recover. Option Default Description failureThreshold 5 In the CLOSED state, this many consecutive failures open the circuit. A success in between resets the counter. successThreshold 2 In the HALF_OPEN state, this many consecutive successes close the circuit. durationOfBreakMs 60000 How long the OPEN state lasts; when it is over, the first call moves to HALF_OPEN . shouldHandle every error except a timeout Which errors count as failures. The default does not count a TimeoutError or a rejection with undefined / null . onStateChange — (old, new) ; 'CLOSED' \| 'OPEN' \| 'HALF_OPEN' . In the OPEN state, execute throws MJX602 without calling action . In HALF_OPEN , a single failure opens the circuit again. Follow the circuit state with onStateChange ; the chain has no "read the state" method.

title: Resilience
heading: bulkhead(options?)
text: Limits the number of action s running at the same time; the rest go into a queue. Option Default Description maxConcurrent 10 The concurrency limit. maxQueue 50 The limit of the waiting queue; when it is full, MJX603 is thrown. The queue is FIFO; when a call finishes, the next one starts.

title: Resilience
heading: rateLimiter(options?)
text: A token bucket: each call spends a token, and tokens refill at intervals. Option Default Description tokensPerInterval 1 Tokens added each interval. intervalMs 1000 The interval. capacity tokensPerInterval The bucket's capacity; the bucket starts full. Give a larger value if you want room for bursts. If there are no tokens, execute does not wait; it throws MJX604 . The defaults mean "at most 1 per second"; for "at most N per second", tokensPerInterval: N is enough. capacity: 10, tokensPerInterval: 1 lets the first 10 calls through at once, then allows 1 per second.

title: Resilience
heading: fallback({ fallback, shouldHandle? })
text: If action fails, the value returned by fallback(error, ctx) (synchronous or a Promise ) becomes the result. If shouldHandle (every error by default) returns false , the error is thrown. Put first in the chain, it catches the last error of every policy inside it.

title: Resilience
heading: decorate(policy, fn)
text: Ties a chain to a function and makes it reusable: decorate(policy: ResiliencePolicy, fn: ResilienceAction<T>) accepts as its first argument any object that has an execute(action, ctx?) method; the Resilience chain implements this interface.

title: Resilience
heading: Error codes
text: Code Policy Meaning MJX602 circuitBreaker The circuit is open; action was not called. MJX603 bulkhead The queue is full. MJX604 rateLimiter No tokens. MJX605 timeout Timeout ( name: 'TimeoutError' ). All four are MotifError s and are thrown from execute ; they can be caught with fallback . With the default shouldHandle , retry and circuitBreaker do not count a timeout, but they do count the other three.

title: Resilience
heading: Next step
text: To learn about routing between pages, go on to Introduction to Routing .

title: Windows
text: A MotifJS component can be moved to another window without being rebuilt: to a window opened with window.open , to the Picture-in-Picture window the browser keeps on top, or to a child window opened by Electron. The component object, its state, bindings, services and events stay in the page's JavaScript world; only the elements go to the other window. This is managed by app.windows , reached as this.context.windows from a component, useApplication().windows in a function component, and Application.main.windows from outside.

title: Windows
heading: Opening a window
text: app.windows.open(component, options) opens the window, moves the component there and returns a handle. The browser call has to happen inside a user gesture, which is why open is called from a click handler. The returned promise resolves once the content is in place. The toolbar that opens the open note's editor in a window or always on top: An empty window is opened with app.windows.create(options) , and content is given later with win.add ; open is a shortcut for these two. A window you already have, the contentWindow of an <iframe> , or a window you opened yourself becomes a managed window with app.windows.attach(win, options) . Option Meaning kind "popup" by default; "pip" for an always-on-top Picture-in-Picture window. fallback What happens if "pip" does not exist in the browser or the request is denied: "popup" by default; with "none" the promise is rejected with MJX419 . width , height , left , top The window's size and position. name The window.open name; if not given, every window gets a name of its own. In Electron this is the frameName the main process sees. features Pieces to add to the window.open feature string. title The window's title; the page's title if not given. styles Mirroring styles and theme: "live" by default, "once" , "none" , or a function that receives the window's document. orphans Content whose origin is gone at closing time: "dispose" by default; "keep" leaves it detached. Applies only to components given with win.add . closeWhenEmpty The window closes when the last content is disposed; true by default. Only components given with win.add are counted; content put directly into host does not keep the window open. closeOnNavigate The window closes when the route changes; false by default. returnOnClose On close, the content returns to its origin; true by default. With false , a component that has an origin also falls under the orphans rule. owner The window is tied to this component's disposal; when the component goes, the window closes. onClosing Called right before the window closes, while the content is still in the window; it receives { window, components, reason } . See Closing rules .

title: Windows
heading: Handle
text: open , create and attach return an AppWindow . Member Meaning window , document The window itself and its document. host The component that wraps the window's body; the content is its child. kind The kind actually opened: "popup" , "pip" , or "attached" for one that came through attach . components The components in the window, in the order they were added. isOpen Whether the window is open. add(...components) Moves components into the window. release(component) Puts the component back at its origin; the window stays open. focus() Brings the window to the front. close() Closes the window; returns the result as { returned, disposed, kept } . closed A promise that resolves with the same result however the window closes. syncStyles() Refreshes the style sheets by hand. A notification or dialog opened by a component in the window should appear in that window too. app.layerOf(component) looks at the component's document: if the component is in a window of this manager it returns the window's host , and if it is on the page it returns app.layer , then adds the given components there (see Page layer ). Content put directly into host this way does not enter the window's components list; orphans and returnOnClose do not look at it, closeWhenEmpty does not count it (when the last component given with win.add goes, the window closes even if there is still a dialog in host ), it is disposed together with host when the window closes, and it does not appear in any list of the closed result. Content that should not go away with the window is given with win.add or written into a Transport slot.

title: Windows
heading: Content, origin and returning
text: When a component is first taken into a window, the manager notes its parent on the page and its next sibling at that moment. The component leaves its old parent and gets onDeactivated , enters the window's body with controls.add and gets onActivated ; if onMounted ran before, it does not run again, and if the component is being placed for the first time there, it runs in that window's queue. Other components can be put into the same window with win.add ; if a component is moved from one window to another, its origin does not change. The origin is kept only for a component given with open or add : the manager does not know about components the application moves itself into a window it connected with attach ; nothing returns for them on close, and they do not appear in the components list. win.release(component) and closing the window put the component back at its origin, in its old order: in front of the remembered sibling if that sibling is still there, in front of that sibling's sibling if the sibling is in the window too, and at the end if there is nobody. Several components taken into the window from the same parent find their old order in controls when they come back. returnOnClose: false turns this return off; a component with an origin counts as having none, while release still puts it back at its origin. If the origin is gone, for example because the route changed and the parent was disposed, orphans decides: the default is to dispose, and with "keep" the component stays alive without a parent and arrives in the kept list of the closed result. An application that wants to keep content whose origin is gone takes it with win.release or with controls.add to another parent before the window closes. A component in the window that is hidden and shown again stays in the window: the marker is left in the window, and motif.show() puts the component there. This also holds for a component whose element the application moves to another document itself. If the marker has been lost, or its holder has left the document, the component is rebuilt under its parent and an MJX106 warning is given.

title: Windows
heading: Closing rules
text: When the window is closed by the user, win.close() is called, or the window gets pagehide , the content returns to its origin and closed resolves. If a component in the window is disposed by the application, it drops out of the list; if the last component goes as well, the window closes, and closeWhenEmpty: false keeps it open. If owner is given, the window closes when the owner component is disposed; closeOnNavigate closes it when the route changes. app.dispose() and the page's own pagehide close every window, and the content inside them is disposed; no empty window is left behind. app.windows.closeAll() does the same job on request. If onClosing is given, the manager calls it before touching the content; when the user closes the window, this is that window's pagehide moment and the document is still standing. At that moment the window counts as closed: isOpen is false , and add throws MJX420. The hook receives { window, components, reason } . components is a copy of the components in the window at that moment; reason is why it is closing: "user" the user closed it or the window got pagehide , "code" win.close() and closeAll , "owner" the owner component was disposed, "empty" the last component went, "navigate" the route changed, "page" the page is closing or app.dispose() was called. A component taken to another parent with controls.add in the hook neither returns nor is disposed; its origin is forgotten and it does not appear in the closed result. win.release can be called as well. If the hook throws, the error is reported with MJX423 and the closing goes on.

title: Windows
heading: Styles and theme
text: A new document has no style sheets. On opening, every <link rel="stylesheet"> and <style> on the page, wherever it is, is copied into the window's head ; those set up with adoptedStyleSheets cannot be given to another document, so they are rebuilt from the text of their rules as a single <style> . The class , lang , dir and data-* attributes of <html> and <body> are mirrored onto the window's root too; if the theme is set up with a data-theme or a root class, it is set up in the window as well. With the default styles: "live" , this continues after opening: a style sheet added to, changed on or removed from the page, and every change to the root attributes, shows up in the open windows. The cost is two MutationObserver s on the page while at least one window is open; they are released when no windows are left. A rule added to adoptedStyleSheets later cannot be observed; you refresh it with win.syncStyles() . "once" copies only on opening, "none" touches nothing, and if you give a function, it is called with the window's document and the rest is up to you.

title: Windows
heading: Kinds
text: popup is opened with window.open("", name, features) ; if the browser does not open it, because of a popup blocker or the lack of a user gesture, the promise is rejected with MJX418 . pip is the browser's documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow window: it needs a user gesture, opens a single window per page and today exists only in Chromium-based browsers; Firefox and Safari have Picture-in-Picture for video only. app.windows.supports("pip") tells you in advance; since fallback defaults to "popup" , a one-line call works in every browser, and win.kind gives what was actually opened. The always-on-top window stays visible even when the main window is minimized. Meanwhile the browser may throttle your application's own setTimeout and requestAnimationFrame calls; the core's transitions and the onMounted queue run from the element's window, so they are not throttled. In Electron the main process decides on a window.open request; the window's name arrives as frameName , and the window options are given there. An always-on-top window does not need Picture-in-Picture; it is achieved with alwaysOnTop . Electron's Chromium recognizes documentPictureInPicture but denies the request, so fallback drops to a popup here too. A child window of the same origin lives in the same renderer process as its opener; the same holds for an application loaded with file:// . On the renderer side the window's name is given as an option: app.windows.open(editor, { name: "motif-popup" }) . A window opened from the main process with new BrowserWindow is a separate renderer process; components cannot be moved there, and the two windows talk over IPC or a MessagePort .

title: Windows
heading: List and events
text: app.windows.list is a reactive list of the open windows; read in a binding, it refreshes as windows open and close. app.windows.of(component) gives the component's window, or null . The application events window-opened and window-closed carry the handle: this.context.on("window-closed", (e) => …) . A component moved into a window sees the router, the services and the application events just as before; a rel="router" link in the window navigates the page's router and does not reload the window.

title: Windows
heading: Error codes
text: Code When MJX418 The browser did not open the window; a popup blocker, or no user gesture. MJX419 With fallback: "none" , Picture-in-Picture does not exist or the request was denied. MJX420 add or focus on a closed handle. MJX421 A value that is not a window was given to attach , or the window belongs to another origin. MJX422 An attempt was made to put a disposed component into a window. MJX423 onClosing threw; it is reported and the closing goes on. All the codes are on the Error and Warning Codes page.

title: Windows
heading: Next step
text: controls and the Component Tree covers the component tree and moving content into slots; for connecting another document to the application without opening a window, app.connectDocument is on the API Reference page.

title: Introduction to Routing
text: MotifJS routing comes with the core. You define routes with a configuration array, place them on screen with RouterView , and navigate in code through Application . The examples in this category come from the notes application in the starter template ( MainLayout , NotesLayout , NotePage ). Note , Folder and NotesService are the ones in the src/services/notes.ts file on the Components page.

title: Introduction to Routing
heading: How an address gets on screen
text: Routes are defined in a single RouteItem[] table. Routes nested with childs form a chain: the parent route is the layout, and the child's component sits in its RouterView . The same component can be given to several routes; the difference between the routes is carried by fields such as meta . An example table: An address matches a chain in the table, and every link of the chain sits in the RouterView of the one before it. During navigation only the links that change are rebuilt: a layout that stays on the same route stays in place, while the component of another route is rebuilt even if it is the same class. In the example, the address /notes/3 matches the chain / ( MainLayout ) → /notes ( NotesLayout ) → /{id} ( NotePage ); going to /notes/5 rebuilds only NotePage , and going to /pinned rebuilds NotesLayout too. The address / goes to /notes through the redirect in the default child. All the fields of the route table are on the Route Table page, and the placement of RouterView on the RouterView page.

title: Introduction to Routing
heading: Turning on the router
text: The route table is given with useRouter while the application is being built: If no root component is given to run , a RouterView is placed at the root and the first link of the chain lands there; in the example the application starts with createApp().run("#app") . When useDevelopment(true) is called before useRouter , the route table is checked in development mode; the situations the check warns about are described on the Route Table page. Option What it does routes The route table. If no other options are needed, pass just the array: app.useRouter(routes) . mode How the address is read and written; see the table below. fallbacks Components for an unmatched address ( notFound ) and for a page that cannot be built ( error ); see The not-found route and the error page . They accept every form the route's control field accepts, () => import(...) included. hooks onEntering , onEnter , onLeave , onUpdate : application-wide hooks for routes that have no hook of their own; see Route Hooks and Guards . scrollMemory Remembers the scroll position of every path; off by default. See Scroll memory . stack Mobile-style stack navigation; off by default. See Stack Navigation . The mode values: Mode Behaviour 'history' The path is the address bar's path and query ( /notes?tag=work ); navigation is written with history.pushState / replaceState . This is the default when mode is not given. 'hash' , 'file' Both work the same way: the path is the part after # ( /index.html#/notes ). When mode is not given and the page is opened from a file: address (as in Electron), this behaviour is chosen. 'history' mode cannot work under file: , because the address's path is a file path: even if mode: 'history' is given explicitly, the router works as in this row and development mode writes an MJX321 warning. 'shell' The address bar and the browser history are never touched; the router always starts with / , and the page's address and query do not enter params . popstate / hashchange are not listened to: the browser's back/forward button or a popstate event does not move the router. stack has no effect in this mode. In 'history' mode the route table matches the whole path of the address; <base href> and Vite's base setting are not taken into account. If the application is published under a subpath ( https://site.com/app/ ), the address becomes /app/notes , the /notes route does not match, and the page opens as not found. For such a deployment, write the routes together with the subpath ( /app/notes ), or use 'hash' mode; in 'hash' mode the path starts after # , so the address /app/#/notes matches the /notes route.

title: Introduction to Routing
heading: The not-found route and the error page
text: If no route matches, the fallbacks.notFound component is rendered into the outlet of the deepest layout that matches as a prefix of the URL (the shell does not disappear), the address bar is updated to the requested URL, and app.router.ok becomes false ( app.router.params.path carries the requested path). If no fallback is defined, a built-in "404 - Not Found" panel is shown. fallbacks.error is used the same way when a route component cannot be loaded or throws ( params.error ); if it is not defined, a built-in error panel appears. In the example, for /notes/3/x the deepest layout whose prefix matches is NotesLayout , and NotFoundPage is rendered into its output; for /missing , the only matching layout is MainLayout .

title: Introduction to Routing
heading: Router error codes
text: The codes the router produces: reports go to console.error and to the errorHandler listeners, warnings are written only in development mode, and thrown errors return to the calling line (see Error Handling ). All the codes are on the Error and Warning Codes page: Code When MJX301 A warning in development mode: the layout's RouterView was not built within 3000 ms, so the child route could not be attached. MJX302 href or navigateByName asked for a route whose name was not found; thrown. MJX303 A warning in development mode: a redirect loop or a redirect chain longer than 10 steps; the error page is shown at the requested address. MJX304 The route page could not be built (the constructor threw, the import failed, there is no default export, a ready instance that has been disposed); the error page is shown. The original cause is in the report's cause . MJX305 The error page could not be built either. MJX306 A route hook, onShow or a guard threw. With a route hook and onShow the navigation goes on; with a guard it is cancelled. MJX307 An error occurred while a route page was being disposed. MJX308 The transition animation of stack navigation failed. MJX309 Navigation was requested without calling useRouter ; thrown. MJX317 Navigation fell over with an unexpected error; navigate returns { ok: false, cancelled: true, reason: 'error' } . The route table's check warnings in development mode ( MJX310 – MJX316 , MJX319 , MJX320 ) are on the Route Table page.

title: Introduction to Routing
heading: Next step
text: To learn how routes are defined, go on to The Route Table .

title: The Route Table
text: RouteItem fields, nested routes, redirect and alias, path parameters, querying the route table, lazy routes and the route check in development mode.

title: The Route Table
heading: Defining a route ( RouteItem )
text: Routes are a RouteItem[] array. Each item maps a path ( path ) to a component ( control ). The example table shows the commonly used fields of RouteItem together: a pattern-constrained, named route ( {id(\d+)} , name ), a layout alias, an optional parameter with a default, and a redirect (an extended version of the table on the Introduction to Routing page): What these fields do: A segment that does not fit the pattern does not match the route: /notes/3 matches, /notes/abc does not, and fallbacks.notFound is shown. The path of a route given a name is produced with href / navigateByName : app.router.href("archive-note", { id: 7 }) → /archive/7 . An alias opens the same route at a second address, and the alias stays in the address bar: /my-notes/3 . An optional parameter that is missing from the address gets its default: at /settings , params.section is "appearance" , and at /settings/notes it is "notes" . {id} in a redirect string is filled with the matched parameter: /n/3 → /notes/3 .

title: The Route Table
heading: RouteItem fields
text: Field Description path The route path. Parameters are in the {name} form. '/' for a layout and the default child; every child path starts with / (otherwise development mode warns with MJX311 ). At the same depth a static segment comes before a parameter ( /archive beats /{slug} ). control The route component. It can be a component class, a ready component instance, () => Component , an Options API factory, () => import(...) (lazy) or a Promise. It is not required only on a route that defines redirect . A route given a ready instance (or a Promise that resolves to one) behaves like keepAlive : the instance is built once, detached from the outlet on leaving, and the same instance is attached again on return; it is not rebuilt on a parameter change ( onUpdate runs). app.router.evict() does not dispose this instance, app.dispose() does. If the route is entered while the instance has been disposed, the page cannot be built: MJX304 is reported (with MJX318 as the cause) and the error route is shown; a page that wants fresh state on every entry gives a class or a factory. childs Child routes. If defined, this route is a layout route. name For reaching the route by name (optional); href and navigateByName use this name. meta Free-form data that guards and hooks can use ( { requiresAuth: true, title: '...' } ). The meta objects in the matched chain (layout → child) are merged; a requiresAuth written on a layout shows up in its children as well. In the example, meta.folder is written on the layout route and read on the note route under it too. extend Extra data attached to the route; merged along the chain like meta . extend.targetOutlet picks the named RouterView the route's component will sit in (see RouterView ). keepAlive If true , the component instance is kept: on leaving it is detached from the outlet and cached ( onDeactivated ), and on return the same instance is attached again in the same position ( onActivated ); both are passed on to the page's visible child components. The cache is emptied with app.router.evict(name \| route) (with no argument: all of them; the instance on screen at that moment is skipped) or app.dispose() . redirect Redirects to another path when this route is reached: a path string with {param} placeholders, or a (to) => path function. Details: Redirect and alias . alias Extra path(s) that open the same route; the alias stays in the address bar. Details: Redirect and alias . validate(e) Called during matching with { uri, key, routes, params } ; if it returns false , this route does not count as matched (another route or fallbacks.notFound takes over). The validate of every route in the chain runs. key is the route's name, or its full path if it has none (its own path for an alias match too); routes is the route table keyed by the same rule (a Map ): routes.get(e.key) is the route being validated, and another route is reached by its name or full path. onShow(component) Called with the component instance every time the route's component is placed in its own RouterView : the first show, rebuilding on a parameter change, coming back from the keepAlive cache, and being placed again when the RouterView is rebuilt. It is called for layout routes too; it is not called again for a layout that stays in place throughout a navigation. An error thrown by the hook is reported with the code MJX306 and does not stop the navigation. The route hooks tied to navigation ( onEntering , onEnter , onLeave , onUpdate ) are described on the Route Hooks and Guards page.

title: The Route Table
heading: Redirect and alias
text: /n/{id} in the example is a redirect in string form. If the target depends on a calculation, give a function: redirect In the string form, the {param} placeholders are filled with the matched parameters. The query string ( ?… ) and #… of the source address are carried over to the target unless the target contains its own query/ # : /n/3?from=mail → /notes/3?from=mail . The function form receives { path, params, meta } ; the path it returns is used as it is. The redirect is applied right after matching, before onLeave and the useGuard guards; guards and hooks run only for the target route. The source route's component is never created. The chain is followed ( /a → /b → /c ). A redirect that goes over 10 steps or comes back to a path passed earlier is stopped, the fallbacks.error page is shown at the requested address, and in development mode an MJX303 warning is written to the console. Only the target enters the browser history. If the address bar already shows the source path (first load, back/forward), the entry is changed with replace , so the "back" button does not get stuck on the redirect. Where the target came from is read through to.redirectedFrom (in the guard and onLeave context) and the redirectedFrom field of the onRouterChanged payload. Only the redirect of the matched leaf route is applied. If a layout has a '/' default child, the leaf that matches at the layout's path is that child; in that case a redirect written on the layout does not run, so write the redirect on the default child. The root route in the example does this: at the address / , the one that redirects is the '/' child of MainLayout . alias An alias is added to the parent path by the same rule as path ( alias: '/detail/{id}' under /notes → /notes/detail/{id} ). Parameters are read from the alias pattern. The children open under a layout's alias too: in the example, /my-notes/5 → NotePage . The alias and the main path are the same route: moving between them with the same parameters keeps the component; if the parameters change, onUpdate runs and the page is rebuilt, as on any parameter change ( keepAlive: true keeps it). The keepAlive cache is shared as well. If an alias clashes with the main path of another route, the main path wins. The check in development mode warns when an alias equals its own path ( MJX315 ), when two routes use the same alias ( MJX316 ), and when a child alias is missing the / prefix ( MJX314 ). app.router.fullPath gives the matched pattern (the alias pattern for an alias), and app.router.aliasOf gives the main pattern ( null if it is not an alias): at /my-notes/5 , /my-notes/{id(\d+)} and /notes/{id(\d+)} . navigateByName and href always produce the main path. RouterLink classes look at the URL: while at /my-notes , a link with to="/notes" does not count as active.

title: The Route Table
heading: Path parameters
text: Parameters are defined with the {name} syntax: Syntax Meaning {id} A required parameter. {id:1} Required; 1 is used only when href / navigateByName produces a path and no value is given (the pattern /h/{id:1} does not match the address /h ). {id?} Optional. {id?:5} Optional, with the default 5 : if it is missing from the address, params.id becomes '5' . {id(\d+)} A pattern constraint: the segment matches only if it fits the regular expression in the parentheses (case-insensitive; capturing groups in the pattern are ignored; ? and : are part of the pattern). It combines with ? and a default: {id(\d+)?:1} . The pattern applies to a single segment and cannot contain / . In a JavaScript string the backslash is written twice: "/{id(\\d+)}" . {path+} One or more segments: for /files/a/b/c , params.path becomes 'a/b/c' (plain text; each segment is decoded separately, and you can split('/') the parts if needed). For href , give 'a/b' or ['a','b'] , and the segments are encoded separately. It combines with a pattern, and the pattern applies to every segment: {ids(\d+)+} . {path*} Like {path+} , but there may be no segment at all (optional like {path?} , and it takes a :default ). A : outside the curly braces and the rest of the segment drop out of the pattern ( /user/:id → /user/ , which matches no address); in development mode the check warns with MJX319 . In the ordering, a route containing {…+} or {…*} comes after routes at the same depth with the same number of static segments: /f/{a}/{b} before /f/{rest+} ; /docs/{rest+} , with its static segment, before /{a}/{b} . For an unusable pattern (one that does not compile, has an unclosed ( or contains / ), the check warns in development mode with MJX320 . href , navigateByName and the redirect string fill the {…} placeholders, and the values are encoded with encodeURIComponent ( href('tag', { name: 'a/b' }) → /tags/a%2Fb , { name: 'café' } → /tags/caf%C3%A9 ). Parameters are reached from the navigation context or the router: params also contains the query string values. Like path parameters, query values are strings and arrive with their percent-encoding decoded ( /notes/5?tab=history → { id: '5', tab: 'history' } , /tags/caf%C3%A9?q=a%20b → { name: 'café', q: 'a b' } ); in the path + is a plain character, while in the query it is a space; values such as true , null , 2025-10-27 or {"a":1} stay text as well. If you need a number, a boolean or a date, convert the value yourself ( Number(params.id) ). A repeated key ( ?tag=work&tag=home ) becomes an array of strings ( ['work', 'home'] ). A path parameter with the same name overrides the query value. The #… part never enters params . router.uri , the uri of the onRouterChanged event, the middleware's ctx.uri and the guard's to.path are in address form: percent-encoded, the same as the address bar ( /tags/caf%C3%A9 ). To display one, use decodeURIComponent ; for the value, use params . navigate , the to of RouterLink and the onActive / onExact path can be written raw ( /tags/café ) or encoded; both go to the same address and make the same link active. The query is read only from the address being navigated to: in history mode, if there is no ? in the address, params contains no query values (the previous page's query is not carried over). In hash / file mode, the query before # ( /?x=1#/a ) is page-level; it reaches params on every route that has no query of its own, and if the route has its own query ( #/b?z=3 ), that one is used instead.

title: The Route Table
heading: Querying the route table — resolve , href , routes
text: app.router carries three members for querying the route table without navigating: The path of a named route is produced with href ; for the to of a RouterLink , for menus and breadcrumbs.
