In the example the link's target is produced from a named route ( nav is the router returned by useNavigation() ): Member Returns resolve(uri) RouteResolution : { chain, result } . chain has the same form as app.router.chain ( string[] , each route's own path with its parameters filled in). result is the ResolveResult that navigate would return when going to that address: { ok, uri, fullPath, route, chain, params, meta, extend, aliasOf } ; result.chain is the route definitions from the root to the route ( RouteItem[] ). If there is no match, result.ok is false and chain is [] . Guards, middleware and redirects do not run. href(name, params?) The path of the named route with its parameters filled in (the same calculation as navigateByName ). 0 and false values are written; for a parameter given as undefined , null or '' , or not given at all, the pattern's default is used (if there is no default, that segment is not written). Parameters that are not in the pattern are not written; if you need a query, append it to the produced path ( href("notes-note", { id: 3 }) + "?tab=history" ). If the name does not exist, it throws MJX302 . routes RouteInfo[] : { fullPath, name, meta, route, chain } . A layout and its default child are separate items; chain is the route definitions from the root to this route.

title: The Route Table
heading: Lazy loading
text: Using () => import(...) in the control field loads the route component only when it is needed and gives automatic code splitting. A page given this way is split into a separate chunk and downloaded the first time the route is visited: The loaded module must export the page as default . For a named export, map it: control: () => import("./pages/SettingsPage").then((m) => m.SettingsPage) . The page cannot be built with a module that has no default export, or with some other object that is not a component: MJX304 is reported (with MJX127 as the cause) and fallbacks.error is shown. fallbacks.notFound and fallbacks.error support the same lazy form. A route's import() does not use a loading view or retries. To lazily load a heavy part inside a page, show a view while it loads and retry on a mobile network, use the Lazy component (see Retrying ).

title: The Route Table
heading: Route check in development mode
text: When app.useDevelopment(true) is called before useRouter , the route table is checked while it is being set up; a problematic definition is written to the console as a warning, and the router keeps working: Code When MJX310 The route path is empty ( '' ); for the default child, write '/' . MJX311 A child route's path does not start with / ( 'notes' ). MJX312 A child route ends up at the same full path as its parent (except the default child '/' ). MJX313 Several routes end up at the same full path. MJX314 A child route's alias does not start with / . MJX315 An alias is equal to the route's own path. MJX316 Several routes use the same alias. MJX319 There is a : outside the curly braces in a path or an alias ( /user/:id ). MJX320 A parameter pattern cannot be used: it does not compile, has an unclosed ( or contains / .

title: The Route Table
heading: Next step
text: To learn where route components are placed on screen, go on to RouterView .

title: RouterView
text: RouterView, where route components are placed, nested and named outlets, and how a route component is built; with and without JSX.

title: RouterView
heading: RouterView — placing a route's output
text: The place where route components are shown on screen is RouterView . Put it inside a layout; without JSX it is built with motifComponent(RouterView) . The component of a layout route puts a RouterView where its child routes should go. The layout in the example places a RouterView next to its own content ( main.detail ) and reads the route's meta data with useNavigation() : If navigation stays on the same layout route, the layout stays in place and only the component in the RouterView changes; when moving to another route, the layout is rebuilt as well (see How an address gets on screen ). RouterView has no element of its own (it is a component without an element, a fragment): the route component sits directly where the RouterView is, inside main.detail in the example. Attributes written on the tag, such as class and style , do not show up in the DOM because there is no element to write them on; if you need a container around the output, put the RouterView inside an element (see Root element ).

title: RouterView
heading: How a route component is built
text: The default export of the module loaded with control: () => import('./pages/SettingsPage') is used as the route component; with a module that has no default export, the page cannot be built, MJX304 is reported (with MJX127 as the cause) and the error route is shown. A class is built with new SomeClass(app) and a function with fn(app) : the first argument is the running Application , and a route component takes no props from a tag. A function that returns an Options API object (or the object itself) becomes a route component too: the function is still called with fn(app) , the returned object is turned into a component as in JSX, and ctor receives no props ( undefined ). The default loaded by Lazy can be one of these forms as well; Lazy builds it without arguments. If the component is registered in DI (an @Injectable class, or a services.addTransient / addScoped / addSingleton registration), the instance is resolved from the provider, and the registration's lifetime decides the page's lifetime: Lifetime Page transient (the default of @Injectable ) A new page is built on every visit and disposed on leaving. scoped One page is built in each navigation's scope and disposed on leaving. With keepAlive: true , a cached page outlives its own navigation scope. singleton A single page for the whole application: like a route given a ready instance, it is not disposed on leaving but detached from the outlet ( onDeactivated ), and the same instance is attached again on return ( onActivated ). It is disposed with app.dispose() .

title: RouterView
heading: Named RouterView
text: By default a route's component sits in the parent route's RouterView named default ; for it to go into another outlet, give extend.targetOutlet on the route. A layout can carry several RouterView s; an outlet without a name is default . In the example the second outlet is named page : Each route goes into a single outlet; only one route is shown at a time at the same level, so while /settings is open the default outlet stays empty, and when you return to a folder the page outlet is emptied. If you do not give app.run a root component, MotifJS automatically places a RouterView with name: 'default' at the root, and the first link of the route table lands there. If the layout's RouterView has not been built yet (for example because it is inside a section waiting with x-wait ), the child route waits and is attached the moment the RouterView is built. If it is not built within 3000 ms in development mode, an MJX301 warning is written; the warning usually means the layout forgot to put a RouterView in. A RouterView built after a navigation has finished fills up the same way: when the layout swaps its output with a Frame , or closes and opens it with {condition && <RouterView />} , the component of the route on screen goes into the new RouterView . No navigation happens for this; guards, onEntering and onEnter do not run, onShow does. A page disposed together with the old RouterView is built again, and if the old outlet has a leave transition, the new page does not wait for it. keepAlive , ready-instance, singleton and scoped pages are not disposed; the same instance is moved to the new RouterView ( onDeactivated , then onActivated ). If the RouterView is removed without a new one being put in its place, these pages wait, and no warning is written. If the page cannot be built, MJX304 is reported and the error route is shown.

title: RouterView
heading: The page that leaves
text: The enter and leave transitions of route pages play during navigation too: the page that leaves finishes its leave transition, and then the incoming page is placed and enters (see Styling and Animation ). The new page does not wait for the leaving page to be disposed. The router takes the leaving page off the screen, places the new page, and disposes the leaving page after the new page has come on screen: As soon as the page leaves, its bindings and the context.on / context.onRouterChanged subscriptions tied to its components stop; content it sent to a slot with TransportTo leaves the slot. The element of a page with its own leave transition is removed when the transition finishes, and that of a page without one right away. onDisposing , onDisposed and cleanup work tied with motif.setDisposable (such as calling destroy() on library components) run after the new page has come on screen, and see the route that was navigated to. A long cleanup does not delay the arrival of the new page. The leaving page uses the scoped instances of its own navigation until its disposal finishes; those instances are disposed after the page (see Lifetimes and Scopes ). keepAlive , ready-instance and singleton pages, and pages kept in the stack, are not disposed but detached from the outlet. If a new navigation starts before one has finished, the page that the interrupted navigation built but could not show is disposed; when that route is visited later, the page is built again. keepAlive , ready-instance and singleton pages are kept. The result of app.navigate and onRouterChanged arrive before the leaving page is disposed. app.dispose() also disposes the pages waiting to be disposed.

title: RouterView
heading: Next step
text: To link pages to each other, go on to Links .

title: Links
text: When an in-app link is clicked, the page does not reload; the router changes the address and builds the link of the route chain that changed. There are three ways to do this: writing rel="router" on a plain <a> tag, the RouterLink component that marks the active link with a class, and enableRouterClassing , which opens the same class logic to any component.

title: Links
heading: With rel="router"
text: Add rel="router" to a standard <a> tag so that MotifJS catches the click and navigates without a full page reload. href can be a fixed path or a getter: In the function component, notes is the service obtained with FromService , and folder() is a local function that returns the folder. rel can also be given together with other values ( rel="router nofollow" ); it is enough for the router token to be in the set. The data-router-link attribute does the same job. Clicks made with Ctrl/Meta/Shift/Alt, links whose target is anything other than _self , and in history mode addresses that go to another origin are not caught. In hash / file mode, href="#/archive" and href="/archive" go to the same place. The catcher listens in the page's document and in every document connected with app.connectDocument ; a rel="router" link in content moved into a popup does not reload that window, it navigates the page's router.

title: Links
heading: The RouterLink component
text: A link component that manages the active/match classes automatically: as the current address matches to , it adds the activeClass / exactClass classes. Its children become the link's content; without JSX, the children are given with childs , and the text of a link that is only text with text : The link is an <a> element; for another tag, give el . Props: Prop Effect to The target path. It is also written as href ; in hash / file mode a # is put in front ( #/archive ), so a link opened in a new tab or copied goes to the right address. href is written according to the router's mode when the link is set up. showHref If false , no href is written; a click still navigates. target Written as an attribute. With any value other than _self , the click is left to the browser and the router does not navigate. text The link's text if it has no children; if it has children, the children are used. bypass If true , the click does not go to the router; the link opens in the browser like a normal link. A click made with Ctrl/Cmd/Shift/Alt is left to the browser. On other clicks, RouterLink calls router.navigate(to) and applies the classes based on the match with the current URL: Class / callback When activeClass , onActive / offActive When the current path starts with to (by segment; an exact match included). While at /notes/5 , to="/notes" is active. exactClass , onExact / offExact Only when the current path matches to exactly (the query string and # are ignored). On an exact match both classes are applied together. to="/" is active only at the root path; it does not count as a prefix of every path.

title: Links
heading: Route classes on any component — enableRouterClassing
text: The class logic of RouterLink is open to every component: when a RouterClassingSettings is written to motif.options.enableRouterClassing , the component's element gets classes as the current address matches path . It is used for elements that are not <a> , such as a menu item, a tab or a sidebar heading. NavItem is an <li> and takes its text as a child: Using it: at the /notes address the first item gets is-active is-exact , and at /notes/5 only is-active : Field Description path The path to compare. to Which matches are handled: 'all' (both), 'active' , 'exact' , 'none' . activeClass / exactClass Class names separated by spaces; they are toggled with classList.toggle according to the match state. onActive / offActive / onExact / offExact Callbacks called on every evaluation according to the match state. The matching rules are the same as for RouterLink (active = a segment prefix or exact; exact = exact; the query and # are ignored). The setting is evaluated once the moment it is written, and then again on every navigation ( onRouterChanged ); the subscription goes away together with the component. An evaluation error is reported as MJX105 . If the router is not set up (no useRouter ), it does nothing. The component must have an element; a component without an element (a fragment) has no element to write classes on (see Root element ).

title: Links
heading: Next step
text: To navigate from code and read the route state, go on to Navigation and Route State .

title: Navigation and Route State
text: navigate and navigateByName, live route state, navigation direction and history entry state, scroll memory.

title: Navigation and Route State
heading: Navigating in code
text: To navigate from code, use this.context (the running Application ) inside a component, and the application instance or useNavigation() outside one: To navigate from code, use useNavigation() in a function component, and the application instance outside one: From the application instance, with navigation options: app.navigate(uri, options?) and app.router.navigate(uri, options?) take the same NavigationOptions type; app.navigate passes the options on to the router. Option Effect replace Replaces the current history entry instead of adding a new one. state A value written to the history entry (see Navigation direction and entry state ). force Navigation to the address on screen is normally ignored; with force: true the middleware, the guards and onRouterChanged still run. The page on screen is not recreated. scroll Scrolling at the end of the navigation: 'top' , 'smooth' , 'instant' or { top, left, behavior } . When given, it overrides scrollMemory . app.navigate returns the result of the navigation: for a completed navigation, the ResolveResult of the route shown ( ok: false for an address that was not found and for the error page); for an ignored navigation, { ok: true, skipped: true, uri } ; for a cancellation by a guard or onLeave , { ok: false, cancelled: true, reason } ( reason : 'guard' , 'onLeave' or the text given by onLeave ); for a navigation stopped by middleware, { ok: false, uri, cancelled: true, reason: 'middleware' } ; if the router was restarted with restartRouter() or shut down with app.dispose() before the navigation finished, { ok: false, uri, cancelled: true, reason: 'restart' | 'dispose' } ; if the navigation falls over with an unexpected error, MJX317 is reported and the result is { ok: false, uri, cancelled: true, reason: 'error', error } . app.router.navigate and app.router.navigateByName return the same result. useNavigation() returns the same object as app.router :

title: Navigation and Route State
heading: Live route state
text: app.router is a single object for the whole application. A router taken into a field, from useApplication().router or from useNavigation() gives the current route on every read. The route fields ( params , route , uri , ok , meta , extend , fullPath , aliasOf , chain , direction , state , stack ) are reactive: read inside a function, they run again on navigation. A layout that stays in place throughout navigation is updated on every navigation by reading the route fields inside a getter; it is not rebuilt. In the example, two attributes are calculated from the route's meta and params values: The attributes become notes / list at /notes , notes / detail at /notes/3 , and page / detail at /settings ; the layout is not rebuilt, only the attributes are updated. Live reading goes through the object. const { params } = useNavigation() or const id = nav.params.id takes the value of that moment and does not change afterwards; for the current value, read nav.params.id every time. The route changes after the leaving page has been taken off the screen and before the new page is attached (in stack navigation, before the transition animation); scoped services move to the new navigation at the same moment. A page taken into the keepAlive cache sees its own route in onDeactivated . The onDisposing and onDisposed hooks of a page being disposed run after the new page has come on screen, and see the route that was navigated to (see The page that leaves ). A new page built by the router sees the route being navigated to in its constructor and in its field initial values. Guards and route hooks ( useGuard , onEntering , onUpdate ) run before the route changes; the route being navigated to is in the context object ( to , params ). In a cancelled navigation the route does not change. keepAlive pages in the cache read the current route even while hidden: when another route is visited, their bindings run again with that route's values. Do route-dependent work (such as loading data) in onActivated . Before useRouter() is called, the route fields are empty ( params {} , uri '' , route null , chain [] ) and navigate throws MJX309 .

title: Navigation and Route State
heading: Listening for route changes
text: For values that show up on screen, reading the reactive fields inside a function is enough; MainLayout above does that. If some side work has to be done after a navigation (the tab title, focus, a measurement), listen to onRouterChanged . app.onRouterChanged(fn) returns a function that removes the subscription. When context.onRouterChanged(fn) is written inside a component ( this.context in a class and in Options, the context of the root component in a function component), the subscription is tied to the component's lifetime: it goes away on its own when the component is disposed, with no need to remove it separately. The payload has the form { uri, params, meta, route, ok, initial, redirectedFrom?, direction?, state? } ; on the startup navigation initial is true (see Navigation guards ).

title: Navigation and Route State
heading: Navigation direction and entry state — direction , state
text: The direction of every navigation arrives in the direction field: 'initial' (startup), 'push' (a new history entry; this includes an address typed into the address bar by hand and an entry opened by a plain anchor link), 'replace' , 'back' , 'forward' , or 'traverse' for a history move whose order cannot be known. The direction shows up in guards ( to.direction ), in the onRouterChanged payload and in app.router.direction . Use it to pick transitions by direction (slide left going forward, right going back). A value given with navigate(uri, { state }) is written to that history entry, and it comes back when returning to the entry with back/forward as well ; it is kept even if the page is reloaded. It suits data that has to travel without being written to the address (which filter the list was reached from, the open tab): Plain objects are stored as they are (the router only adds its own stamp, and app.router.state removes it); values that are not plain, such as Date and Map , are not touched at all. For an entry without state , app.router.state is undefined .

title: Navigation and Route State
heading: Scroll memory — scrollMemory
text: In a single-page application navigation changes the document but not the scroll position, and the browser does not manage that for an SPA on its own. When scrollMemory is turned on, the router keeps the last scroll position of every path and puts the position back when that path is returned to (back/forward, a link, a reload): The rules: A path never seen before starts at the top of the page (turned off with top: false ). If there is an anchor in the address ( /notes/5#history ), the anchor overrides the memory and the page scrolls to the matching id . If there is a fixed top bar, give scroll-margin-top in CSS. Scrolling is instant , even if CSS has scroll-behavior: smooth : returning to a saved position, the top of a new page, an anchor arriving from another page, and back/forward all settle into place without waiting, as in the browser's own page transitions. An anchor link within the same page ( /notes/5 → /notes/5#history , including a plain <a href="#history"> in history mode) follows the scroll-behavior rule in CSS; if smooth is given, it slides smoothly. The navigation-specific scroll option overrides the memory: app.router.navigate('/x', { scroll: 'top' }) always goes to the top; it scrolls the container if container is set, and the window otherwise. When leaving the page navigated to, the position is still saved under that page's name. Positions are kept in memory: they survive a restart with restartRouter() and are cleared when the page is reloaded. If they should be remembered after a reload too, you do the saving; where to write them (browser storage, a server) is up to you. For saving, app.router gives three methods: saveScrollPositions(fn) calls the callback with the current positions every time saving is needed (when leaving a page, on pagehide , when the page is hidden, and on app.dispose() ) and returns a function that removes the subscription; the subscription survives a restart as well. restoreScrollPositions(positions) adds the given positions to the memory ( limit applies); it can be called at startup, before run() too. scrollPositions() returns the current positions, including that of the page on screen, in the form { "/notes": 1200 } . While scrollMemory is off, scrollPositions() returns an empty object, restoreScrollPositions has no effect and the callback is never called. Fine-tuning with a settings object: If scrolling happens inside a container (like mobile shells with a fixed header and a tab bar), give container . The container is looked up again on every navigation, so it is fine if it is not in the DOM yet on the first load; if it is not found, window scrolling is used. If content is drawn asynchronously (remote data, markdown, a virtual list, rows chunked with x-chunk ), do not worry: restoring is not a one-off, it is retried on every frame until the target is reached or settleMs runs out. If the user steps in meanwhile with the wheel, a touch, a key or a mouse click, the attempt is dropped. The cost: zero at rest. The scroll event is not listened to; the position is read once per navigation: after the guards have passed, right before the address is applied and the content is changed. At that moment the leaving page is still on screen and its position is real; in a cancelled navigation the position is not read. While it is on, history.scrollRestoration is set to 'manual' ; on pagehide / when the page is hidden, the position of the page on screen is also taken into memory and the saving callback is called. While it is off (the default), no listener is attached and history.scrollRestoration is not touched. Where the anchor comes from depends on the mode. The #… in the address bar is read as an anchor only in history mode. In hash / file (and shell ) mode only the route's own anchor ( /page#section ) is used; the # part of the address is the route, so it does not count as an anchor. In these modes the memory works with the default anchor setting.

title: Navigation and Route State
heading: Next step
text: To control and stop navigation, go on to Route Hooks and Guards .

title: Route Hooks and Guards
text: A navigation goes through several steps between the address changing and the page coming on screen. You can step into these from three places: the route's own hooks ( onEntering , onEnter , onLeave , onUpdate ), application-level guards that run on every navigation ( useGuard ), and middleware that runs before the address is resolved ( app.use ).

title: Route Hooks and Guards
heading: Route lifecycle hooks
text: Hooks tied to the navigation lifecycle can be defined on a RouteItem : Hook When onEntering(ctx) Before the route component is created (after the guards; the page is not in the DOM yet); on a parameter change on the same route, after onUpdate . onEnter(ctx) After the route component has been mounted and onShow has run. onLeave(ctx) When leaving the route (also on a parameter change on the same route), before the useGuard guards. It cancels the navigation by returning false or { cancel: true, reason } . onUpdate(ctx) Only when the parameters change on the same route; onEntering runs after it and the page is rebuilt with the new parameters. With keepAlive: true the same instance is kept and only the hooks run. The order: onLeave (the route being left) → useGuard → onUpdate (only on a parameter change) → onEntering → creating and placing the component → onShow → onEnter → onRouterChanged → disposing the leaving page after the new page has come on screen (see The page that leaves ). Context objects: onEntering / onEnter get { path, params, meta, to: { path, params, meta } } ; onLeave gets { from: { path, params, meta }, to: { path, params, meta, redirectedFrom?, direction?, options?, state? } } ; onUpdate gets { from: { path, params }, to: { path, params }, meta } . Hooks can be async ; the router waits for the result. An error thrown by these hooks (including a rejected promise in an async hook) and an error thrown by onShow (including the rejected promise of an async onShow ) are reported with the code MJX306 ; the navigation goes on. If the route component cannot be created (the constructor throws, the import fails), MJX304 is reported and the fallbacks.error page is shown. With useRouter({ hooks }) the same four hooks ( onEntering , onEnter , onLeave , onUpdate ) are defined application-wide; a global hook runs only for routes that have no hook of their own, and a route's own hook replaces the global one. onLeave receives the context of the route being left; since it also runs on a parameter change on the same route, from.params is always the parameters of the address being left. The hook reaches services through useApplication().services . In the example, the note being left is deleted if it is empty: To stop the navigation, the hook returns false or { cancel: true, reason: "…" } ; the result of app.navigate becomes { ok: false, cancelled: true, reason } .

title: Route Hooks and Guards
heading: Navigation guards and hooks (application level)
text: Global guards and hooks are defined on Application . useGuard runs before every navigation and gives its decision with next : next() continues, next("/path") redirects to another address, and next(false) cancels the navigation; if next is never called, the navigation is blocked. onRouterChanged runs after every navigation (startup and not-found addresses included); to tell startup apart, read the initial field in the payload. A guard makes its decision by looking at the target's to.params and to.meta values; onRouterChanged runs with the values in the payload after the navigation is over. In the example the guard changes the address if the target note is archived, and onRouterChanged writes the tab title: Guards run on every navigation, the startup navigation included, in the order they were added; the first guard that redirects or cancels ends the chain. If the address bar shows the blocked path (first load, back/forward), a guard's next('/login') redirect replaces the history entry with replace , so the "back" button does not return to the blocked path and get stuck on the same guard again. In a programmatic navigation (from another page), the target is added to the history as usual. If a guard throws (or the promise it returns is rejected), the navigation is cancelled and the error is reported with the code MJX306 ( The guard hook threw. ); the result of app.navigate becomes { ok: false, cancelled: true, reason: 'guard' } . In a back/forward navigation the address is rolled back, as with other cancellations. If back/forward is cancelled, the address is rolled back. The browser's back/forward button (and the system back gesture on Android) changes the address before the navigation starts. If a guard, onLeave or middleware cancels this navigation, the router returns the address with history.go to the entry of the page on screen; the address and the screen do not drift apart, and the history is not damaged. Thanks to this, an "unsaved changes" confirmation works correctly on the back button too. For this, the router writes a namespaced order stamp ( __motifHistory ) into the history.state of every history entry; if some other code calls history.pushState directly, the order calculation can slip.

title: Route Hooks and Guards
heading: Middleware — app.use
text: To add a middle layer to the navigation resolution chain: Middleware runs in the order it was added, before redirects ( redirect ), onLeave and the guards. Middleware that does not call next() cancels the navigation. The address given with rewritePath becomes the address navigated to and written to the address bar. Middleware does not run on the router's startup navigation ( run() and restartRouter() ); guards do.

title: Route Hooks and Guards
heading: Restarting and shutting down the router
text: app.restartRouter(uri?) sets up a new router and disposes the old one. If useRouter was called again after run() , the latest configuration is used, and otherwise the current one; a new configuration given after run() takes effect only through restartRouter() , and until then the running router carries on with the page on screen, the navigation and the route fields under the old table. The new router starts at the root ( / ); the address of the old table is not carried over to the new one. If it should start at another address, give the address: app.restartRouter("/notes/7") . If the address bar changes, the current history entry is overwritten, and no entry is added to the history; the entry's state value is kept if the address stays the same and cleared if it changes. In shell mode the address bar is not touched. The route table is rebuilt, and the keepAlive cache and the pages kept in the stack are dropped; scrollMemory positions are kept. The page and layout on screen leave like the page that leaves : their bindings stop right away, their leave transitions play, the new page is built after that, and the cleanup work runs after the new page has come on screen. A layout given as a ready instance or as a singleton stays in place if it is in the same spot in the new table; onDeactivated / onActivated do not run. The route fields move to the new route in a single step after the leaving page has come off the screen; a layout that stays in place goes from the old route to the new one without seeing an empty value in between. Guards run on the restart's startup navigation as well ( from is null , to.direction is 'initial' ), and at that moment app.router shows the old route. A redirect ( next("/login") ) is applied, and the address is again written over the current entry. A cancellation ( next(false) , a next that is never called, or a guard that throws) does not undo the restart, it only keeps the page from being shown: the old page leaves with its leave transition, then the route fields are emptied ( uri '' , ok false ), the address bar does not change and onRouterChanged does not arrive; the next navigation works normally with the new table. onLeave does not run. onRouterChanged runs with initial: true and direction: 'initial' . The return value is the result of the startup navigation (see Navigating in code ); if the restarted router was ended by a new restartRouter() or by app.dispose() before that navigation finished, reason is 'restart' or 'dispose' . Called before run() , it does nothing and returns undefined . app.dispose() disposes the router too (listeners, the keepAlive cache, the pages in the stack) and rolls back the address only if the router set it: in history mode it makes it / with history.replaceState , in hash / file mode it removes only the # part (the document's path and query stay), and in shell mode or without a router it does not touch the address; no entry is added to the history. It returns a promise that resolves once the route pages, the RouterView , the shell and then the services have been disposed; the host element given to run() stays on the page, and the same host can be used with a new run() .

title: Route Hooks and Guards
heading: Next step
text: For mobile-style back navigation, go on to Stack Navigation .

title: Stack Navigation
text: Mobile-style stack navigation; kept pages, the transition animation and swiping back.

title: Stack Navigation
heading: Stack navigation — stack
text: By default, when you leave a page the old page is thrown away, and it is recreated when you come back. In mobile apps, though, the expected behaviour is a stack : going forward keeps the previous page with its state, its scroll position and its form, and going back brings back the same instance. stack turns this on: stack: true turns it on with the default values. If the option is not given, the behaviour is as described above and nothing changes. In shell mode it has no effect, because there is no history. The rules: A kept page is tied to the history entry, not to the route. /notes/1 → /notes/2 → back: the very instance of /notes/1 comes back. (With the stack on, going forward to the same route with different parameters creates a new instance; onUpdate is still called.) Going forward (push/forward) keeps the page being left; going back (back) throws it away. The browser's forward button recreates that page. A page replaced with replace is not kept. Going back and then somewhere new throws away the pages of the forward entries. When a kept page is hidden, onDeactivated runs, and when it comes back, onActivated and the route's onShow hook run. The positions of scrollable items inside the page are kept. With retain: true , the hidden page stays in the DOM with display: none , inert and aria-hidden ; its styles are put back exactly as they were when it returns. If the page has no element (a fragment), it is kept by detaching it from the DOM. keepAlive routes keep using their own cache. When the application or the router is disposed, all kept pages are disposed. app.router.stack gives the current list of the stack: [{ index, uri, current, retained }] . Use it for work such as showing the previous page's name on a back button. With persist: true this list comes back after a page reload too; on reload the previous pages are not recreated, they are created as you go back. The transition animation. animation: 'slide' slides the new page in from the right when going forward, and slides the current page out to the right when going back; meanwhile the other page stays underneath. The animation works independently of the retain setting: with retain: false , the page being left stays in the DOM until the animation finishes and is detached after that. If the user has chosen "reduce motion" in the system, the animation is skipped. To write your own animation, give a function; the two pages arrive positioned on top of each other, and the styles are rolled back when the function finishes: In a navigation where the stack animation runs, the pages' own transitions ( motif.options.transition , see Styling and Animation ) do not play; only the stack animation does the transition. The pages' own transitions. If animation is not given, the stack uses the pages' own enter/leave transitions, and there is no need to define a stack animation separately. The order is the same as with the stack off: first the leave of the page being left finishes, then the incoming page enters. Going forward, the page being left plays its leave transition and is kept in the stack once it finishes (detached or hidden, depending on the retain setting). Going back, the page being left plays its leave transition and is thrown away. The incoming page plays its enter transition; a kept page coming back from the stack also plays its enter transition again, whatever the value of retain . A page without a transition leaves or arrives instantly. For the duration of the transition, the page element's data-nav-direction attribute carries the direction of the navigation ( initial , push , back , forward , replace , traverse ); it is removed when the transition finishes. With the same CSS you can write different animations for forward and back: Swiping back. With swipeBack: true , a horizontal touch starting from the left edge of the screen (24px by default) slides the page along with the finger. For the previous page to show underneath while dragging, retain: true is needed; with retain: false the previous page is not in the DOM, so the page background shows underneath, and going back still works on release. Passing 35% of the width ( threshold ) or a quick flick goes back; otherwise the page settles back into place. If a guard cancels going back, the page slides back and the address is kept. When going back by swiping, the drag is the animation itself; the pages' own transitions do not play. Settings: swipeBack: { edge: 24, threshold: 0.35 } . The touch listener becomes active only on a touch that starts from the edge; it does not affect the page's vertical scrolling or content that scrolls horizontally.

title: Stack Navigation
heading: Next step
text: To learn how services are registered and injected, go on to Introduction to Dependency Injection .

title: Introduction to Dependency Injection
text: MotifJS includes a built-in dependency injection (DI) system. You register services when the application starts, and then resolve them from components or from other services. A service is a class or a value that holds state and work shared between components. A component does not build the service itself; it asks the provider ( ServiceProvider ) for it, and the provider gives either the same instance or a new one, depending on the registration's lifetime.

title: Introduction to Dependency Injection
heading: From registration to use
text: Services are registered on the services collection of Application.CreateBuilder() , before build() . addSingleton(token, { useClass }) registers the class with a single instance; a singleton given startup: true is created at the start of app.run() without a component asking for it. The two registrations in the example ( NotesService and SettingsService from the Components page): A component gets a registered service from the provider: a class component and an Options object use this.getService(token) , and a function component uses FromService(token) . When the service's reactive state is read inside a getter, the binding refreshes as the state changes. FolderBadge in the example shows the number of notes in a folder: The component is used with its tag: Every component that asks for a service registered as a singleton gets the same instance. If the service keeps its state in a reactive object, a change made by one component (for example notes.create() ) refreshes every binding that reads that state; no separate event or notification is needed. A function component has no this , so FromService takes the service from the application's provider; for a scoped service, this also gives the handle of the current navigation. The details are on the Resolving Services page, the other registration forms and automatic registration with @Injectable on the Registering Services page, and how long a service lives on the Lifetimes and Scopes page.

title: Introduction to Dependency Injection
heading: DI error codes
text: Thrown codes arrive as an error on the line that made the call; warnings are written only in development mode, to the console and to the DevTools warning list, and do not go to the errorHandler listeners (see Error Handling ). All the codes are on the Error and Warning Codes page: Code When MJX401 A token that is not registered was asked for with get , getAsync or inject ; thrown. MJX402 A service registered with an async factory or a Promise was asked for with get (a startup service included); thrown, use getAsync . MJX403 The registration definition is invalid; thrown. MJX404 A circular dependency; thrown. MJX405 A second ApplicationBuilder was set up; thrown. MJX406 app.run could not find the host element given as a selector; thrown. MJX407 getService could not find a provider for the component; a warning in development mode, returns null . MJX408 The getService resolution failed; a warning in development mode, returns null . MJX409 inject was called outside the setup of a service; thrown. MJX410 Several sources were given in one registration; a warning in development mode, the precedence is useValue > useFactory > useClass . MJX411 deps is not an array; a warning in development mode, the invalid deps is ignored. MJX413 A function that cannot be constructed (an arrow function, an async function, an object method) was registered as a class; thrown on the registration line. MJX414 FromService could not resolve; a warning in development mode, returns null . MJX415 startup was given to a registration that is not a singleton; a warning in development mode, the service is created on its first resolution.

title: Introduction to Dependency Injection
heading: Next step
text: To learn how services are registered, go on to Registering Services .

title: Registering Services
text: ServiceCollection registration forms, singletons created at startup, automatic registration with @Injectable and its options.

title: Registering Services
heading: Registering a service
text: Services are registered on the services collection ( ServiceCollection ) of the builder returned by Application.CreateBuilder() , before build() . Each registration ties a token (usually the class itself; it can also be a string or a symbol) to an implementation and a lifetime; the lifetimes are on the Lifetimes and Scopes page:

title: Registering Services
heading: Registration forms
text: In the add*(token, impl) methods, impl can be one of these: The deps array works for both class and factory registrations: the entries are resolved in order and passed to the constructor/factory in the same order; in a factory the last parameter is always the ServiceProvider . The provider builds only a class registration ( useClass ) with new . A value given with useValue and the value a factory returns are handed out as they are; get and getAsync return the same value. To hand out a function or the class itself as a service, use { useValue: fn } or a factory that returns it; a factory that wants an instance writes the new itself. A function given directly to add*(token, impl) is constructed as a class. A function that cannot be constructed (an arrow function, an async function, an object method) gives a compile error in TypeScript, and at run time it throws MJX413 on the registration line: ServiceCollection methods: Method Description addSingleton/addScoped/addTransient(token, impl) Registration. tryAddSingleton/tryAddScoped/tryAddTransient(token, impl) Adds only if not registered yet; returns a boolean . replace(token, impl, lifetime?) Replaces an existing registration. remove(token) / has(token) Remove / check. reset() Clear everything. buildServiceProvider() Produces a ServiceProvider ( build() does this automatically).

title: Registering Services
heading: Singletons created at startup
text: For a singleton to be created when the application starts, without being asked for from anywhere, give startup: true on the registration. Services whose constructor does work on its own (writing an attribute to the document, attaching a listener, opening a connection) are registered this way. The service in the example opens an effect while it is being built and writes the selected theme to the <html> element; it has to run even if no component asks for it: In an explicit registration startup is given in the object form; it works with useClass and useFactory , and tryAddSingleton takes the same form: The services are created inside app.run() , before the shell and the first page are built; build() does not create them. The useDevelopment and useLogging settings called before run() apply in the constructor. The creation order is the registration order: the add* calls before build() in the order they are written, then the @Injectable classes. Dependencies are built first, as usual. A service resolved with get before run() is not created again; components, FromService and inject get the same instance. If the constructor throws, run() throws the same error and the application does not start. The services are created synchronously, with get : for a service registered with an async factory or a Promise, run() throws MJX402 . Do not give these services startup ; start them with await app.provider.getAsync(token) . startup applies only to a singleton registration. On transient and scoped registrations it is ignored, and in development mode an MJX415 warning is written; the service is created on its first resolution. Of the @Injectable classes, the ones whose module is loaded at the time of run() are created. A class whose module loads after run() (a service imported only by a lazy page) is not created when it loads; it is created on its first resolution. replace(token, impl) keeps the previous registration's startup value if startup is not written in the new registration; startup: false turns it off. While the application is running, builder.rebuild() sets up a new provider and immediately creates the startup singletons again in that provider; if a constructor throws, rebuild() throws the same error. Components, app.provider and the ServiceProvider token give the new provider. The old provider is disposed; rebuild() does not wait for this disposal. A rebuild() called before run() does not create the services; run() does.

title: Registering Services
heading: Automatic registration with decorators
text: @Injectable marks a class for automatic registration, so no explicit add* line is needed. When the application is built ( autoRegisterInjectables is called inside builder.build() ), the marked classes are registered with their options. Classes whose module loads after build() (services imported only by a lazy page) are registered too: when the descriptor is not found, the registration happens at the moment of the first resolution. An explicit registration ( addSingleton / addScoped / addTransient ) always overrides the decorator, and the decorator cannot override an explicit registration. @Injectable is a standard (TC39) class decorator; it needs no extra setting in tsconfig.json or in Vite's esbuild setting. @motifx/compiler compiles decorators in .ts and .js files just as in .tsx files; vite dev and vite build give the same result. Files whose nearest tsconfig.json has experimentalDecorators: true are left to TypeScript's legacy decorator transform; @Injectable works in that form as well.

title: Registering Services
heading: @Injectable options
text: Option Meaning lifetime 'singleton' , 'scoped' or 'transient' ; 'transient' if not given. deps Tokens resolved in order as constructor parameters (see deps ). startup Singleton only: the service is created inside run() without being asked for (see Singletons created at startup ).

title: Registering Services
heading: Next step
text: To learn how long a service lives, go on to Lifetimes and Scopes .

title: Lifetimes and Scopes
text: singleton, scoped and transient; the navigation scope and scoped handles.

title: Lifetimes and Scopes
heading: Lifetimes
text: Lifetime Behaviour singleton A single instance for the whole application. scoped One instance per navigation. Everything on screen in the same navigation (the layout, the page, child components, FromService , singleton dependencies) sees the same instance; details below. Without a router, it is a single instance in the root provider. transient A new instance on every resolution (the default). The lifetime is given on the registration ( addSingleton / addScoped / addTransient , or @Injectable({ lifetime }) ; see Registering Services ). If a route component itself is registered in DI, the registration's lifetime decides the page's lifetime (see How a route component is built ).

title: Lifetimes and Scopes
heading: scoped : a single instance per navigation
text: The router opens a scope on every navigation. Everyone who asks for a scoped service ( getService , inject , deps , FromService ) gets not the service itself but a handle that leads to it. The handle is used like the service (fields, methods, #private fields, instanceof ) and goes to the instance of the right navigation on every access. In the example, the layout and the page use the same scoped selection: The counter in the layout and the button on the note page ask for the same service: The layout places the counter with <SelectedCount /> , and the note page places the button with <SelectButton note={note} /> . The layout places the counter with new SelectedCount() , and the note page places the button with new SelectButton({ note }) . The layout places the counter with motifComponent(SelectedCount) , and the note page places the button with motifComponent(SelectButton, { note }) . The layout sees a change made by the page at the same moment; both are on the same navigation's instance. When moving to another page, the layout's handle moves to the new navigation's instance on its own, and the counter's binding refreshes. The previous navigation's instance is disposed ( dispose() ) after the leaving page has been disposed. The leaving page stays tied to the previous navigation's instance; the instance is alive while the page is being disposed ( onDisposing , onDisposed ) too. Work that completes after the page has left (after an await ) writes to its own navigation's instance, not to the new page's service. A parameter change on the same route ( /notes/1 → /notes/2 ) is a new navigation as well. A keepAlive page keeps its own navigation's instance alive while it waits in the cache; when it is shown again, it moves to the current navigation's instance before onActivated runs, so a value written to the service inside onActivated stays in the current instance. Pages waiting in the mobile stack follow the same rule. If the state in the service should be kept across navigations, the service should be a singleton . Back and forward navigation is a new navigation too, and opens a new instance. If the navigation does not happen (a guard cancels it, the page fails to build), the current instance does not change; the scope that was opened is disposed. While a page is being built (in the constructor, or in work the constructor starts), the new navigation's instance is used. A scope opened in code with app.provider.createScope() is outside this arrangement: it gives the service itself, which lives only in that scope. For transient instances produced in such a scope to be disposed together with the scope, see Disposing Services . A handle is a separate object per component: the handles two components get are not equal with === even though they go to the same instance; compare services by their content. Since the fields of a disposed component are cleared, checking the component's isDisposed field in long-running work is still a good habit.

title: Lifetimes and Scopes
heading: Next step
text: To learn where and how services are obtained, go on to Resolving Services .

title: Resolving Services
text: ServiceProvider.get and getAsync, getService in a component, FromService, inject, deps and useApplication.

title: Resolving Services
heading: Resolving a service
text: A registered service is asked for from the provider. In a component you use getService or FromService , while a service is being built inject or deps , and anywhere else the provider itself ( app.provider ).

title: Resolving Services
heading: ServiceProvider.get
text: The router resolves a route component from the provider if it is registered there ( add* or @Injectable ), and builds it directly if it is not. If a registered component cannot be resolved (a missing dependency, a cycle, a constructor error), the navigation fails with MJX304 , the original error is carried in cause , and fallbacks.error is shown. get is synchronous and throws an error ( MJX402 ) for a service registered with an async factory or a Promise; resolve those with await provider.getAsync(token) . provider.createScope(name?) produces a new child scope; scoped services have a single instance per scope. From a place that has no access to the application instance (a helper module, a route hook), the running application's provider is reached through Application.main.provider :

title: Resolving Services
heading: getService from a component
text: getService finds the nearest provider and resolves the token; if none is found or the resolution fails, it returns null (in development mode an MJX407 / MJX408 warning is written). In the example, the header of the notes list writes the total number of notes to its title attribute while it is being built: In class and Options components getService is on the component itself; these lines are written with this in a hook ( onConfig , onConfigured ) or in a field initializer. In a function component getService is on the component itself ( head in the example): in JSX, the component that reaches the root's onConfig hook or ref , and without JSX, the component received by the function of the motifComponent call that builds the root. When the component is not at hand, FromService does the same job. If the service is not registered, getService and FromService return null ; inject , provider.get and provider.getAsync throw when they cannot find it. When a class token is given, the return type is that class; this includes classes whose constructor takes parameters, abstract classes and classes with a protected constructor. getService and FromService give a nullable type ( T | null ), while inject , provider.get and provider.getAsync give a non-null type. Writing the generic explicitly ( getService<NotesService>(NotesService) ) gives the same type; it can be used to type the class through an interface: FromService<NoteStore>(NotesService) . For a string or symbol token, the type is given with the generic: getService<{ apiUrl: string }>("config") .

title: Resolving Services
heading: The FromService helper
text: For quick resolution anywhere (outside components as well): If the service is not registered, there is a circular dependency, or the constructor throws, it returns null ; in development mode an MJX414 warning is written together with the original error. For a scoped service it gives the handle that leads to the current navigation's instance.

title: Resolving Services
heading: inject(token) — taking a dependency
text: inject is called in a class's field initializers and constructor while the provider is building that class, or inside a useFactory factory while the provider is calling it. It resolves the dependency from the provider that builds the class: a scoped service is the instance of the route scope that asks for it. The return type comes from the token. inject works only at setup time. Inside a method, in a setTimeout callback, or when the class is built by hand with new SearchIndex() , it throws an MJX409 error. A token that is not registered gives MJX401 , and a circular dependency MJX404 . inject is synchronous; take async registrations that need getAsync with deps or getAsync . In class and Options components, use this.getService(token) for a dependency. In a function component, use FromService(token) for a dependency.

title: Resolving Services
heading: deps — constructor parameters
text: Dependencies can also be given to the constructor as parameters. The tokens in the deps array are resolved in order and passed to the constructor in the same order: TypeScript does not check the order; deps and the constructor parameters have to be written in the same order. In this form the class can be built by hand in a test with fake dependencies: new SearchIndex(fakeNotes, { apiUrl: "/test" }) .

title: Resolving Services
heading: The useApplication hook
text: useApplication() gives the running application, its provider and the router in a single object; attach(...components) adds components to the application shell:

title: Resolving Services
heading: Next step
text: To learn when and how services are disposed, go on to Disposing Services .

title: Disposing Services
text: Cleaning up services with app.dispose and provider.dispose, closing the navigation scope, tracking transient instances.

title: Disposing Services
heading: Disposing services
text: The provider disposes the instances it built itself. If a service holds a resource such as a timer, a listener or a connection, write a dispose() method that releases it; calling it is the provider's job: When they are disposed: app.dispose() disposes the services after the component tree has been torn down (leave animations included); until then, every component's onDisposing / onDisposed sees the same services, and await app.dispose() also waits for async dispose s. app.dispose() and provider.dispose() dispose the instances the provider built: the singleton cache, the scoped instances of scopes, and the navigation scopes. A navigation scope closes when a new navigation takes its place or when the navigation is cancelled, and its scoped instances are disposed. If a page tied to the scope is still alive (a leaving page whose disposal is in progress, a page in the keepAlive cache or kept in the stack), the scope stays open until that page is disposed or shown again. How: on every instance, dispose() , close() , [Symbol.dispose]() and [Symbol.asyncDispose]() are called in order if they exist; an error thrown by one does not stop the others. Only instances that have been built are disposed: a singleton that was never asked for was never built, so it is not disposed either; a value given with useValue goes through this only if it has been resolved at least once. transient instances are not tracked by default; when provider.enableAutoDisposeTransients() is turned on, transient instances produced in a child scope ( createScope , a navigation scope) are disposed together with that scope. Transients resolved from the root provider are still not tracked. provider.getAllServices() gives the ServiceCollection the provider uses.

title: Disposing Services
heading: Next step
text: For the mechanisms that writing packages on MotifJS relies on, go on to Writing Packages on Motif .

title: Writing Packages on Motif
text: A MotifJS package is made of the same material as application code: components, services and reactive objects. Whether the package is written with or without JSX does not concern the application that uses it, because the code the compiler produces from JSX is also the framework's public API; there is no separate template representation in between.

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Compiler output
text: The compiler turns this piece of the notes list into the calls in the table below: This piece of the notes list is the hand-written version of the calls the compiler produces from the JSX form of the same piece; the table maps the two forms line by line: JSX expression The call it compiles to Tracked class="list" section.class.add("list") nothing; written once {folder.title} node.bindings.add("textContent", folder, "title") on a text node folder.title only x-wait={() => !state.loading} p.bindings.wait(() => !state.loading) , before the element is built ( preconfig ) every field the getter reads {state.items.map(…)} holder.bindings.list(() => state.items, (note) => motifComponent("li", …)) on a holder without an element the array's length and item identity key={note.id} indexkey: () => note.id — class={note.pinned ? "pinned" : ""} li.class.add([() => (note.pinned ? "pinned" : "")]) every field the getter reads every element motifComponent("h2", …) and controls.add(h2) on the parent — The calls in the right-hand column are the form without JSX itself (see Views without JSX ). motif-explain , which comes with @motifx/compiler , gives this table for a file; --code also prints the whole generated code: So whichever form a package writes its own components in, the application uses them the same ways: with a tag in JSX ( <NoteList /> ), and without JSX with new NoteList(props) for a class and motifComponent(NoteList, props) for functions and Options.

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Package types
text: Each of the types below relies on a mechanism in the core; the details are on that mechanism's page.

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Theme and design system
text: A theme is a property of the document, not of components. The selected theme and density are kept as reactive state in a singleton service; the service writes them to the <html> element as an attribute ( data-theme ), and the CSS reads the attribute. If the service is registered with startup: true , it runs when the application opens without any component asking for it (see Singletons created at startup ). If a subtree needs to look different, the same attribute is written to that tree's root element; no separate service scope is needed. The package's CSS comes inside an @layer : an unlayered rule overrides all of the application's layered rules regardless of specificity (see Styles and CSS ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Dialogs, notifications and overlays
text: A dialog is part of the component that opens it, but it has to appear in the page's top layer. The layer is ready in the core: app.layer is the layer component at the end of <body> , and app.layerOf(opener) gives that window's layer if the opening component is in a window (see Page layer ). The package can put the dialog there directly with this.context.layerOf(this, dialog) ; then the dialog's lifetime is the layer's, and removing it on close is the package's job ( remove or the dialog's own dispose ). If the dialog has to go away together with the component that opened it, the package puts a Transport slot in the layer and writes the content inside the opening component with a TransportTo : the content appears in the slot, its bindings and event handlers work with the state of the component it was written in, and when the opening component is disposed, the content leaves the slot as well. For notifications to pile up in the same slot, the slot is set up with mode: "merge" (see Transport and TransportTo ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Layout and moving panels
text: In split, tab and docking panel packages, a panel moves from one region to another but must not lose its state. When a component is given to another parent's controls.add , it leaves its old parent on its own; it is not disposed, and its bindings and state stay in place. It gets onDeactivated when removed from the DOM and onActivated when placed again (see Moving without disposing ). Transporter.transport does the same move (see Moving in code ). For a panel that is a route page, keepAlive: true keeps its instance across navigations (see Route Definitions ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Application shell and plugins
text: A shell package gives the application its skeleton: the sidebar, the toolbar, the status line. Plugins add pieces to this skeleton. Every region of the skeleton is a named Transport slot; a plugin sends content to that region with a TransportTo of the same name in its own component. Whether the slot is built before or after the sender does not change the result. A plugin's services are registered in the application's ServiceCollection , and the shell gets them from the provider (see Registering Services ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Data components
text: In table, grid and long list packages, the list binding recognizes a row by the item object, not by key : when the same object moves to a new position, its row is moved, not rebuilt (see key and item identity ). For thousands of rows, or data that arrives page by page from a server, Virtualization builds only the visible rows and asks for the data with dataRequest (see Virtual Lists ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Library wrappers
text: A library that manages its own DOM (a chart, a map, an editor) is set up on the component's element. The setup is done in onBuilt or initializeComponent , and the library's own cleanup is tied to the component with motif.setDisposable . The full set of rules is on the Wrapping Third-Party Libraries page.

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Language and user settings
text: Settings such as the language, the time zone and the density sit in a single singleton service as a reactive object. Components read the value inside a binding; when a setting changes, only the bindings that read that value refresh, and components are not rebuilt (see Reactivity , Lifetimes and Scopes ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Transition packages
text: A transition package provides CSS class names and keyframe definitions. A class based transition is attached by its transition name ( fade → fade-enter-from …), and an animation defined in code is given with motif.options.transition.in / out . The application decides the order of enter and leave with app.useTransitions({ mode }) (see Styling and Animation ).

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Publishing the package
text: The package format, the build, the types, CSS, the prop contract and the pre-publish checks are on the Publishing an npm Library for MotifJS page. A package carrying compiled JSX must be compiled with a compiler contract supported by the @motifx/core it is used with; with an unsupported contract, development mode writes an MJX121 warning.

title: Writing Packages on Motif
heading: Next step
text: To turn a library that manages its own DOM into a component, go on to Wrapping Third-Party Libraries .

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
text: In real applications not everything is written in MotifJS. Work such as charts, rich text editors, maps and drag and drop is left to mature libraries that manage their own DOM. This section covers the rules for turning those libraries into MotifJS components; the examples use Chart.js and SortableJS.

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: First decide: do you need to wrap it?
text: Wrap it: If the library produces its own DOM (it draws a canvas , builds a tree, moves nodes). If it has an imperative lifecycle ( new X() / x.destroy() ). If doing the job with MotifJS's fine-grained bindings makes no sense (drawing a chart, a text editor). Do not wrap it: Libraries that only compute (dates, money, validation). Call them directly. Packages tied to another UI framework's component tree. They do not work in MotifJS; look for a framework-independent (headless) version. Work MotifJS already does (rendering lists, conditional rendering, virtualization).

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: Four rules
text: The rules are explained on the same example: a chart that draws the number of notes in each folder with Chart.js.

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: 1. Setup inside onBuilt or initializeComponent
text: The library instance is set up the moment the element is created: in the onBuilt or initializeComponent hook. The element exists on the component at that moment; it does not have to be attached to the document. onMounted is only for cases where the library wants the element in the document: libraries that take measurements, read layout or want a live DOM. onBuilt can fire while the element is still inside a detached piece (ternary and list branches are built in a detached fragment), and these libraries give wrong results there. onMounted runs once , in the task after the element is attached to document ; the setup of several wrappers is split into slices and does not lock up the page. The chart is placed with <FolderChart /> . The chart is placed with new FolderChart() . The chart is placed with motifComponent(FolderChart) .

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: 2. Cleanup with motif.setDisposable
text: The library's destroy() / disconnect() call is tied to the component's lifetime; in the example chart.destroy() is tied this way. When the component is disposed, the library goes too, and nothing else needs to be called. Side resources such as timers, ResizeObserver and WebSocket are registered in the same place (see Memory Management and Disposal ).

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: 3. Reads are tracked, writes happen inside untracked
text: There are two traps when passing reactive data to a library: If you hand the data directly to the library, the library reads that object during its own update. If this read is in a tracked region, the effect triggers itself and a loop forms. If you put the reading entirely inside untracked , then the inner fields are not tracked at all, and nothing updates when the data changes. The right form is the one in the example: inside bindings.watch , a plain copy ( counts ) is taken in the tracked region, and the write to the library is done inside untracked . The copy catches deep changes too: when a note is pinned, count("pinned") reads the notes' pinned field, so the effect runs again and the chart updates.

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: 4. Setup errors are reported
text: An exception thrown from inside onBuilt (or the rejected promise of an async onBuilt ) is not swallowed: MotifJS reports it to errorHandler as a MotifError with the code MJX122 ( The component onBuilt hook threw. ), with the original error in the cause field. The report is written to the console in production mode too ( app.useLogging(false) turns it off) and reaches the errorHandler.addListener(fn) listeners. The same report is produced for the other lifecycle hooks, onMounted included. The wrapper does not need to write console.error itself. Leaving the component in a consistent state when setup fails (tearing down the half-built instance, giving a fallback view) is the wrapper's job; for that, the error is caught, handled and then rethrown, and the report still happens. config is the chart's settings object:

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: DOM ownership conflicts
text: The hardest case is when the library moves nodes that MotifJS drew. Drag-and-drop libraries do exactly this: at the moment of the drop they reorder the DOM themselves. But those nodes are owned by the list binding; if the two owners clash, the binding can no longer calculate correctly. The solution pattern: Undo the library's DOM change. Apply the same change to the model . Let MotifJS draw the DOM again. Since the effect queue is emptied on a microtask, the undo and the redraw complete in the same frame; there is no flicker on screen. The simplest form, for a single list with SortableJS: In use, list is given the very reactive array whose rows are drawn, and every row carries a key . In the example the array being sorted is in a local reactive object that keeps the order of the folders in the sidebar: const order = reactive({ folders: ["notes", "pinned", "archive"] as Folder[] }) . The ref calculation in the undo is deliberately not from.children[oldIndex] ?? null . MotifJS draws the list inside a fragment; the container's last child is usually a comment node that is the list's closing marker . If the item was dragged from the end, insertBefore(item, null) puts it outside that marker, that is, outside the list, and the list binding cannot find the item on the next update. The nextSibling of the last element, on the other hand, gives the spot in front of the marker, and the item stays inside the list. This simple form is for a single list. If the library manages the inside of its own container completely (a chart, an editor), there is no clash: the component only provides an empty container, and MotifJS draws nothing inside it.

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: Root element
text: Most libraries want a real element ( canvas , div ). In a class, the root element is decided not by view() but by the class itself. When you write Component<HTMLCanvasElement> in TypeScript, @motifx/compiler takes the element type from the generic, and the root is created as a <canvas> on its own. In JavaScript, and in a file that does not go through the compiler, write static elementTag = "canvas" . A tag name or a ready element can also be given as the first parameter of the super call in the constructor: super("canvas", props) , super(document.createElement("canvas"), props) ; this form does not depend on the generic, so it works in a package not compiled with @motifx/compiler as well. In a function component, the root is the returned element: <canvas … /> in JSX, and motifComponent("canvas", …) without JSX. In Options, the root is the el field: el: "canvas" . If no root element is declared, the root is a fragment (a comment node), and the content takes the place of this fragment. A fragment is not a real element, so it cannot be given to a library as a container; always declare the root element in a wrapper. In a component that does not write view() , the children are added inside the root element: in a class if the root is declared with the generic or static elementTag , and in Options with el . That is why SortableList keeps its rows inside its own element. In a class that builds its root with super("div", props) , you place the children yourself.

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: Careful with prop names
text: The options prop belongs to the framework: it is the component's own settings object, read in the constructor, and the recognized keys are copied into motif.options : hideStrategy , disableDisposal (see Hide strategy ) and isSvg , which creates the root element in the SVG namespace. Library options are not passed with this prop; pick an explicit name such as chartOptions or sortableOptions : The component reads this value from its props during setup and hands it to Chart.js: new Chart(canvas, { type: "bar", data, options: chartOptions }) . Props starting with on stay in the props and can be used as callbacks; those that carry a DOM event name are the exception. A prop such as onChange , onCopy , onResize , onSelect , onReset or onContextMenu on a component tag is attached to the root element as a DOM listener and never reaches the props; for the camelCase spelling the compiler prints an MJX002 warning. Make the name specific to the domain ( onChartUpdate , onCodeCopy ).

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: The single-copy rule
text: If the wrapper is a separate package, the wrapped library and @motifx/core must be a single copy in the application. If there are two copies: The library's global registry (for example Chart.registry ) splits in two; your registration does not reach the copy the package sees. Two separate reactivity engines come about; untracked does not recognize the effect on the other side. Both errors are silent . In Vite the fix is a single line:

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: Prove the cleanup
text: A wrapper's correctness is not measured by "it seems to work". Write a round-trip test that builds and tears down the component many times: at the end of the rounds, the number of live components and the number of live external instances should return to where they started. For the measurement hooks, see the disposableTracker section in Memory Management and Disposal .

title: Wrapping Third-Party Libraries
heading: Next step
text: To publish the wrapper or a set of components on npm, go on to Publishing an npm Library for MotifJS .

title: Publishing an npm Library for MotifJS
text: If you are writing a UI library, a wrapper or a set of services and want others to use it through npm install , this section is for you. The package must attach to the same @motifx/core instance the application uses, carry its JSX already compiled , and impose nothing on the consumer's build setup. The setup below makes that happen.

title: Publishing an npm Library for MotifJS
heading: The package's boundary
text: There are two kinds of packages, and the difference in setup is small: Package Content Is the compiler needed? A package without JSX .ts components that do not use JSX ( super('canvas') , controls.add , bindings.* ) No, if the root element is declared with static elementTag or super(...) and no decorators are used; tsc or any bundler is enough. If the root element is to be produced from the generic, the compiler plugin is needed. A JSX library (a UI kit) .tsx components Yes; the package is compiled with @motifx/compiler before it is published. In both cases @motifx/core is a peer dependency : the package does not bundle it, it uses the copy the consumer installs. Two copies mean two reactivity engines, and that error is silent (see The single-copy rule ).

title: Publishing an npm Library for MotifJS
heading: package.json
text: The same @motifx/core major in peerDependencies and devDependencies : one is a requirement for the consumer, the other is for your own build and tests. @motifx/compiler is only in devDependencies ; the consumer does not have to install it, because the package carries compiled code. sideEffects: false turns on tree-shaking; in that case do not have a module that does work when imported (global CSS injection, a global registration). If you need something like that, export it as an explicit function ( registerX(app) ). A third-party library you wrap (such as chart.js ) becomes a peer dependency too; add it to the external list as well.

title: Publishing an npm Library for MotifJS
heading: Build
text: What happens: vite build runs in library mode; @motifx/compiler brings the JSX in every .tsx file down to bindings.* calls. The output is plain JavaScript with no JSX left; the @motifx/core imports ( motifComponent , motifCompiled …) are external , so they stay outside the package and attach to the consumer's copy. tsc -p tsconfig.build.json produces only .d.ts ; the compiler does not touch the types. The static elementTag produced from the Component<HTMLDivElement> generic exists in the compiled JS; it does not appear on the type side, and it does not need to.
